rd-school-c9-maths.number-systems.title: Number Systems
rd-school-c9-maths.number-systems.subtitle: From counting cows to √2: the whole family of real numbers and where each one lives on the line

sections.h: A number that refused to be a fraction
sections.md:
About 2,500 years ago, the followers of **Pythagoras** in Greece believed that every length in the universe could be written as a ratio of two whole numbers. Then they looked at a simple square with sides of 1 unit. By Pythagoras' own theorem its diagonal is **√2**. Try as they might, they could not write √2 as p/q. A story (probably a legend) says that **Hippasus**, the one who revealed this, was drowned at sea for it.

This chapter is the story of how mathematicians made room for such numbers. In NCERT order:
1. **Introduction**: natural numbers, whole numbers, integers and rational numbers, and how they sit on the number line
2. **Irrational numbers**: what they are and how to locate √2, √3 … on the line
3. **Real numbers and their decimal expansions**: terminating, non-terminating recurring and non-terminating non-recurring
4. **Representing real numbers on the number line** (successive magnification)
5. **Operations on real numbers**: surds, rationalising the denominator, and √x for any x on the number line
6. **Laws of exponents for real numbers**

**Did you know?** India's mathematicians were way ahead here. The **Sulbasutras** (about 800–500 BCE) gave an approximation of √2 equal to 1 + 1/3 + 1/(3·4) − 1/(3·4·34) ≈ **1.4142156**, correct to five decimal places.

check.q: Why was √2 a shock to the Pythagoreans?
options: It cannot be written as a ratio of two integers
check.why: √2 is irrational: no fraction p/q equals it, which broke the belief that every length is a ratio of whole numbers.

sections.md:
| Set | Symbol | Members | Comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| Natural numbers | **N** | 1, 2, 3, … | counting |
| Whole numbers | **W** | 0, 1, 2, 3, … | N together with zero |
| Integers | **Z** (from German *zählen*, to count) | …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … | W together with negatives |
| Rational numbers | **Q** (from *quotient*) | p/q, with p, q integers and q ≠ 0 | ratios |
| Irrational numbers | — | √2, √3, π, 0.10110111… | numbers that are not ratios |
| Real numbers | **R** | all rationals together with all irrationals | every point on the line |

Each set sits inside the next: **N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R**. Every natural number is a whole number, every whole number is an integer, and every integer is rational, because 5 = 5/1 and −3 = −3/1.

### Rational numbers have many names
1/2 = 2/4 = 10/20 = 50/100. These are **equivalent** rational numbers. When we write p/q we usually take p and q **co-prime** (no common factor except 1) and q > 0.

### Infinitely many rationals between any two
Between 1 and 2 there is 3/2, between 1 and 3/2 there is 5/4, and so on forever. **Method 1:** take the average, (a + b)/2. **Method 2:** to find, say, 5 rationals between 3/5 and 4/5, write them as 18/30 and 24/30. Then 19/30, 20/30, 21/30, 22/30 and 23/30 lie in between. Multiplying the numerator and denominator by a larger number gives more room.

check.q: Is every integer a rational number?
check.why: Any integer n can be written as n/1 with denominator 1 ≠ 0, so every integer is rational.

sections.md:
A number **s** is **irrational** if it **cannot be written in the form p/q**, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.

Examples: **√2, √3, √5, √15, π, 0.10110111011110…** (a pattern, but one that never repeats).

- The square root of any positive integer that is **not a perfect square** is irrational. So √4 = 2 is rational, but √8 is irrational.
- **π is irrational.** The values 22/7 and 3.14 are only **approximations**. This was proved by Lambert in 1761. The Indian mathematician **Aryabhata** (476–550 CE) gave π ≈ 62832/20000 = 3.1416.

### Placing √2 on the number line
1. On the number line, draw a unit square OABC with O at 0 and A at 1.
2. By Pythagoras, OB = √(1² + 1²) = √2.
3. With compass centre O and radius OB, draw an arc to cut the number line at P. **P represents √2.**

### The square-root spiral
Next, at B draw BD of 1 unit perpendicular to OB. Then OD = √(2 + 1) = **√3**. Keep going: each new perpendicular of length 1 adds 1 under the root, giving √4, √5, √6 … This beautiful figure is the **square root spiral**, sometimes called the Spiral of Theodorus. It is an NCERT activity.

sections.h: 3. Decimal expansions: the fingerprint of a number
sections.md:
Divide p by q and look at the remainders. There are only q possible remainders (0 to q − 1), so the division either **stops** or **repeats**.

**Case 1: terminating.** 7/8 = 0.875 and 1/2 = 0.5. The remainder becomes 0. This happens when q (in lowest terms) has **only 2s and 5s** as prime factors.

**Case 2: non-terminating recurring.** 1/3 = 0.333… = 0.3̄, 1/7 = 0.142857142857… = 0.\overline{142857}, 10/3 = 3.3̄. A block of digits repeats forever.

**Case 3: non-terminating non-recurring.** √2 = 1.41421356…, π = 3.14159265…, 0.01001000100001… These never stop and never repeat. **These are exactly the irrational numbers.**

> A number is **rational** if and only if its decimal expansion is terminating or non-terminating recurring. It is **irrational** if and only if its decimal expansion is non-terminating non-recurring.

### Converting a recurring decimal into p/q
**Example: 0.6̄.** Let x = 0.666… Then 10x = 6.666… Subtracting, 9x = 6, so x = **2/3**.
**Example: 0.4̄7̄ (0.474747…).** 100x = 47.4747… and x = 0.4747…, so 99x = 47 and x = **47/99**.
**Example: 1.27̄ (1.2777…).** 10x = 12.777… and 100x = 127.777… Subtracting, 90x = 115, so x = 115/90 = **23/18**.
**Surprise: 0.9̄ = 1.** Let x = 0.999… Then 10x = 9.999…, so 9x = 9 and x = 1. The two decimals name the same number.

### Finding an irrational between two numbers
Between 5/7 = 0.714285… and 9/11 = 0.8181…, write a decimal that never repeats, such as **0.75075007500075…**

sections.h: 4. Real numbers on the number line: successive magnification
sections.md:
How do we locate **3.765** exactly? Use a magnifying glass, mathematically:
1. 3.765 lies between **3 and 4**. Divide that interval into 10 parts.
2. It lies between **3.7 and 3.8**. Zoom in and divide into 10 again.
3. It lies between **3.76 and 3.77**. Zoom in again.
4. The **5th mark** after 3.76 is **3.765**.

For a recurring number such as **4.26̄ = 4.2626…**, zoom in to about 4 decimal places and mark it between 4.2626 and 4.2627. We can make the approximation as close as we like.

The **real number line** has no gaps. **Every real number has a unique point on the line, and every point on the line represents a unique real number.** Dedekind and Cantor proved this idea in the 1870s.

sections.md:
### Mixing rationals and irrationals
- rational + irrational = **irrational** (2 + √3)
- rational × irrational (with the rational non-zero) = **irrational** (5√2)
- irrational + irrational can be **either**: √2 + (−√2) = 0 is rational, while √2 + √3 is irrational.
- irrational × irrational can be **either**: √2 × √2 = 2 is rational, while √2 × √3 = √6 is irrational.

### Identities for square roots (a, b > 0)
1. √(ab) = √a √b
2. √(a/b) = √a / √b
3. (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b
4. (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b
5. (√a + √b)(√c + √d) = √(ac) + √(ad) + √(bc) + √(bd)
6. (√a + √b)² = a + 2√(ab) + b

**Examples:** (5 + √7)(2 + √5) = 10 + 5√5 + 2√7 + √35. (√11 + √7)(√11 − √7) = 11 − 7 = 4. (3 + √3)² = 9 + 6√3 + 3 = 12 + 6√3.

### Rationalising the denominator
We prefer a denominator with no root in it. Multiply the top and bottom by a suitable factor:
- 1/√2 = √2/2
- 1/(2 + √3) = (2 − √3)/((2 + √3)(2 − √3)) = (2 − √3)/(4 − 3) = **2 − √3**
- 5/(√3 − √5) = 5(√3 + √5)/(3 − 5) = **−5(√3 + √5)/2**
- 1/(√7 − 2) = (√7 + 2)/(7 − 4) = **(√7 + 2)/3**

The factor (a − √b) is called the **conjugate** of (a + √b).

### √x for any positive real x, geometrically
To locate √9.3:
1. Mark AB = 9.3 units on a line, then extend it 1 unit further to C.
2. Find the midpoint O of AC and draw a semicircle with centre O and radius OC.
3. Draw a perpendicular at B to meet the semicircle at D. Then **BD = √9.3**.
*Why it works:* OD = (x + 1)/2, OB = (x + 1)/2 − 1 = (x − 1)/2, so BD² = OD² − OB² = x.

sections.h: 7. Rational numbers between any two numbers
sections.md:
Between any two rational numbers lie **infinitely many** rational numbers. Two methods:

**Method 1 — averages.** Between a and b, (a + b)/2 is rational and lies between them. Between 1 and 2: 3/2; between 1 and 3/2: 5/4; and so on forever.

**Method 2 — common denominators.** To find 5 rationals between 3/5 and 4/5, multiply top and bottom by 6 (one more than 5): 18/30 and 24/30. Now 19/30, 20/30, 21/30, 22/30, 23/30 lie between.

**Irrationals between two numbers.** Between 1/7 and 2/7 (0.142857… and 0.285714…), write a non-terminating, non-recurring decimal such as 0.150150015000150000… — it never repeats a fixed block, so it is irrational.

**Types of intext question:** 'Is zero rational?' Yes — 0 = 0/1 = 0/5, with q ≠ 0. 'Is every whole number natural?' No — 0 is whole but not natural. 'Is every integer rational?' Yes — −3 = −3/1. 'Is every rational an integer?' No — 1/2.

check.q: Which statement is FALSE?
options: Every natural number is a whole number
Every integer is a rational number
Every rational number is an integer
check.why: 1/2 is rational but not an integer, so not every rational number is an integer.

sections.md:
Every recurring decimal is rational, and we can find its fraction with a neat trick.

**One digit repeats:** x = 0.333… Multiply by 10: 10x = 3.333… Subtract: 9x = 3, x = 1/3.

**Two digits repeat:** x = 1.272727… Multiply by 100: 100x = 127.2727… Subtract: 99x = 126, x = 126/99 = 14/11.

**Non-repeating digit first:** x = 0.2353535… Multiply by 10: 10x = 2.3535… and by 1000: 1000x = 235.3535… Subtract: 990x = 233, x = 233/990.

**Surprising fact:** 0.999… = 1. Using the trick, 10x − x = 9.999… − 0.999… = 9, so 9x = 9, x = 1. Two different decimal names, one number.

**Predicting the type of decimal.** A fraction p/q in lowest terms has a *terminating* decimal exactly when q has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. So 7/8, 13/125 and 3/20 terminate; 1/3, 2/7 and 5/12 recur. The length of the repeating block of 1/q is less than q: 1/7 = 0.142857 repeating, six digits (less than 7). Knowing 1/7, you can write 2/7, 3/7… without dividing: they use the same digits in rotated order (2/7 = 0.285714…).

sections.h: 9. Locating √x on the number line and rationalising
sections.md:
**√2 and √3 (spiral).** Draw OA = 1 on the line, AB = 1 perpendicular: OB = √2 by Pythagoras. Swing an arc from O through B to mark √2. Then draw BC = 1 perpendicular to OB: OC = √3. Repeating gives the beautiful *square-root spiral*.

**√x for any x > 0 (e.g. √9.3).** Mark AB = 9.3 units, then BC = 1 unit further. Find the mid-point O of AC; draw a semicircle with centre O. At B raise a perpendicular meeting the semicircle at D. Then **BD = √9.3**. Why? Radius r = (x + 1)/2, OB = r − 1 = (x − 1)/2, so BD² = r² − OB² = [(x+1)² − (x−1)²]/4 = x. Swing BD onto the line to mark √9.3.

**Identities for surds** (a, b > 0):
- √(ab) = √a·√b; √(a/b) = √a/√b
- (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b
- (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b
- (√a + √b)² = a + 2√(ab) + b

**Rationalising the denominator** means making the denominator rational by multiplying by a suitable factor:
- 1/√2 = √2/2.
- 1/(2 + √3) = (2 − √3)/[(2)² − 3] = 2 − √3.
- 5/(√3 − √5) = 5(√3 + √5)/(3 − 5) = −(5/2)(√3 + √5).

**Sums and products:** a rational + an irrational is irrational; a non-zero rational × an irrational is irrational. But two irrationals can give a rational: √2 × √2 = 2, and (2 + √3) + (2 − √3) = 4.

**Did you know?** π is irrational (proved by Lambert in 1761). 22/7 and 3.14 are only approximations.

rd-school-c9-maths.polynomials.subtitle: Degrees, zeroes, the Remainder and Factor Theorems, and the identities that make algebra fast

sections.h: A box, a garden and a cube of sweets
sections.md:
A sweet-shop owner in Kolkata packs rasgullas in cube-shaped boxes. If the side of a box is x cm, its volume is **x³** cm³. If the side grows by 2 cm, the new volume is **(x + 2)³** = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8. A gardener has a rectangular plot whose area is **x² + 5x + 6** m². What could its length and breadth be? The answer is **(x + 2) and (x + 3)**. Expressions like these are **polynomials**, and this chapter teaches you to read them, evaluate them, split them into factors and multiply them quickly.

The NCERT chapter, in order:
1. **Introduction**: algebraic expressions, terms, coefficients
2. **Polynomials in one variable**: definitions, degree, types
3. **Zeroes of a polynomial**
4. **Remainder Theorem** (in the older edition)
5. **Factorisation of polynomials**: the Factor Theorem and splitting the middle term
6. **Algebraic identities**: squares, cubes and the three-variable identity

### Recall
In the expression 5x² − 3x + 7, the **terms** are 5x², −3x and 7. The **coefficients** are 5 and −3, and 7 is the **constant term**. The **variable** is x, which can take any real value.

check.q: What is the coefficient of x in 5x² − 3x + 7?
check.why: The number multiplying x in the term −3x is −3.

sections.md:
A **polynomial in one variable x** is an algebraic expression of the form

aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁x + a₀

where a₀, a₁, …, aₙ are **constants (real numbers)** and the powers of x are **whole numbers** (0, 1, 2, …). We name polynomials p(x), q(x), r(x) and so on.

**Polynomials:** 4x + 2, 2y² − 3y + 4, 5t − √2, x³ − x² + 4x + 7, and even the constant 7.
**Not polynomials:** x + 1/x (this has x⁻¹), √y + 3 (this has y^(1/2)), and 1/(x − 1). The powers must be whole numbers.

### Counting terms
- **Monomial**: one term, such as 2x or 5y³.
- **Binomial**: two terms, such as x + 1 or y² − 7.
- **Trinomial**: three terms, such as x² + x + 1.

### Degree
The **degree** of a polynomial in one variable is the **highest power** of the variable.
| Degree | Name | General form | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | constant | a | 7 |
| 1 | linear | ax + b (a ≠ 0) | 2x − 5 |
| 2 | quadratic | ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0) | x² − 4x + 3 |
| 3 | cubic | ax³ + bx² + cx + d (a ≠ 0) | x³ − 1 |

A linear polynomial has at most 2 terms, a quadratic at most 3 and a cubic at most 4.

- The degree of a **non-zero constant** polynomial is **0**.
- The **zero polynomial** (the constant 0) has **no defined degree**.

### More than one variable
x² + y² + xyz is a polynomial in three variables. The degree of a term is the **sum of its exponents**: xyz has degree 3. The degree of the polynomial is the highest of these.

check.why: 3/x = 3x⁻¹ has a negative power, so x + 3/x is not a polynomial.

sections.md:
The **value** of p(x) at x = k is found by replacing x with k, and is written **p(k)**.
For p(x) = 5x³ − 2x² + 3x − 2: p(1) = 5 − 2 + 3 − 2 = **4**, and p(0) = **−2**.

A real number k is a **zero** of p(x) if **p(k) = 0**. The zeroes are where the graph crosses the x-axis.

- For p(x) = x − 1, the zero is **1**.
- For p(x) = x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), the zeroes are **1 and −1**.
- For a linear p(x) = ax + b with a ≠ 0, the only zero is **x = −b/a**.

### Facts about zeroes
1. A zero of a polynomial **need not be 0**.
2. **0 can be a zero**: for x² − 2x, p(0) = 0.
3. A **non-zero constant polynomial has no zero**, because 5 is never 0.
4. **Every real number is a zero of the zero polynomial.**
5. A polynomial can have **more than one zero**. A polynomial of degree n has **at most n** real zeroes.

**Did you know?** Finding zeroes is called **solving the equation p(x) = 0**. Engineers do this to find when a ball thrown upward returns to the ground. A height of h(t) = 20t − 5t² metres is zero at t = 0 and t = 4 seconds.

check.q: What is the zero of p(x) = 3x − 2?
check.why: 3x − 2 = 0 gives x = 2/3.

sections.md:
Divide numbers first: 15 ÷ 6 gives 15 = 6 × 2 + 3, so the **remainder is 3**. In the same way, for polynomials:

**Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder**, where the remainder is 0 or has a degree **less than** the divisor's.

**Long division example:** (3x² + x − 1) ÷ (x + 1).
- 3x² ÷ x = 3x. Multiply: 3x(x + 1) = 3x² + 3x. Subtract: −2x − 1.
- −2x ÷ x = −2. Multiply: −2(x + 1) = −2x − 2. Subtract: **1**.
So 3x² + x − 1 = (x + 1)(3x − 2) + 1, with **remainder 1**.

Now evaluate p(−1) = 3 − 1 − 1 = **1**. It is the same number!

**Remainder Theorem:** *If p(x) has degree ≥ 1 and is divided by the linear polynomial (x − a), the remainder is p(a).*

**Why:** p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. Put x = a: p(a) = 0 · q(a) + r = r.

**Examples:**
- Remainder of x³ + 3x² + 3x + 1 ÷ (x + 1): p(−1) = −1 + 3 − 3 + 1 = **0**.
- ÷ (x − ½): p(½) = 1/8 + 3/4 + 3/2 + 1 = **27/8**.
- ÷ (5 + 2x): the zero of the divisor is −5/2, so the remainder is p(−5/2) = −125/8 + 75/4 − 15/2 + 1 = **−27/8**.

The Remainder Theorem saves you from long division. It is a shortcut for finding a remainder.

check.q: What is the remainder when x³ − 2x + 1 is divided by (x − 2)?
check.why: By the Remainder Theorem the remainder is p(2) = 8 − 4 + 1 = 5.

sections.md:
**Factor Theorem:** *If p(x) has degree n ≥ 1 and a is a real number, then (i) (x − a) is a factor of p(x) if p(a) = 0, and (ii) p(a) = 0 if (x − a) is a factor of p(x).*

This is the Remainder Theorem with remainder 0.

**Check:** is (x + 2) a factor of x³ + 3x² + 5x + 6? p(−2) = −8 + 12 − 10 + 6 = **0**, so **yes**.
**Find k:** if (x − 1) is a factor of kx² − 3x + k, then p(1) = k − 3 + k = 0, so **k = 3/2**.

### Factorising quadratics: splitting the middle term
For **ax² + bx + c**, find two numbers p and q with **p + q = b** and **pq = ac**.

**Example: 6x² + 17x + 5.** Here ac = 30 and b = 17. Since 15 × 2 = 30 and 15 + 2 = 17:
6x² + 15x + 2x + 5 = 3x(2x + 5) + 1(2x + 5) = **(3x + 1)(2x + 5)**.

**Example: y² − 5y + 6.** Since −2 × −3 = 6 and −2 + (−3) = −5: **(y − 2)(y − 3)**.

**Example (Factor Theorem method):** for x² − 5x + 6, try x = 2: 4 − 10 + 6 = 0, so (x − 2) is a factor. The other factor is (x − 3).

### Factorising cubics
**Example: x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120.**
1. Try factors of the constant 120: ±1, ±2, ±3, …
2. p(1) = 1 − 23 + 142 − 120 = **0**, so (x − 1) is a factor.
3. Divide (or regroup): x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120 = (x − 1)(x² − 22x + 120).
4. Split the quadratic: −10 and −12 multiply to 120 and add to −22, so x² − 22x + 120 = (x − 10)(x − 12).
5. **Answer: (x − 1)(x − 10)(x − 12).**

**Tip:** if the sum of all the coefficients is 0, then x = 1 is a zero. If the sum of the coefficients of the even powers equals the sum for the odd powers, then x = −1 is a zero.

sections.md:
An **identity** is an equality that is true for **every** value of the variables.

| No. | Identity |
|---|---|
| I | (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y² |
| II | (x − y)² = x² − 2xy + y² |
| III | x² − y² = (x + y)(x − y) |
| IV | (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab |
| V | (x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + 2xy + 2yz + 2zx |
| VI | (x + y)³ = x³ + y³ + 3xy(x + y) |
| VII | (x − y)³ = x³ − y³ − 3xy(x − y) |
| VIII | x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx) |

Also: **x³ + y³ = (x + y)(x² − xy + y²)** and **x³ − y³ = (x − y)(x² + xy + y²)**.

### Special consequence of VIII
If **x + y + z = 0**, then **x³ + y³ + z³ = 3xyz**.
Example: (−12)³ + 7³ + 5³. Since −12 + 7 + 5 = 0, the value is 3(−12)(7)(5) = **−1260**. Check: −1728 + 343 + 125 = −1260 ✓.

### Mental maths with identities
- 105 × 106 = (100 + 5)(100 + 6) = 10000 + 1100 + 30 = **11130** (IV)
- 104³ = (100 + 4)³ = 1,000,000 + 64 + 3·100·4·104 = 1,000,000 + 64 + 124,800 = **1,124,864** (VI)
- 99³ = (100 − 1)³ = 1,000,000 − 1 − 3·100·1·99 = 1,000,000 − 1 − 29,700 = **970,299** (VII)
- 103 × 97 = 100² − 3² = **9991** (III)

### Area and volume pictures
Identity I can be seen as a square of side (x + y) split into an x² square, a y² square and two x·y rectangles. Identity VI can be seen as a cube of side (x + y) cut into 8 blocks.

sections.h: 6. Vocabulary check: degree, terms and types
sections.md:
Before factorising, be fluent with the names.

| Example | Terms | Name by terms | Degree | Name by degree |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 1 | monomial | 0 | constant |
| 3x | 1 | monomial | 1 | linear |
| x² + 1 | 2 | binomial | 2 | quadratic |
| y³ − y + 4 | 3 | trinomial | 3 | cubic |
| 0 | — | zero polynomial | not defined | — |

Which are **not** polynomials? Any expression where a variable has a negative or fractional exponent: x + 1/x (exponent −1), √y + 2 (exponent ½). But √2·x + 3 **is** a polynomial — the root is on the coefficient, not the variable.

**Polynomials in more than one variable** also exist (x² + xy + y²), and the degree of a term is the sum of its exponents: x²y³ has degree 5.

A linear polynomial ax + b has exactly one zero, −b/a. A polynomial can have more than one zero (x² − 1 has 1 and −1), and the zero polynomial has every real number as a zero. A non-zero constant has no zero at all.

check.q: Which is a polynomial?
check.why: In √3·x² − 5 the variable has a whole-number exponent; the root sits only on the coefficient.

sections.h: 7. Factorising quadratics by splitting the middle term
sections.md:
To factorise ax² + bx + c, find two numbers p and q with **p + q = b** and **pq = ac**. Split bx as px + qx, then group.

Example: 6x² + 17x + 5. ac = 30; we need two numbers adding to 17 and multiplying to 30: 15 and 2.
6x² + 15x + 2x + 5 = 3x(2x + 5) + 1(2x + 5) = **(3x + 1)(2x + 5)**.

Example: y² − 5y + 6. Numbers adding to −5, multiplying to 6: −2 and −3. Answer (y − 2)(y − 3).

Example: 2x² + 7x + 3: ac = 6; 6 and 1 → 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = (2x + 1)(x + 3).

Example: 3x² − x − 4: ac = −12; −4 and 3 → 3x² − 4x + 3x − 4 = x(3x − 4) + 1(3x − 4) = (3x − 4)(x + 1).

**Alternative using the Factor Theorem.** For x² − 5x + 6, test x = 2: 4 − 10 + 6 = 0, so (x − 2) is a factor; divide or compare to get (x − 3).

check.q: Factorise 2x² + 7x + 3.
check.why: Splitting 7x as 6x + x gives 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = (2x + 1)(x + 3).

sections.h: 8. Factorising cubics with the Factor Theorem
sections.md:
For a cubic like x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120:
1. List divisors of the constant term (±1, ±2, ±3, … ±120).
2. Test them: p(1) = 1 − 23 + 142 − 120 = 0. So (x − 1) is a factor.
3. Divide: x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120 = (x − 1)(x² − 22x + 120).
4. Split the quadratic: −10 and −12 → (x − 10)(x − 12).
Answer: **(x − 1)(x − 10)(x − 12)**.

Tip: if the coefficients add to 0, x = 1 is a zero; if the sum of odd-power coefficients equals the sum of even-power ones, x = −1 is a zero.

Example: x³ + 13x² + 32x + 20. Coefficients of even powers (13 + 20 = 33) equal those of odd powers (1 + 32 = 33), so x = −1 is a zero. Quotient x² + 12x + 20 = (x + 2)(x + 10). Answer (x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 10).

**Finding unknown coefficients.** If x − 1 is a factor of kx² − √2x + 1, then p(1) = 0 → k − √2 + 1 = 0 → k = √2 − 1.

check.q: Which value is certainly a zero of 2x³ − 3x² + x?
check.why: The coefficients 2 − 3 + 1 + 0 add to 0, so p(1) = 0.

sections.md:
Besides (x + y)², (x − y)², (x + y)(x − y) and (x + a)(x + b), Class 9 adds:
- (x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + 2xy + 2yz + 2zx
- (x + y)³ = x³ + y³ + 3xy(x + y)
- (x − y)³ = x³ − y³ − 3xy(x − y)
- x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx)

**Special case:** if x + y + z = 0, then **x³ + y³ + z³ = 3xyz**. So (−12)³ + 7³ + 5³ = 3(−12)(7)(5) = −1260, because −12 + 7 + 5 = 0.

**Mental maths:** 104 × 96 = (100 + 4)(100 − 4) = 10000 − 16 = 9984. 103 × 107 = (100 + 3)(100 + 7) = 10000 + 1000 + 21 = 11021. 99³ = (100 − 1)³ = 1000000 − 1 − 300(99) = 970299.

**Area/volume puzzles:** a rectangle of area 25a² − 35a + 12 has sides (5a − 3) and (5a − 4); a cuboid of volume 3x² − 12x has dimensions 3, x and (x − 4).

sections.h: The kite, the carrom board and the folding gate
sections.md:
Look around: a **carrom board** is a square, a **door** is a rectangle, a **kite** flown on Makar Sankranti is, well, a kite, and the **collapsible gate** of a shop is made of rhombuses that squash and stretch. All of these are **quadrilaterals**, four-sided figures. Why does a folding gate stay neat as it moves? Because each rhombus in it stays a **parallelogram**, and parallelograms obey some very reliable rules.

This chapter proves those rules. In NCERT order:
1. **Angle sum property of a quadrilateral** (older edition)
2. **Types of quadrilaterals**
3. **Properties of a parallelogram**: theorems and their converses
4. **Another condition for a quadrilateral to be a parallelogram**
5. **The Mid-point Theorem** and its converse

A **quadrilateral ABCD** has 4 sides (AB, BC, CD, DA), 4 angles (∠A, ∠B, ∠C, ∠D) and 2 diagonals (AC and BD). The vertices are named in order around the figure. **Opposite sides** do not share a vertex (AB and CD), and **adjacent sides** do (AB and BC).

check.q: How many diagonals does a quadrilateral have?
check.why: A quadrilateral has two diagonals, each joining a pair of opposite vertices.

sections.md:
**The sum of the angles of a quadrilateral is 360°.**

**Proof:** Draw diagonal AC. It splits ABCD into △ABC and △ADC.
- In △ABC: ∠CAB + ∠B + ∠BCA = 180°.
- In △ADC: ∠DAC + ∠D + ∠ACD = 180°.
- Adding: (∠CAB + ∠DAC) + ∠B + ∠D + (∠BCA + ∠ACD) = 360°.
- But ∠CAB + ∠DAC = ∠A and ∠BCA + ∠ACD = ∠C.
- So **∠A + ∠B + ∠C + ∠D = 360°**. ∎

**Example:** the angles of a quadrilateral are in the ratio 3 : 5 : 9 : 13. Then 30x = 360°, so x = 12°, and the angles are **36°, 60°, 108° and 156°**.

**Did you know?** In general, a polygon with n sides has an angle sum of (n − 2) × 180°, because it can be split into (n − 2) triangles. For a quadrilateral, n = 4 gives 2 × 180° = 360°.

sections.md:
| Type | Definition | Extra facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Trapezium** | one pair of opposite sides parallel | an isosceles trapezium has equal non-parallel sides |
| **Parallelogram** | both pairs of opposite sides parallel | opposite sides and angles equal; diagonals bisect each other |
| **Rectangle** | parallelogram with one angle 90° (so all are) | diagonals are equal |
| **Rhombus** | parallelogram with all sides equal | diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of each other |
| **Square** | rectangle with all sides equal (also a rhombus with a right angle) | diagonals are equal and perpendicular, and bisect each other |
| **Kite** | two pairs of equal adjacent sides | not a parallelogram; one diagonal bisects the other at 90° |

### The family tree
Square ⊂ Rectangle ⊂ Parallelogram ⊂ Trapezium ⊂ Quadrilateral, and Square ⊂ Rhombus ⊂ Parallelogram.
So **every square is a rectangle and a rhombus**, but a rectangle need not be a square.

**Did you know?** NCERT's older edition defines a trapezium as having *exactly* one pair of parallel sides, so a parallelogram would not count as a trapezium. Many books today use "at least one pair". Read the question's wording carefully.

sections.md:
**Theorem 8.1:** *A diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles.*
**Proof:** In parallelogram ABCD with diagonal AC: ∠BCA = ∠DAC (alternate angles, AD ∥ BC), ∠BAC = ∠DCA (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC), and AC = CA (common). So **△ABC ≅ △CDA by ASA**.

**Theorem 8.2:** *In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal.* (By CPCT from 8.1: AB = CD and AD = BC.)
**Theorem 8.3 (converse):** *If each pair of opposite sides of a quadrilateral is equal, it is a parallelogram.* (Use SSS, then alternate angles.)

**Theorem 8.4:** *In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal.*
**Theorem 8.5 (converse):** *If each pair of opposite angles is equal, it is a parallelogram.* (∠A + ∠B = 180° by the angle sum, so the co-interior angles are supplementary and the sides are parallel.)

**Theorem 8.6:** *The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.* (△AOB ≅ △COD by ASA, so OA = OC and OB = OD.)
**Theorem 8.7 (converse):** *If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, it is a parallelogram.*

**Also:** adjacent angles of a parallelogram are **supplementary**, ∠A + ∠B = 180° (co-interior angles).

### Special parallelograms (standard exercises)
- **A parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle.** *Proof idea:* △ABC ≅ △DCB (SSS), so ∠B = ∠C. Since they also add to 180°, each is 90°.
- **If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other at right angles, it is a rhombus.**
- **The diagonals of a square are equal and bisect each other at right angles**, and the converse also holds.
- **A diagonal of a parallelogram that bisects ∠A also bisects ∠C, and the figure is a rhombus.**
- **Angle bisectors of a parallelogram form a rectangle.**

sections.md:
**Theorem 8.8:** *A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if one pair of its opposite sides is both equal and parallel.*

**Proof:** In ABCD, let AB = CD and AB ∥ CD. Draw diagonal AC. In △ABC and △CDA: AB = CD (given), ∠BAC = ∠DCA (alternate angles, AB ∥ CD), and AC = CA (common). So △ABC ≅ △CDA (SAS). Then ∠BCA = ∠DAC (CPCT), and these are alternate angles for AD and BC, so **AD ∥ BC**. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so ABCD is a parallelogram. ∎

### All the ways to prove a quadrilateral is a parallelogram
1. Both pairs of opposite sides are **parallel** (the definition).
2. Both pairs of opposite sides are **equal**.
3. Both pairs of opposite angles are **equal**.
4. The diagonals **bisect each other**.
5. **One pair** of opposite sides is **equal and parallel**.

### Classic exercise
*In parallelogram ABCD, E and F are the midpoints of AB and CD. Show that AECF is a parallelogram.*
AE = ½AB = ½CD = CF, and AE ∥ CF (parts of AB ∥ CD). One pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel, so AECF is a parallelogram by Theorem 8.8.

*Exercise style:* in parallelogram ABCD, points P and Q on diagonal BD with DP = BQ. Show APCQ is a parallelogram. Use △APD ≅ △CQB (SAS) to get AP = CQ, and similarly AQ = CP, so both pairs of opposite sides are equal.

check.q: Which of these conditions alone guarantees a parallelogram?
options: One pair of opposite sides parallel
One pair of opposite sides equal and parallel
check.why: Theorem 8.8 says one pair of opposite sides that are both equal and parallel is enough to make a parallelogram.

sections.md:
Draw any triangle ABC. Mark E, the midpoint of AB, and F, the midpoint of AC, and join EF. Measure: **EF is exactly half of BC and parallel to it.** Every time.

**Theorem 8.9 (Mid-point Theorem):** *The line segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half of it.*

**Proof:** Through C draw a line parallel to BA, meeting EF extended at D.
- In △AEF and △CDF: AF = CF (F is the midpoint), ∠AFE = ∠CFD (vertically opposite), and ∠EAF = ∠DCF (alternate angles, BA ∥ CD).
- So △AEF ≅ △CDF (ASA), which gives EF = DF and AE = CD.
- But AE = BE, so BE = CD. Also BE ∥ CD, so **EBCD is a parallelogram** (Theorem 8.8).
- Hence ED ∥ BC, so **EF ∥ BC**, and ED = BC with EF = ½ED, so **EF = ½BC**. ∎

**Theorem 8.10 (converse):** *The line drawn through the midpoint of one side of a triangle, parallel to another side, bisects the third side.*

### Consequences
- **Joining the midpoints of the sides of ANY quadrilateral gives a parallelogram** (Varignon's theorem). Each side of the inner figure is parallel to a diagonal and half its length.
- Joining the midpoints of a **rectangle** gives a **rhombus**; of a **rhombus**, a **rectangle**; of a **square**, a **square**.
- The triangle formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of △ABC has **one quarter** of its area, and its perimeter is **half** that of △ABC. The four small triangles are congruent.
- In a **trapezium**, the line through the midpoint of one non-parallel side, parallel to the bases, bisects the other non-parallel side. Its length is ½(sum of the parallel sides).

sections.md:
**Type A: angle calculations** in parallelograms, rhombuses and rectangles. Use opposite angles equal, adjacent angles supplementary, the angle sum of 360°, and the facts that rhombus diagonals meet at 90° and bisect the vertex angles.

**Type B: prove a figure is a parallelogram**, rectangle, rhombus or square. Pick the shortest condition from the list of five above, then add the special condition (a right angle, equal sides, or perpendicular diagonals).

**Type C: congruence inside parallelograms.** Perpendiculars from opposite vertices to a diagonal are equal (AP = CQ), proved by AAS.

**Type D: isosceles trapezium.** In trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ CD and AD = BC, show that ∠A = ∠B, ∠C = ∠D, △ABC ≅ △BAD and AC = BD. Draw CE ∥ DA to make a parallelogram AECD, then use the isosceles triangle BCE.

**Type E: Mid-point Theorem.** Find lengths, prove figures formed by midpoints, prove that a line bisects a side. Look for a triangle with two midpoints, or a line parallel to a side through one midpoint.

**Type F: right triangle median.** In right △ABC with ∠C = 90°, if M is the midpoint of hypotenuse AB, then **CM = MA = MB = ½AB**. Draw a line through M parallel to BC; it bisects AC at D (converse of the theorem) and is perpendicular to AC. Then △AMD ≅ △CMD (SAS), so MC = MA.

**Tip:** in every parallelogram proof, list the parallel pairs first. Then alternate and co-interior angles appear almost by themselves.

steps: Opposite angles are equal: 3x − 20 = x + 40, so 2x = 60 and x = 30.

steps: The diagonals bisect each other at 90°, giving half-diagonals of 8 cm and 6 cm.

workedExamples.q: ABCD is a rhombus and ∠ABD = 35°. Find ∠BAD and ∠ACB.
steps: In a rhombus the diagonal BD bisects ∠B, so ∠ABC = 70°.

workedExamples.q: In △ABC, D, E and F are the midpoints of BC, CA and AB. If AB = 10 cm, BC = 12 cm and CA = 8 cm, find the perimeter of △DEF.
steps: By the Mid-point Theorem, EF = ½BC = 6, DF = ½CA = 4 and DE = ½AB = 5.
Perimeter = 6 + 4 + 5 = 15 cm, which is half of 30 cm.

workedExamples.q: ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC. E is the midpoint of AD, and a line through E parallel to AB meets BC at F. Show that F is the midpoint of BC.
steps: Join AC, which meets EF at G.
In △ADC, E is the midpoint of AD and EG ∥ DC, so G is the midpoint of AC (converse of the Mid-point Theorem).
In △CAB, G is the midpoint of AC and GF ∥ AB, so F is the midpoint of BC (converse again).
workedExamples.answer: F is the midpoint of BC

sections.h: 6. The parallelogram family tree and its diagonals
sections.md:
Every square is a rhombus and a rectangle; every rhombus and rectangle is a parallelogram; every parallelogram is a trapezium (in the NCERT definition, a trapezium has at least one pair of parallel sides). A kite is *not* a parallelogram in general.

| Shape | Diagonals bisect each other | Diagonals equal | Diagonals perpendicular | Diagonals bisect angles |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parallelogram | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ |
| Rectangle | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ |
| Rhombus | ✔ | ✘ | ✔ | ✔ |
| Square | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ |
| Kite | one bisects the other | ✘ | ✔ | one does |

The table is a goldmine for 'prove it is a ___' questions:
- A parallelogram with **equal diagonals** is a rectangle.
- A parallelogram whose **diagonals are perpendicular** is a rhombus.
- A quadrilateral whose diagonals are **equal and bisect each other at right angles** is a square.
- If a diagonal of a parallelogram **bisects one angle**, it is a rhombus.

Each is proved with congruent triangles (SAS or SSS) using what the book has already established.

check.q: A parallelogram has perpendicular diagonals. It must be a:
check.why: Perpendicular diagonals that bisect each other make all four sides equal by SAS congruence, giving a rhombus.

sections.h: 7. Converses: how to show a quadrilateral IS a parallelogram
sections.md:
The book proves each property and then its converse. A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if **any one** of these holds:
1. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel (definition).
2. Both pairs of opposite sides are equal.
3. Both pairs of opposite angles are equal.
4. The diagonals bisect each other.
5. **One pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel** (the 'another condition' theorem).

Useful extra results from the exercises:
- The **angle bisectors of a parallelogram** form a rectangle.
- In parallelogram ABCD, points P and Q on diagonal BD with DP = BQ make APCQ a parallelogram (its diagonals AC and PQ bisect each other).
- If ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC and AD = BC (isosceles trapezium), then ∠A = ∠B, ∠C = ∠D, triangles ABC and BAD are congruent and diagonals AC = BD.
- In a parallelogram, the perpendiculars from opposite vertices to a diagonal are equal (AAS).

check.q: Which single condition is enough to make ABCD a parallelogram?
check.why: One pair of opposite sides that is both equal and parallel guarantees a parallelogram.

sections.h: 8. The converse of the mid-point theorem and its family
sections.md:
**Mid-point Theorem:** the segment joining mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half of it.

**Converse:** a line through the mid-point of one side, **parallel to another side**, bisects the third side. Proof idea: in △ABC, E is the mid-point of AB, and the line l through E parallel to BC meets AC at F. Draw CD ∥ BA meeting EF extended at D. Then △AEF ≅ △CDF (ASA), so AF = CF.

**Applications (exercise types):**
- Joining mid-points of the sides of **any** quadrilateral gives a parallelogram (each side is parallel to a diagonal and half of it).
- If the original is a rhombus, the mid-point figure is a rectangle; if a rectangle, a rhombus; if a square, a square.
- In a trapezium ABCD (AB ∥ DC), a line through the mid-point of AD parallel to AB bisects BC.
- The line segments joining the mid-points of opposite sides of a quadrilateral bisect each other.
- In right △ABC (right angle at C), the mid-point M of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices: CM = MA = MB = ½AB.
- The three mid-point segments of a triangle divide it into four congruent triangles.

**Did you know?** Engineers use the mid-point idea in truss bridges and scissor lifts: linkages joined at mid-points stay parallel while the structure folds.

1. **Assuming what you must prove.** Do not say 'since it is a rhombus' when the question asks you to show it is one.
2. **Naming congruence wrongly.** △ABD ≅ △CDB must match A↔C, B↔D, D↔B in order.
3. **Skipping the reason in brackets.** Write (Alternate angles, AB ∥ DC) or (CPCT) every time.
4. **Using measurement.** A figure that 'looks' like a rectangle proves nothing; use given facts only.
5. **Mixing up opposite and adjacent angles.** Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal; adjacent angles add to 180°. Read carefully which pair the question gives — using the wrong rule can produce an impossible angle bigger than 180°, which is a sign to recheck.

rd-school-c9-maths.revision-practice.subtitle: Every chapter's key ideas, formulas, traps and practice, before the exam

sections.h: How to use this revision read
sections.md:
It is the week before your exam. The textbook has twelve chapters, and you have a notebook full of half-remembered formulas. This read is your map. For each chapter you get the **big idea**, the **must-know results** in textbook order, **worked mini-examples**, the **classic traps** and a **check**. At the end are worked examples and mixed practice in exam style.

| Strand | Chapters |
|---|---|
| Numbers & algebra | 1 Number Systems, 2 Polynomials, 4 Linear Equations in Two Variables |
| Coordinates | 3 Coordinate Geometry |
| Geometry & proof | 5 Euclid's Geometry, 6 Lines & Angles, 7 Triangles, 8 Quadrilaterals, 9 Circles |
| Mensuration & data | 10 Heron's Formula, 11 Surface Areas & Volumes, 12 Statistics |

**A revision method that works:** read a section, close the page, and write the key results from memory on a blank sheet. Then check. What you could not recall is exactly what you need to study. Short, repeated recall beats long re-reading.

**Exam habits:** write the formula before substituting; draw a neat labelled figure for every geometry question; give a reason in brackets for every step of a proof; write units in the final answer; and check arithmetic by a second method when time allows.

check.q: Which revision method does research support most strongly?
check.why: Active recall followed by checking shows you exactly what you have not yet learnt and strengthens memory.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** every point on the number line is a **real number**; real numbers are either **rational** or **irrational**.

- Natural N = {1, 2, 3, …} ⊂ Whole W = {0, 1, 2, …} ⊂ Integers Z ⊂ Rationals Q ⊂ Reals R.
- **Rational number**: can be written as p/q, p and q integers, q ≠ 0. Between any two rationals there are **infinitely many** rationals (take averages, or write with a common large denominator).
- **Irrational number**: cannot be written as p/q — √2, √3, √5, π. Pythagoreans (c. 400 BCE) found √2 is irrational; it can be located on the number line by the **spiral of square roots** (right triangles with sides 1 and √n give hypotenuse √(n+1)).
- **Decimal expansions**: rational ⇔ **terminating** (1/8 = 0.125) or **non-terminating recurring** (1/3 = 0.333…, 1/7 = 0.142857…). Irrational ⇔ **non-terminating non-recurring** (√2 = 1.41421…).
- **Recurring decimal to p/q**: x = 0.333… ⇒ 10x = 3.333… ⇒ 9x = 3 ⇒ x = 1/3. For 1.272727…: 100x − x = 126 ⇒ x = 126/99 = 14/11. For 0.2353535…: 1000x − 10x = 233 ⇒ x = 233/990.
- **Operations**: rational + irrational = irrational; rational (non-zero) × irrational = irrational; but irrational + irrational may be rational (√2 + (−√2) = 0).
- **Identities with roots** (a, b > 0): √(ab) = √a√b; √(a/b) = √a/√b; (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b; (√a + √b)² = a + 2√(ab) + b.
- **Rationalising the denominator**: 1/(√7 − 2) = (√7 + 2)/(7 − 4) = (√7 + 2)/3.
- **Laws of exponents** (a > 0, p, q rational): aᵖ·a^q = a^(p+q); (aᵖ)^q = a^(pq); aᵖ/a^q = a^(p−q); aᵖbᵖ = (ab)ᵖ; a⁰ = 1; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ. Example: 125^(1/3) = 5; 9^(3/2) = 27; 32^(−2/5) = 1/4.
- **Trap:** √(a + b) ≠ √a + √b.

check.q: The decimal expansion of an irrational number is:
check.why: Irrational numbers have decimal expansions that never end and never fall into a repeating block.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** expressions like 3x² − 5x + 2 behave like numbers; their zeroes and factors follow neat theorems.

- A **polynomial in one variable** has whole-number powers only: x³ + 2x − 1 is a polynomial; x^(1/2) or 1/x is not.
- **Degree**: highest power. Constant (degree 0; the zero polynomial's degree is not defined), linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3). By number of terms: monomial, binomial, trinomial.
- **Zero of p(x)**: a number c with p(c) = 0. A linear polynomial ax + b has exactly one zero, −b/a. A polynomial can have several zeroes; a non-zero constant has none.
- **Factor theorem**: if p(x) has degree ≥ 1 and a is a real number, then (x − a) is a **factor** of p(x) if p(a) = 0, and conversely. Check: is x + 1 a factor of x³ + x² + x + 1? p(−1) = −1 + 1 − 1 + 1 = 0 ✓.
- (Older editions also had the **Remainder theorem**: remainder of p(x) ÷ (x − a) is p(a).)
- **Factorising quadratics** ax² + bx + c by **splitting the middle term**: find two numbers with sum b and product ac. 6x² + 17x + 5: ac = 30, numbers 15 and 2 ⇒ 6x² + 15x + 2x + 5 = 3x(2x + 5) + 1(2x + 5) = (3x + 1)(2x + 5).
- **Factorising cubics**: guess a zero from the factors of the constant term (try ±1, ±2 …), then divide. x³ − 23x² + 142x − 120: p(1) = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor; quotient x² − 22x + 120 = (x − 10)(x − 12).
- **Algebraic identities**:
  - (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y²; (x − y)² = x² − 2xy + y²; x² − y² = (x + y)(x − y)
  - (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab
  - (x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + 2xy + 2yz + 2zx
  - (x + y)³ = x³ + y³ + 3xy(x + y); (x − y)³ = x³ − y³ − 3xy(x − y)
  - x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx); so if x + y + z = 0 then x³ + y³ + z³ = 3xyz.
- Quick use: 104 × 96 = (100 + 4)(100 − 4) = 10000 − 16 = 9984. (−12)³ + 7³ + 5³: sum is 0, so = 3 × (−12) × 7 × 5 = −1260.

check.q: If x + y + z = 0, then x³ + y³ + z³ equals:
check.why: From x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(…), a zero sum gives x³ + y³ + z³ = 3xyz.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** two perpendicular number lines turn every point of a plane into a pair of numbers. The idea is due to **René Descartes** (17th century) — hence 'Cartesian' plane.

- The horizontal line X′OX is the **x-axis**; the vertical Y′OY is the **y-axis**; they meet at the **origin O (0, 0)**.
- A point P is written **(x, y)**: x = **abscissa** (perpendicular distance from the y-axis), y = **ordinate** (distance from the x-axis).
- The axes divide the plane into **four quadrants**, numbered anticlockwise:

| Quadrant | Signs | Example |
|---|---|---|
| I | (+, +) | (3, 2) |
| II | (−, +) | (−3, 2) |
| III | (−, −) | (−3, −2) |
| IV | (+, −) | (3, −2) |

- Points on the **x-axis** are (x, 0); on the **y-axis** (0, y). They lie in no quadrant.
- **(x, y) ≠ (y, x)** unless x = y: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points.
- **Plotting**: move x units along the x-axis (right if positive, left if negative), then y units parallel to the y-axis (up if positive, down if negative).
- **Trap:** the 'ordinate' is the *y*-value — remember 'abscissa' comes first alphabetically and in the pair.

check.q: The point (−4, −7) lies in quadrant:
check.why: Both coordinates are negative, which is the case only in the third quadrant.

sections.h: Ch 4 — Linear Equations in Two Variables
sections.md:
**Big idea:** an equation like 2x + 3y = 12 has **infinitely many solutions**, and they all lie on a **straight line**.

- Standard form: **ax + by + c = 0**, with a and b not both zero. Write x − 2y = −√3 as 1·x + (−2)·y + √3 = 0; x = 3y as 1·x − 3y + 0 = 0; y = 3 as 0·x + 1·y − 3 = 0.
- A **solution** is a pair (x, y) that satisfies the equation. For 2x + 3y = 12: x = 0 gives y = 4 → (0, 4); y = 0 gives x = 6 → (6, 0); x = 3 gives y = 2 → (3, 2). Is (1, 1) a solution? 2 + 3 = 5 ≠ 12, so no.
- A linear equation in one variable (ax + b = 0) has a **unique** solution; in two variables, **infinitely many**.
- **Word problems**: 'The cost of a notebook is twice the cost of a pen' ⇒ x = 2y, i.e. x − 2y = 0. 'The total of Ravi's and Rahul's runs is 176' ⇒ x + y = 176.
- (In fuller editions: the **graph** of every linear equation in two variables is a straight line; every point on the line is a solution, and every solution lies on the line. Lines y = k are parallel to the x-axis; x = k parallel to the y-axis; y = mx passes through the origin.)
- **Finding k**: if (2, 1) satisfies 2x + 3y = k, put in ⇒ k = 4 + 3 = 7.

check.q: How many solutions does 2x + 5y = 7 have?
check.why: Every value of x gives a matching y, so a linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** all of geometry can be built logically from a few **definitions, axioms and postulates**.

- Geometry began with practical measuring — Egyptian land surveys after Nile floods, Indus Valley town planning with fired bricks of fixed ratio 4 : 2 : 1, and the **Sulbasutras** (800–500 BCE) for building Vedic fire-altars. Greek thinkers like Thales and Pythagoras turned it into reasoning.
- **Euclid** (c. 300 BCE, Alexandria) collected the knowledge in the *Elements*, 13 books.
- **Definitions** (some): a point is that which has no part; a line is breadthless length; the ends of a line are points; a straight line lies evenly with the points on itself; a surface has length and breadth only. Point, line and plane are taken as **undefined terms** today.
- **Axioms** (common notions — used throughout maths): things equal to the same thing are equal to one another; if equals are added (or subtracted) to equals, the wholes (or remainders) are equal; things that coincide are equal; **the whole is greater than the part**; things that are double (or halves) of the same things are equal.
- **Postulates** (specific to geometry): (1) a straight line may be drawn from any one point to any other point — and it is **unique** (Axiom 5.1 today: given two distinct points, there is a unique line through them); (2) a terminated line can be produced indefinitely; (3) a circle can be drawn with any centre and radius; (4) all right angles are equal; (5) the **parallel postulate** — if a line falling on two lines makes the interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, the two lines, if produced, meet on that side.
- **Equivalent of Postulate 5 (Playfair's axiom)**: for every line l and point P not on l, there is a **unique** line through P parallel to l.
- **Theorem**: two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common.
- **Euclid's Proposition 1**: an **equilateral triangle** can be constructed on any given segment (draw circles of radius AB with centres A and B).
- Attempts to prove the fifth postulate failed for 2,000 years and led to **non-Euclidean geometries** in the 19th century.

check.q: 'The whole is greater than the part' is one of Euclid's:
check.why: It is a common notion (axiom) — a general truth used across mathematics, not just geometry.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** where lines meet or are cut by a transversal, angles come in equal or supplementary pairs.

- **Terms**: line segment, ray, collinear points; acute (< 90°), right (90°), obtuse (90°–180°), straight (180°), reflex (180°–360°) angles; **complementary** (sum 90°) and **supplementary** (sum 180°); **adjacent** angles (common vertex, common arm, non-common arms on opposite sides); **linear pair** (adjacent angles whose non-common arms are opposite rays, sum 180°); **vertically opposite** angles.
- **Linear pair axiom**: if a ray stands on a line, the two adjacent angles sum to 180°; conversely, if two adjacent angles sum to 180°, the non-common arms form a line.
- **Theorem 6.1**: if two lines intersect, the **vertically opposite angles are equal**. (Proof: ∠AOC + ∠AOD = 180° = ∠AOD + ∠BOD ⇒ ∠AOC = ∠BOD.)
- **Parallel lines and a transversal**: corresponding angles equal; alternate interior angles equal; interior angles on the same side of the transversal (co-interior) are supplementary. Each of these, conversely, proves the lines parallel.
- **Lines parallel to the same line are parallel** to each other.
- **Angle sum property**: the angles of a triangle sum to **180°** (draw a line through a vertex parallel to the opposite side and use alternate angles). **Exterior angle theorem**: an exterior angle = sum of the two interior opposite angles.
- **Example**: lines AB and CD intersect at O, and ray OE lies between OA... in the textbook figure, ∠AOC, ∠COE and ∠EOB together make the straight angle AOB. If ∠AOC + ∠BOE = 70° and ∠BOD = 40°: ∠AOC = ∠BOD = 40° (vertically opposite), so ∠BOE = 30°; ∠COE = 180° − 70° = 110°; reflex ∠COE = 360° − 110° = **250°**.
- **Example**: angles of a triangle in ratio 2 : 3 : 4 ⇒ 9k = 180° ⇒ 40°, 60°, 80°.

check.q: If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, co-interior angles are:
check.why: Interior angles on the same side of the transversal add up to 180°.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** three well-chosen equal parts are enough to prove two triangles are exact copies.

- **Congruent** = same shape and size; ∆ABC ≅ ∆PQR means A↔P, B↔Q, C↔R. Order of letters matters.
- **CPCT** — corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal.
- **Criteria**:
  - **SAS** (axiom): two sides and the *included* angle.
  - **ASA**: two angles and the included side.
  - **AAS**: two angles and any corresponding side (third angle follows from the angle sum).
  - **SSS**: three sides.
  - **RHS**: right angle, hypotenuse, one side.
  - **Not** criteria: AAA (same shape, different sizes) and SSA (may give two triangles).
- **Isosceles triangle**: angles opposite equal sides are equal (Theorem 7.2, proved by bisecting the vertex angle and using SAS), and the converse (sides opposite equal angles are equal). Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.
- The bisector of the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is also its median, altitude and the perpendicular bisector of the base.
- (Older editions also had **inequalities**: the larger side has the larger angle opposite to it; the sum of any two sides is greater than the third side.)
- **Proof layout**: Given; To prove; Construction; Proof (three equalities with reasons); conclusion with the rule; then CPCT.

check.q: Which is NOT a valid congruence rule?
check.why: Two sides and a non-included angle can fit two different triangles, so SSA does not guarantee congruence.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** a parallelogram's diagonals and sides obey neat rules, and the mid-point theorem links triangles to parallel lines.

- **Angle sum** of a quadrilateral = **360°** (a diagonal splits it into two triangles).
- **Types**: trapezium (one pair of parallel sides), parallelogram (both pairs parallel), rectangle (parallelogram with one right angle), rhombus (parallelogram with all sides equal), square (rectangle with all sides equal), kite (two pairs of equal adjacent sides).
- **Properties of a parallelogram** (each with its converse — any one proves a quadrilateral is a parallelogram):
  - A diagonal divides it into **two congruent triangles**.
  - **Opposite sides are equal**.
  - **Opposite angles are equal**.
  - **Diagonals bisect each other**.
  - A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if **one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel**.
- **Special diagonals**: rectangle — equal; rhombus — perpendicular bisectors of each other; square — equal and perpendicular bisectors.
- Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary.
- **Mid-point theorem**: the segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is **parallel to the third side** and **half of it**. **Converse**: a line through the mid-point of one side parallel to another side **bisects the third side**.
- **Example**: in ∆ABC with D, E, F the mid-points of the sides, the four small triangles are congruent and the perimeter of DEF is half that of ABC.
- **Example**: the quadrilateral formed by joining the mid-points of the sides of any quadrilateral is a **parallelogram**; of a rectangle — a rhombus; of a rhombus — a rectangle.
- **Example**: in parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 70° ⇒ ∠C = 70°, ∠B = ∠D = 110°.

check.q: The diagonals of a rhombus:
options: bisect each other at right angles
check.why: A rhombus is a parallelogram with equal sides, and its diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of each other.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** chords, angles and arcs in a circle follow equal-for-equal rules, culminating in cyclic quadrilaterals.

- **Terms**: centre, radius, diameter (longest chord), chord, arc (minor/major), segment, sector, circumference; **congruent circles** have equal radii.
- **Theorem**: equal chords subtend **equal angles at the centre** (and conversely).
- **Theorem**: the **perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord**; conversely, the line from the centre to the mid-point of a chord is perpendicular to it.
- **There is one and only one circle through three non-collinear points** (find the meeting point of the perpendicular bisectors).
- **Equal chords are equidistant from the centre**, and chords equidistant from the centre are equal.
- **Angle subtended by an arc**: the angle at the centre is **double** the angle at any point on the remaining part of the circle.
- **Angles in the same segment are equal**. The **angle in a semicircle is a right angle**.
- **Cyclic quadrilateral** (all four vertices on a circle): **opposite angles sum to 180°**; conversely, if a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is supplementary, it is cyclic.
- **Example**: a chord of length 8 cm is 3 cm from the centre ⇒ radius = √(4² + 3²) = 5 cm.
- **Example**: arc AB subtends 100° at the centre ⇒ 50° at a point on the major arc; the angle at a point on the minor arc = 180° − 50° = 130°.
- **Example**: in cyclic ABCD, ∠A = 80° ⇒ ∠C = 100°.

fig.alt: Circle with moving inscribed angle and fixed central angle.

check.q: The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are:
check.why: For a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, each pair of opposite angles adds up to 180°.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** you can find the area of any triangle from its three sides alone — no height needed.

- Usual formula: Area = ½ × base × height. For a right triangle with legs a and b: ½ab. For an equilateral triangle of side a: (√3/4)a².
- **Heron's formula** (Heron of Alexandria, c. 10–75 CE): for sides a, b, c and **semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c)/2**:

**Area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)]**

- **Example**: sides 40 m, 24 m, 32 m: s = 48; area = √(48 × 8 × 24 × 16) = √147456 = **384 m²**. (Check: it is a right triangle 24-32-40, area ½ × 24 × 32 = 384 ✓.)
- **Example (park)**: triangular park with sides 120 m, 80 m, 50 m: s = 125; area = √(125 × 5 × 45 × 75) = √2109375 = 375√15 ≈ 1452.36 m².
- **Example (ratio)**: sides in ratio 3 : 5 : 7, perimeter 300 m ⇒ sides 60, 100, 140; s = 150; area = √(150 × 90 × 50 × 10) = √6750000 = 1500√3 ≈ 2598 m².
- **Example (isosceles)**: equal sides 12 cm, perimeter 30 cm ⇒ base 6; s = 15; area = √(15 × 3 × 3 × 9) = 9√15 cm².
- **Quadrilaterals**: split along a diagonal into two triangles and add their Heron areas. E.g. ABCD with AB = 3, BC = 4, CD = 4, DA = 5, AC = 5 cm: ABC is right (3-4-5) with area 6; ACD has sides 5, 4, 5: s = 7, area = √(7 × 2 × 3 × 2) = √84 ≈ 9.2; total ≈ 15.2 cm².
- **Trap:** forgetting to halve the perimeter, or mixing units.

check.q: For a triangle with sides 5, 12 and 13 cm, s equals:
check.why: Semi-perimeter s = (5 + 12 + 13)/2 = 15 cm.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** cones and spheres, with Archimedes' beautiful ratios.

| Solid | Curved/lateral SA | Total SA | Volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cuboid l×b×h | 2h(l + b) | 2(lb + bh + hl) | lbh |
| Cube a | 4a² | 6a² | a³ |
| Cylinder r, h | 2πrh | 2πr(r + h) | πr²h |
| **Cone** r, h, l | **πrl** | **πr(l + r)** | **⅓πr²h** |
| **Sphere** r | 4πr² | 4πr² | **(4/3)πr³** |
| **Hemisphere** r | **2πr²** | **3πr²** | **(2/3)πr³** |

- Slant height **l = √(r² + h²)**.
- A cone holds one-third of a cylinder with the same base and height; a sphere is two-thirds of its enclosing cylinder.
- Doubling the radius multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8.
- 1 m³ = 1000 L; 1 L = 1000 cm³.
- **Example**: cone r = 7 cm, h = 24 cm ⇒ l = 25; CSA = 22/7 × 7 × 25 = 550 cm²; V = ⅓ × 22/7 × 49 × 24 = 1232 cm³.
- **Example**: sphere d = 14 cm ⇒ SA = 4 × 22/7 × 49 = 616 cm²; V = (4/3) × 22/7 × 343 = 1437.33 cm³.
- **Trap:** open bowls use curved area only; if a diameter is given, halve it first.

check.q: The volume of a hemisphere of radius r is:
check.why: A hemisphere is half a sphere: ½ × (4/3)πr³ = (2/3)πr³.

sections.md:
**Big idea:** organise raw data into tables, then picture it.

- **Data**: primary (collected by you) and secondary (from others). **Frequency** = number of times a value occurs.
- **Grouped frequency table**: class intervals such as 10–20, 20–30 (a value of 20 goes to 20–30); class size = upper − lower; **class mark = (upper + lower)/2**.
- Inclusive classes (10–19, 20–29) are made continuous by subtracting/adding half the gap: 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.
- **Bar graph**: bars of equal width with equal gaps; heights ∝ values; for categories.
- **Histogram**: touching rectangles for continuous classes; **area ∝ frequency**. For **unequal widths**, adjusted height = (minimum class width ÷ class width) × frequency.
- **Frequency polygon**: join mid-points of the tops of histogram bars (or plot (class mark, frequency)), closing with zero-frequency classes at both ends. Good for comparing two data sets.
- Use a **kink** on an axis that does not start at zero.
- (Older syllabus / Class 10: mean = Σx/n; median = middle value; mode = most frequent value.)

check.q: In a histogram with unequal class widths, frequency is represented by the rectangle's:
check.why: The area of each rectangle must be proportional to frequency, so heights are adjusted for width.

sections.md:
**Seven-day plan**

| Day | Focus |
|---|---|
| 1 | Number systems + polynomials (identities by heart) |
| 2 | Coordinate geometry + linear equations |
| 3 | Euclid + lines & angles |
| 4 | Triangles + quadrilaterals (write 5 proofs) |
| 5 | Circles (theorem statements + 5 problems) |
| 6 | Heron + surface areas & volumes + statistics graphs |
| 7 | One full timed sample paper; review mistakes |

**Top 12 traps**
1. √(a + b) ≠ √a + √b.
2. 0.999… = 1 (it is rational!).
3. The degree of the zero polynomial is not defined.
4. Points on axes are in no quadrant.
5. (x, y) and (y, x) are different points.
6. Euclid's 'axioms' are general; 'postulates' are geometric.
7. Vertically opposite angles are equal; a linear pair adds to 180° — don't mix them.
8. AAA and SSA are not congruence rules.
9. Every square is a rhombus and a rectangle, but not conversely.
10. Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference — only for the *same* arc.
11. In Heron's formula, s is **half** the perimeter.
12. Histograms have no gaps; adjust heights for unequal widths.

**Did you know?** The decimal place-value system and zero, which you use in Chapter 1 without a thought, were developed in India — Brahmagupta (628 CE) gave rules for arithmetic with zero.

check.q: Which statement is true?
check.why: A square has all sides equal and is a parallelogram, so it is always a rhombus; the converse is false.

summary: Real numbers = rationals (terminating or recurring decimals) + irrationals (non-terminating, non-recurring).
Laws of exponents and rationalising denominators simplify surds.
Factor theorem: (x − a) is a factor of p(x) iff p(a) = 0; know all algebraic identities including x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz.

ax + by + c = 0 has infinitely many solutions lying on a straight line.
Euclid: definitions, axioms, 5 postulates; the fifth is equivalent to Playfair's axiom.
Vertically opposite angles are equal; parallel lines give equal corresponding/alternate angles; triangle angles sum to 180°.
Congruence: SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS, RHS; angles opposite equal sides are equal.
Parallelogram: opposite sides/angles equal, diagonals bisect; mid-point theorem.
Circles: equal chords ↔ equal angles/distances; perpendicular from centre bisects a chord; central angle = 2 × inscribed angle; cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles sum to 180°.
Heron: area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)].
Cone: πrl, πr(l + r), ⅓πr²h; sphere: 4πr², (4/3)πr³; hemisphere: 2πr², 3πr², (2/3)πr³.
Statistics: bar graphs, histograms (area ∝ frequency), frequency polygons.

rd-school-c9-maths.statistics.title: Statistics
rd-school-c9-maths.statistics.subtitle: Turning a pile of numbers into pictures that tell a story

sections.md:
Open any newspaper on a weekday morning and count the numbers on the front page. The Sensex closed at some value; Mumbai received 112 mm of rain; India's run rate in the last ten overs was 9.4; onion prices rose 18% in a month; a state's literacy rate is 82%. A cricket analyst, a weather scientist at the IMD, a shopkeeper in Indore and a district health officer all collect numbers and use them to make decisions.

Facts or figures — numerical or otherwise — collected with a definite purpose are called **data** (the word is plural; one piece is a *datum*). The branch of mathematics that deals with the **collection, presentation, analysis and interpretation** of data is called **statistics**. In everyday speech the word 'statistics' is also used for the numbers themselves ('the statistics of the match'), so the word has two meanings: the subject, and the numerical data.

India has a proud tradition in this subject. **Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis** founded the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata in 1931 and helped design the National Sample Survey after Independence. His birthday, 29 June, is celebrated as National Statistics Day.

In this chapter you will learn:

- what data is and how it is collected (primary and secondary),
- how raw data is organised into frequency distribution tables — ungrouped and grouped,
- how to draw data as **bar graphs**, **histograms** (with equal and unequal class widths) and **frequency polygons**.

> Note: In the current rationalised NCERT book, the chapter focuses on graphical representation. Earlier editions also had collection of data and mean, median and mode. We cover the organising ideas briefly here because you need them to draw any graph — and mean/median/mode return in Class 10.

check.q: Which of these best describes 'statistics' as a subject?
options: Collecting, presenting, analysing and interpreting data
check.why: Statistics covers the whole journey of data — from collecting it to drawing conclusions from it.

sections.md:
Before you can draw a graph, someone must collect the numbers. There are two kinds of data:

- **Primary data**: collected by the investigator herself, first-hand, for her own purpose. Example: Riya measures the heights of all 40 students of her class with a tape for her science project. Primary data is reliable for that purpose because you know exactly how it was collected, but it takes time and effort.
- **Secondary data**: data collected by someone else, which you use from a published or stored source. Example: Riya takes population figures from the Census of India website, or rainfall from IMD records. It is quick and cheap, but you must check that the source is trustworthy and that the data really fits your question.

**Raw data.** When data is first collected it is usually a jumble: 40 heights written in the order the students stood in line. This is called raw data. It is hard to read anything from it. The next step is to **organise** it.

**Range.** The difference between the largest and smallest value is the range. If the tallest student is 168 cm and the shortest is 139 cm, the range is 168 − 139 = 29 cm. The range tells you how spread out the data is and helps you decide how to group it.

**Did you know?** India's Census, held every ten years since 1881, is one of the largest secondary data sources in the world. Students and researchers all over the world use it.
keyTerms: Data — facts or figures collected for a purpose
Primary data — collected first-hand by the investigator
Secondary data — collected by someone else, used by you
Raw data — data in the unorganised form it was collected
Range — highest value minus lowest value

check.q: A student uses IMD's published rainfall records for Chennai for her project. This is:
check.why: The data was collected by IMD, not by the student, so for her it is secondary data.

sections.md:
Suppose the marks (out of 20) of 30 students in a test are:

10, 12, 15, 18, 10, 12, 14, 15, 10, 20, 16, 12, 14, 15, 18, 10, 12, 15, 15, 14, 16, 18, 12, 10, 15, 14, 12, 16, 18, 15

Count how many times each value occurs — its **frequency**. On paper we use **tally marks**: four upright strokes and a fifth across them make a bundle of five.

| Marks | Frequency |
|---|---|
| 10 | 5 |
| 12 | 6 |
| 14 | 4 |
| 15 | 7 |
| 16 | 3 |
| 18 | 4 |
| 20 | 1 |
| Total | 30 |

This is an **ungrouped frequency distribution table**. At a glance: 15 is the most common score; only one student got full marks. Always check that frequencies add up to the total number of observations (5+6+4+7+3+4+1 = 30 ✓).

**Grouped frequency distribution.** If the data has many different values — like the weights of 40 students from 30 kg to 62 kg — a table with one row per value would be too long. We group values into **classes** (class intervals) such as 30–35, 35–40, 40–45, …

- In 30–35, 30 is the **lower class limit** and 35 the **upper class limit**.
- **Class size (width)** = upper limit − lower limit = 5.
- **Class mark** (mid-point) = (lower + upper)/2 = (30 + 35)/2 = 32.5.
- In such **exclusive** (continuous) classes, a value equal to an upper limit goes into the *next* class: 35 kg is counted in 35–40.

**Inclusive classes and adjusting them.** Sometimes classes are written 30–34, 35–39, 40–44. There is a gap between 34 and 35. To make them continuous for drawing a histogram, find half the gap: (35 − 34)/2 = 0.5. Subtract 0.5 from every lower limit and add 0.5 to every upper limit. The classes become 29.5–34.5, 34.5–39.5, 39.5–44.5 — now touching, with width 5.

How many classes? Usually 5 to 10. Too few hide the pattern; too many make the table almost as messy as raw data.

head: Class (kg)
Tally count
Frequency
Class mark
fig.caption: A grouped frequency table for the weights of 40 students. Width of every class = 5 kg.

check.q: In the exclusive classes 40–50, 50–60, the value 50 is placed in:
check.why: In exclusive classes the upper limit is not included, so 50 belongs to the class 50–60.

sections.md:
A table is organised, but a picture is faster. Your eye can compare the heights of bars in a fraction of a second; it cannot compare ten numbers that quickly. That is why companies put graphs in annual reports and news channels show bar charts on election night.

The chapter teaches three graphs:

1. **Bar graph** — for data in separate categories (subjects, states, months, modes of transport).
2. **Histogram** — for grouped *continuous* data (heights, weights, marks in class intervals). Bars touch each other.
3. **Frequency polygon** — a line graph joining the mid-points of the tops of the histogram rectangles, or drawn directly from class marks.

General rules for any graph:

- Give the graph a **title**.
- Label both **axes** with names and units.
- Choose a sensible **scale** and write it (for example, 1 cm = 10 students).
- Start the frequency axis at 0 so heights are honest.
- If the horizontal axis does not start at 0, show a **kink** (a small zig-zag) near the origin to say 'values have been skipped here'.

check.q: Why must the frequency axis of a bar graph start at zero?
options: So that bar heights are honestly proportional to the values
NCERT says so for no reason
check.why: If the axis starts above zero, small differences look huge and the graph misleads the reader.

sections.md:
A **bar graph** shows data using bars of **uniform width** drawn with **equal spacing** between them, on one axis (usually horizontal). The **height (or length)** of each bar is proportional to the value it represents. The gaps show that the categories are separate — 'Bus' and 'Cycle' have nothing between them.

**Example.** A survey of 120 students of a school in Pune asked how they come to school:

| Mode | Bus | Walk | Cycle | Car | Metro |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Students | 40 | 25 | 30 | 15 | 10 |

Steps:
1. Draw two perpendicular axes. Mark the modes on the horizontal axis with equal width bars and equal gaps.
2. Choose a scale on the vertical axis: 1 unit = 5 students. The largest value 40 needs 8 units — fits well.
3. Draw each bar to its height: Bus 8 units, Walk 5, Cycle 6, Car 3, Metro 2.
4. Title: 'How students travel to school'.

**Reading a bar graph** is just as important. From the graph you can answer: Which mode is most popular? (Bus.) How many more cycle than come by car? (30 − 15 = 15.) What fraction walk? (25/120 = 5/24.)

**Double bar graphs** put two bars side by side for each category — for example, boys and girls, or 2024 and 2025 sales — so you can compare both at once. Use a key (legend) to show which colour means what.

check.why: All bars have the same width; only the height changes, and it is proportional to the value.

sections.md:
A **histogram** is a graph of a grouped frequency distribution of **continuous** data. It looks like a bar graph but with two key differences:

- There are **no gaps** between the bars — the classes are continuous (30–35 runs straight into 35–40).
- Strictly, the **area** of each rectangle is proportional to the frequency. When all classes have the same width, area ∝ height, so we simply draw heights equal to the frequencies.

**Example.** Weights of 40 students (from Section 3): 30–35: 4, 35–40: 8, 40–45: 12, 45–50: 9, 50–55: 5, 55–60: 2.

Steps:
1. On the horizontal axis mark class limits 30, 35, 40, …, 60 with a scale (1 cm = 5 kg). Since the axis does not start from 0, draw a kink near the origin.
2. On the vertical axis mark frequency (1 cm = 2 students).
3. Draw touching rectangles: base 30–35, height 4; base 35–40, height 8; and so on.

Reading it: the tallest rectangle is over 40–45 kg — the most common weight group. The shape rises then falls, a typical pattern for body measurements.

**If classes are inclusive** (30–34, 35–39 …), first convert them to continuous classes (29.5–34.5 …) as shown earlier; otherwise the rectangles would have gaps, which is wrong for a histogram.
