check.q: In the potato-cup activity, why does the boiled-potato cup with sugar stay dry?
options: Boiling kills cells, so osmosis through living membranes stops
check.why: Osmosis in the potato needs living, selectively permeable membranes, and boiling destroys them.

sections.md:
Cells come in two grand designs.

**Prokaryotic cells** (bacteria, and blue-green algae/cyanobacteria) are usually tiny (1–10 µm). They have **no nuclear membrane**: the genetic material lies in a region called the **nucleoid**. They lack membrane-bound organelles like mitochondria and Golgi bodies, though they do have ribosomes, and in photosynthetic bacteria chlorophyll is found on membranous vesicles. They usually have a single chromosome.

**Eukaryotic cells** (protists, fungi, plants, animals) are larger (5–100 µm), with a **true nucleus** bounded by a nuclear membrane, more than one chromosome, and membrane-bound organelles.

| Feature | Prokaryote | Eukaryote |
|---|---|---|
| Size | 1–10 µm | 5–100 µm |
| Nucleus | nucleoid, no membrane | true nucleus |
| Chromosomes | one | more than one |
| Membrane organelles | absent | present |

**Did you know?** Mitochondria and plastids have their own DNA and ribosomes, so they can make some of their own proteins — one reason scientists think they were once free-living bacteria.

check.q: Which feature is found in a prokaryotic cell?
check.why: A prokaryote's DNA lies in an undefined nucleoid region because it has no nuclear membrane.

sections.h: 12. Mitosis and meiosis, and how organelles work together
sections.md:
New cells come only from existing cells. Two kinds of division:

- **Mitosis** — one mother cell gives **two identical daughter cells**, each with the same number of chromosomes as the mother. It is used for growth and repair of tissues (healing a cut knee, a growing root tip).
- **Meiosis** — happens in the reproductive organs to make gametes (egg and sperm). One cell divides twice to give **four cells with half the number of chromosomes**. When gametes fuse at fertilisation, the full number is restored.

**The cell as a factory.** Think of a cell making a protein for export: the **nucleus** holds the plan (DNA), **ribosomes** on the **rough ER** assemble the protein, the ER carries it, the **Golgi apparatus** packages and dispatches it in vesicles, **mitochondria** supply ATP energy, and **lysosomes** clear worn-out parts. When a cell is badly damaged, lysosomes may burst and digest the cell itself — hence the nickname *suicide bags*. The **smooth ER** helps make lipids and detoxify poisons in liver cells, and the ER also makes lipids and proteins for building the cell membrane (**membrane biogenesis**).
keyTerms: Mitosis — division giving 2 identical cells
Meiosis — division giving 4 cells with half chromosomes
Membrane biogenesis — making new membrane using ER products

check.q: A cell with 46 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. Each resulting cell has:
check.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so 46 becomes 23 in each gamete.

workedExamples.q: A shrivelled raisin is put in water and becomes plump. Name and explain the process.
steps: Inside the raisin the sugar solution is more concentrated than plain water.
Water moves from dilute outside to concentrated inside through the skin (selectively permeable).
This movement of water into the cell is endosmosis.
workedExamples.answer: Endosmosis (osmosis of water into the raisin).

summary: Onion peel cells show walls and nuclei after safranin staining; cheek cells have no wall.
Cell shape is linked to function (nerve, blood, muscle cells).
Unicellular organisms do all life functions in one cell; multicellular ones show division of labour.
De-shelled egg and raisins show endosmosis and exosmosis.
Living membranes are needed for osmosis (boiled potato cup fails).
Hypotonic → cell swells; isotonic → no change; hypertonic → cell shrinks.
Plant cells become turgid, not burst, due to the cell wall.
Prokaryotes: nucleoid, no membrane organelles; eukaryotes: true nucleus.
Mitosis → 2 identical cells for growth and repair; meiosis → 4 cells with half chromosomes.
Lysosomes are 'suicide bags'; ER helps in membrane biogenesis.

rd-school-c9-science-a.is-matter-around-.title: Is Matter Around Us Pure?
rd-school-c9-science-a.is-matter-around-.subtitle: 'Pure' milk, 'pure' ghee — what a chemist really means by pure

sections.md:
The packet says *pure desi ghee*, the dairy promises *100% pure milk*, and the bottle of water is *pure mineral water*. To a shopkeeper 'pure' means 'not adulterated'. To a scientist, though, milk is a mixture of water, fat, proteins, lactose and more; mineral water has dissolved salts. None of them is pure!

For a scientist, a **pure substance** consists of **a single type of particles** — all its constituent particles have the same chemical nature. A **mixture** contains **more than one** pure substance mixed in any proportion.

This chapter answers: What is a mixture, and what kinds are there? What are solutions, suspensions and colloids? How do we separate the parts of a mixture? What is the difference between physical and chemical changes? And what are the two kinds of pure substances — elements and compounds?

check.q: To a scientist, which of these is a pure substance?
check.why: Distilled water has only one type of particle (water molecules); the others are mixtures.

sections.md:
Mixtures are made of more than one kind of pure substance. Dissolved sodium chloride can be separated from water by evaporation — but sodium chloride itself is a pure substance that cannot be separated into its chemical constituents by physical processes.

**Types of mixtures**, depending on the nature of the components:

- **Homogeneous mixture**: has a **uniform composition** throughout; you cannot see the separate parts. Examples: salt in water, sugar in water, air, a copper sulphate solution, brass. Two solutions of copper sulphate of different strengths (light and dark blue) are both homogeneous — so a homogeneous mixture can have a variable composition, but each sample is uniform.
- **Heterogeneous mixture**: contains **physically distinct parts** and has **non-uniform** composition. Examples: sodium chloride and iron filings; salt and sulphur; oil and water; sand and water; a fruit salad.

**Activity idea.** Stir a pinch of copper sulphate into 50 mL water in one beaker, and a spoonful of chalk powder into another. The first is clear blue throughout; in the second, chalk particles float and settle — heterogeneous.

check.q: Which is a heterogeneous mixture?
check.why: Sand and water form visible separate layers, so the composition is not uniform.

sections.md:
A **solution** is a **homogeneous mixture of two or more substances**. Lemonade (nimbu pani), soda water and sugar syrup are solutions. We usually think of a liquid with a solid, liquid or gas dissolved in it, but there are **solid solutions** (alloys) and **gaseous solutions** (air) too.

- **Alloys** are mixtures of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, that cannot be separated by physical methods but still show the properties of their constituents and have **variable composition**. **Brass** is about 30% zinc and 70% copper.
- A solution has a **solvent** (the component in larger amount, which dissolves the other) and a **solute** (the component dissolved, present in lesser quantity).
  - Sugar in water: sugar = solute, water = solvent (solid in liquid).
  - Tincture of iodine: iodine in alcohol (solid in liquid).
  - Soda water: CO₂ in water (gas in liquid).
  - Air: mainly oxygen (21%) and nitrogen (78%) — gas in gas; nitrogen is the solvent.

**Properties of a solution:**
1. It is **homogeneous**.
2. Particles are smaller than **1 nm** (10⁻⁹ m) in diameter — they cannot be seen even with a microscope.
3. Because the particles are so small, they **do not scatter a beam of light** — the path of light is not visible.
4. The solute particles **cannot be separated by filtration**, and they do not settle on standing: a solution is **stable**.

check.q: In tincture of iodine, the solvent is:
check.why: Iodine (the solute) is dissolved in alcohol, which is the solvent.

sections.md:
If you keep adding salt to a glass of water while stirring, it dissolves at first — but at some point, no more dissolves and salt starts collecting at the bottom. The solution is now **saturated**.

- **Saturated solution**: at a given temperature, it has dissolved as much solute as it can.
- **Solubility**: the amount of solute present in a saturated solution at that temperature.
- **Unsaturated solution**: contains less solute than the saturation level.
- Different substances have different solubilities in the same solvent. Solubility usually rises with temperature for solids (hot water dissolves more sugar — think of making chashni for gulab jamun).

A solution may be dilute, concentrated or saturated — these words are only comparative. The **concentration** of a solution is the amount of solute present in a given amount (mass or volume) of solution or solvent. Common ways to express it:

**(i) Mass by mass percentage** = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100
**(ii) Mass by volume percentage** = (mass of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100

(mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent)

**Example 1.** A solution contains 40 g of common salt in 320 g of water. Mass of solution = 40 + 320 = 360 g. Concentration = 40/360 × 100 = **11.1%** (mass by mass).

**Example 2.** How much sugar is needed to make 500 g of a 5% (mass/mass) sugar solution? 5/100 × 500 = 25 g sugar in 475 g water.

**Example 3.** 2 g of salt dissolved to make 100 mL of solution: 2/100 × 100 = 2% (mass by volume).

check.q: 10 g of sugar is dissolved in 90 g of water. The concentration (mass by mass) is:
check.why: Mass of solution = 10 + 90 = 100 g, so concentration = 10/100 × 100 = 10%.

sections.md:
### Suspension
In a **suspension**, a solid is dispersed in a liquid but the particles **do not dissolve** and are **visible to the naked eye**. Chalk powder in water, muddy river water and sand in water are suspensions.

**Properties:** heterogeneous; particles can be seen; they **scatter a beam of light**, making its path visible; they **settle down** when left undisturbed — the suspension is **unstable** — and can be separated by **filtration**.

### Colloidal solution
Milk, starch solution, ink and soap solution look homogeneous but are actually **heterogeneous**. Their particles are too small to see with the eye (between about 1 nm and 100 nm) but big enough to scatter light. These are **colloids**.

**Tyndall effect**: the scattering of a beam of light by colloidal particles, making the beam's path visible. You see it when sunlight streams through a gap in a dense forest canopy at dawn, through the window of a dusty room, or as the beam of a cinema projector.

**Properties of colloids:** heterogeneous but appear homogeneous; particles too small to be seen individually; they scatter light (Tyndall effect); they **do not settle** on standing — quite stable; they **cannot be separated by filtration**, but can be separated by **centrifugation**.

**Components:** the **dispersed phase** (the solute-like particles) and the **dispersion medium** (the component in which they are spread).

head: Dispersed phase
Dispersion medium
Type
Example
fig.caption: Common examples of colloids.

check.q: The Tyndall effect is shown by:
check.why: Milk is a colloid; its particles are large enough to scatter light, unlike those of true solutions.

sections.md:
| Property | True solution | Colloid | Suspension |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nature | Homogeneous | Heterogeneous (looks homogeneous) | Heterogeneous |
| Particle size | < 1 nm | 1–100 nm | > 100 nm |
| Visible? | No | Not to the eye | Yes |
| Tyndall effect | No | Yes | Yes |
| Settles on standing? | No | No | Yes |
| Separation by filter paper | No | No | Yes |
| Example | Sugar in water | Milk, ink | Muddy water |

**Did you know?** The blue colour of the sky and the red of a sunset come from scattering of sunlight by tiny particles in the atmosphere — a cousin of the Tyndall effect you will study in Class 10.

check.why: Suspension particles (as in muddy water) are big enough to be stopped by filter paper.

sections.h: 7. Separating the components of a mixture
sections.md:
Heterogeneous mixtures can be separated by simple physical methods like **hand-picking, sieving and filtration** (used at home for stones in rice or tea leaves from chai). Special techniques are needed for others:

1. **Evaporation** — to separate a **volatile** component (solvent) from a **non-volatile** solute. *Example:* heating blue/black ink in a china dish over a water bath: water evaporates, the dye remains. Salt is obtained from sea water in salt pans of Gujarat this way.
2. **Centrifugation** — spinning a mixture very fast so denser particles are forced to the bottom and lighter ones stay on top. *Uses:* diagnostic labs for blood and urine tests; dairies and homes to separate butter from cream; washing machines to squeeze water from clothes.
3. **Separating funnel** — for **two immiscible liquids** (oil and water, kerosene and water). The denser liquid forms the lower layer and is drained through the stopcock. Also used to separate iron from its ore in a blast furnace (lighter slag on top of molten iron).
4. **Sublimation** — for a mixture containing a **sublimable** component (one that turns directly from solid to vapour), such as **ammonium chloride, camphor, naphthalene, anthracene** — e.g. salt + ammonium chloride. Heat in a china dish under an inverted funnel; the vapours solidify on the cool funnel.
5. **Chromatography** — to separate **coloured components (dyes)** of a mixture, or very small amounts of substances. Put a spot of ink on filter paper and dip its edge in water: the more soluble dye rises faster with the water and separates. (*Kroma* = colour in Greek.) *Uses:* separating colours in a dye or pigments from natural colours; drugs from blood.
6. **Distillation** — for two **miscible liquids** that boil without decomposing and whose boiling points differ greatly (e.g. acetone 56 °C and water 100 °C). Heat; the lower-boiling liquid vaporises first, is condensed and collected.
7. **Fractional distillation** — when boiling points differ by **less than 25 K**. A **fractionating column** packed with glass beads gives surfaces for repeated condensing and evaporating. *Uses:* separating gases of **air**; separating petroleum products.
8. **Crystallisation** — to purify a solid by separating it as pure crystals from a solution. Better than evaporation because some solids decompose or char on heating to dryness, and impurities may stay dissolved. *Example:* purifying salt from sea water; separating alum (phitkari) from impure samples; making pure copper sulphate crystals.

check.q: Which method would you use to separate the gases of air?
check.why: The gases of liquefied air have close boiling points, so they are separated by fractional distillation.

sections.h: 8. Getting gases from air and purifying water
sections.md:
### Obtaining gases from air
Air is a homogeneous mixture. To separate it:
1. Compress air and cool it by increasing pressure and decreasing temperature → **liquid air**.
2. Allow liquid air to warm slowly in a fractional distillation column; gases separate at different heights as they boil:

| Gas | Boiling point (°C) | % in air (approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | −183 | 20.9 |
| Argon | −186 | 0.9 |
| Nitrogen | −196 | 78.1 |

Nitrogen boils first (lowest b.p.). Oxygen collects as liquid at the bottom.

### Water purification in a waterworks
River water from a reservoir passes through:
1. **Sedimentation tank** — heavy particles settle.
2. **Loading tank** with **alum** — helps fine particles clump and settle (loading/coagulation).
3. **Filtration tank** — layers of sand and gravel remove remaining particles.
4. **Chlorination tank** — chlorine kills germs.
5. **Water tank** → supply to homes.

sections.md:
**Physical properties** — colour, hardness, rigidity, fluidity, density, melting point, boiling point — can be observed and specified. Changing the **state** of a substance (ice → water → steam) or its shape is a **physical change**: the chemical nature (composition) stays the same, and it is usually easy to reverse.

A **chemical change** brings change in the chemical properties of matter and **we get new substances**. It is also called a **chemical reaction**. Burning candle wax is a chemical change (a new substance, CO₂, forms) though melting the wax is physical. Other chemical changes: rusting of iron, burning of paper or LPG, cooking of food, curdling of milk, ripening of fruit, digestion.

| Physical change | Chemical change |
|---|---|
| No new substance | New substance formed |
| Usually reversible | Usually irreversible |
| Melting ice, dissolving sugar, cutting wood, breaking glass, boiling water | Burning wood, rusting, cooking, curd from milk, growth of a plant |

**Activity: iron and sulphur.** Mix iron filings and sulphur powder in one dish (group I) and heat a similar mixture strongly in another (group II).
- A magnet pulls the iron out of group I but not group II.
- Carbon disulphide dissolves the sulphur in group I, not in group II.
- With dilute acid, group I gives hydrogen (odourless, burns with a pop); group II gives hydrogen sulphide (rotten-egg smell).
Group I is a **mixture**; group II has become a **compound**, iron sulphide (FeS), with new properties.

check.q: Which is a chemical change?
check.why: Rusting forms a new substance (iron oxide) with different properties.

sections.h: 10. What are the types of pure substances?
sections.md:
Pure substances are of two kinds: **elements** and **compounds**.

### Elements
**Robert Boyle** (1661) first used the term element. **Antoine Lavoisier**, the French chemist, first gave a useful definition: an **element is a basic form of matter that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions**.

Elements are divided into:
- **Metals**: lustrous (shiny); conduct heat and electricity; ductile (drawn into wires); malleable (hammered into sheets); sonorous (ring when struck). Examples: gold, silver, copper, iron, sodium, potassium. **Mercury** is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
- **Non-metals**: show a variety of colours; poor conductors of heat and electricity; not lustrous, sonorous or malleable. Examples: hydrogen, oxygen, iodine, carbon (coal, coke), bromine (a liquid at room temperature), chlorine.
- **Metalloids**: properties intermediate between metals and non-metals — boron, silicon, germanium.

Over 118 elements are known; 92 occur naturally. Most are solids; 11 are gases at room temperature; 2 are liquids (mercury and bromine); gallium and caesium become liquid just above room temperature (303 K).

### Compounds
A **compound** is a substance composed of **two or more elements, chemically combined** with one another **in a fixed proportion**.

| Mixture | Compound |
|---|---|
| Elements/compounds just mix; no new compound | Elements react to form new compounds |
| Variable composition | Fixed composition |
| Shows properties of its constituents | Properties totally different from its constituents |
| Separated by physical methods | Separated only by chemical or electrochemical reactions |

Water (H₂O) is a liquid that puts out fire, though it is made of hydrogen (which burns) and oxygen (which supports burning) — a striking example of a compound having entirely new properties.

check.q: Which property shows that iron sulphide is a compound and not a mixture?
options: Its properties differ from those of iron and sulphur
check.why: A compound has new properties different from its elements; a mixture keeps its components' properties.

Add water to the rest and stir: salt dissolves.
Filter: sand stays on the filter paper.
Evaporate/crystallise the filtrate to get salt.

summary: A pure substance has only one kind of particle; a mixture has more than one substance in any proportion.
Homogeneous mixtures (solutions) are uniform; heterogeneous mixtures have visible distinct parts.
A solution = solute + solvent; particles < 1 nm, no Tyndall effect, stable, not filterable.
Alloys like brass are solid solutions; air is a gaseous solution.
Saturated solutions hold the maximum solute at a temperature; that amount is the solubility.
Concentration = mass of solute/mass of solution × 100 (or per volume of solution).
Suspensions are heterogeneous, visible, settle on standing and can be filtered.
Colloids (1–100 nm) look homogeneous, show the Tyndall effect, do not settle and need centrifugation to separate.
Colloids have a dispersed phase and a dispersion medium: aerosol, foam, emulsion, sol, gel, solid sol.
Separation methods: evaporation, centrifugation, separating funnel, sublimation, chromatography, distillation, fractional distillation, crystallisation.
Physical changes form no new substance; chemical changes form new substances.
Elements cannot be broken down by chemical reactions: metals, non-metals, metalloids.
Compounds have elements combined in fixed proportions with entirely new properties.

sections.h: 11. Mixture or compound? The iron and sulphur activity
sections.md:
The chapter's most famous activity compares a mixture with a compound made from the same two substances.

Take about 5 g of iron filings and 3 g of sulphur powder. Divide into two groups.

- **Group I** just mixes and crushes them. This is a **mixture**.
- **Group II** heats the mixture strongly in a china dish until it glows red, then cools it. This forms **iron sulphide (FeS)**, a **compound**.

Now test both:

| Test | Mixture (Group I) | Compound (Group II) |
|---|---|---|
| Look with a hand lens | yellow sulphur and grey iron visible separately | uniform black-grey mass |
| Bring a magnet near | iron filings are attracted | not attracted |
| Add carbon disulphide | sulphur dissolves | nothing dissolves |
| Add dilute sulphuric or hydrochloric acid (teacher only) | hydrogen gas — colourless, odourless, burns with a pop | hydrogen sulphide gas — smells of rotten eggs |

**Conclusions — mixture vs compound:**
1. In a mixture the components keep their own properties; in a compound the properties are totally different from the elements.
2. A mixture has variable composition; a compound always has a fixed ratio by mass.
3. Mixtures are separated by physical methods; compounds only by chemical or electrochemical reactions.
4. Forming a compound usually involves energy change (heat, light); making a mixture usually does not.

check.q: Which gas is given off when dilute acid is added to iron sulphide?
check.why: Iron sulphide reacts with acid to give hydrogen sulphide, recognised by its rotten-egg smell, while free iron in the mixture gives hydrogen.

sections.md:
Robert Boyle (1661) first used the word *element*, and Antoine Lavoisier defined an element as a basic form of matter that cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical reactions.

**Metals** usually have lustre (shine), silvery-grey or golden-yellow colour, conduct heat and electricity, are **ductile** (drawn into wires), **malleable** (beaten into sheets) and **sonorous** (ring when struck). Examples: gold, silver, copper, iron, sodium, potassium. **Mercury** is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

**Non-metals** show a variety of colours, are poor conductors, and are not lustrous, sonorous or malleable. Examples: hydrogen, oxygen, iodine, carbon (coal, coke), bromine, chlorine. **Bromine** is the non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.

**Metalloids** have properties in between: boron, silicon, germanium.

Over 100 elements are known; 92 occur naturally, the rest are man-made. Most are solids, eleven are gases and two (mercury and bromine) are liquids at room temperature; gallium and caesium become liquid just above room temperature (about 303 K).

check.q: Which element is a metalloid?
check.why: Silicon shows properties between metals and non-metals, so it is a metalloid.

sections.h: 13. More on separation — choosing the right method
sections.md:
Exams often give a mixture and ask for the method. Use this decision table:

| Mixture | Method | Why it works |
|---|---|---|
| Dye from blue/black ink | evaporation | water evaporates, dye stays |
| Cream from milk | centrifugation | denser particles forced down on fast spinning |
| Kerosene and water | separating funnel | immiscible liquids form layers |
| Ammonium chloride and salt | sublimation | NH₄Cl turns straight to vapour |
| Colours in ink, pigments | chromatography | dyes travel at different speeds on paper |
| Acetone and water | distillation | boiling points far apart (56 °C vs 100 °C) |
| Oxygen, nitrogen, argon from air | fractional distillation of liquid air | boiling points close together |
| Pure copper sulphate from impure | crystallisation | impurities stay in solution |
| Butter from curd | centrifugation/churning | |
| Iron pins from sand | magnet | iron is magnetic |

**Centrifugation** is used in diagnostic labs (blood and urine tests), dairies and in washing machines to squeeze water from clothes. **Chromatography** — from the Greek *kroma*, colour — is used to separate drugs from blood and coloured dyes.

check.q: Which method separates two miscible liquids whose boiling points differ by less than 25 K?
check.why: When boiling points are close, a fractionating column is needed, so fractional distillation is used.

rd-school-c9-science-a.matter-in-our-sur.title: Matter in Our Surroundings
rd-school-c9-science-a.matter-in-our-sur.subtitle: Why ice melts, why a matka cools water, and why you smell biryani from the next street

sections.md:
The air you breathe, the food you eat, stones, clouds, stars, plants, animals, even a single drop of water or a grain of sand — everything in this universe is made of **matter**. Anything that **occupies space and has mass** is matter.

Ancient Indian philosophers classified matter into five basic elements — the **Panch Tatva**: air, earth, fire, sky and water. Ancient Greek thinkers had a similar idea. Modern scientists classify matter in two ways: by **physical properties** (this chapter) and by **chemical nature** (next chapters).

**Is everything matter?** Feelings like love, hate, thought or a smell's *sensation* are not matter — they occupy no space and have no mass. But the *molecules* that carry a smell are matter.

In this chapter: the physical nature of matter (particles), the characteristics of particles, the three states of matter, how states change with temperature and pressure, latent heat, and evaporation and its cooling effect.

check.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
check.why: A feeling has no mass and occupies no space, so it is not matter.

sections.h: 2. Physical nature of matter — made of particles
sections.md:
For a long time, people argued: is matter continuous like a block of wood, or made of particles like sand?

**Activity: salt or sugar in water.** Take a 100 mL beaker, fill half with water and mark the level. Dissolve some salt or sugar with a glass rod. The level does **not** rise noticeably, and the salt seems to vanish. Where did it go? The particles of salt fit into the **spaces between particles of water**. This is evidence that matter is **made of particles**.

**How small are these particles?** Activity: dissolve 2–3 crystals of potassium permanganate in 100 mL water. Take 10 mL of this into 90 mL of clear water — still purple. Repeat 5–8 times. The water is still faintly coloured. A few crystals can colour a huge volume of water, so each crystal must contain **millions of tiny particles** that keep dividing among more water. The same works with 2 mL of Dettol in 1000 mL of water — you can still smell it.

**Did you know?** The particles of matter are so small that they are beyond imagination — far too small to be seen even with an ordinary microscope.

check.q: When sugar dissolves in water, the water level hardly rises because:
options: sugar particles occupy the spaces between water particles
check.why: Particles of water have gaps between them, into which sugar particles fit.

sections.md:
### (i) Particles of matter have space between them
As we saw with salt, sugar, Dettol and potassium permanganate, particles of one substance get into the spaces between particles of another. Tea, coffee or nimbu pani are made this way.

### (ii) Particles of matter are continuously moving
Light an incense stick (agarbatti) in one corner: soon the whole room smells. A drop of ink or honey in water spreads out by itself. Particles possess **kinetic energy** (energy of motion). As **temperature rises, particles move faster** — the kinetic energy increases.

The intermixing of particles of two different types of matter on their own is called **diffusion**. It becomes **faster with increasing temperature**: a crystal of copper sulphate in hot water spreads colour much quicker than in cold water. Diffusion of gases is fastest, then liquids, and diffusion in solids is extremely slow. This is how oxygen and CO₂ from air dissolve into water — aquatic animals and plants depend on it.

### (iii) Particles of matter attract each other
There is a **force of attraction** between particles that holds them together. Its strength varies from one kind of matter to another.

*Activity:* Try to break an iron nail, a piece of chalk and a rubber band with your hand. Iron is hardest, chalk breaks easily — attraction is strongest in the iron. Open a water tap and try to break the stream with your finger — it rejoins, because water particles attract each other.

**Did you know?** When you smell hot sizzling food (like jalebis being fried) from several metres away, but must go close to smell cold food — this is because hot food's particles move faster and diffuse quicker.

sections.h: 4. States of matter — solid, liquid, gas
sections.md:
Matter around us exists in three states, decided by the arrangement and motion of particles.

### Solid
Definite **shape**, distinct boundaries and fixed **volume**; **negligible compressibility**; **rigid** — tends to keep its shape under force. May break under force but it is difficult to change shape.
- A **rubber band** changes shape when stretched but regains it — it is a solid; it breaks under too much force.
- **Sugar and salt** take the shape of the jar but each crystal keeps its shape — solids.
- A **sponge** has tiny holes full of air; when squeezed the air goes out, so it can be compressed — still a solid.

### Liquid
**No fixed shape** but a **fixed volume**; takes the shape of the container. Liquids **flow** — they are **fluid**, not rigid. Gases (O₂, CO₂) and solids (salt, sugar) can **diffuse into liquids**. Rate of diffusion in liquids is higher than in solids because particles move freely and have more space between them.

### Gas
Neither fixed shape nor fixed volume; fills any container. **Highly compressible** — that is why **LPG** cylinders for cooking and **CNG** cylinders for vehicles can store large amounts of gas in small volumes, and oxygen cylinders go to hospitals. Gases diffuse very fast because particles move at high speed with lots of space between them. The particles hit the container walls; the force per unit area is the **pressure** of the gas.

| Property | Solid | Liquid | Gas |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shape | Fixed | Of container | Of container |
| Volume | Fixed | Fixed | Fills container |
| Compressibility | Negligible | Very low | High |
| Interparticle spaces | Least | More | Most |
| Force of attraction | Strongest | Weaker | Weakest |
| Kinetic energy | Least | More | Most |
| Density | Highest | Lower | Lowest |

sections.h: 5. Can matter change its state? — effect of temperature
sections.md:
Water exists as ice (solid), water (liquid) and steam/water vapour (gas). What makes the difference?

**Activity.** Put ice cubes in a beaker with a thermometer. Heat slowly on a low flame. Note the temperature when ice starts melting, then when all of it has melted, then when water starts boiling. Keep heating and note what happens.

Observations:
- Ice melts at **0 °C (273.15 K)** and the temperature **stays at 0 °C** until all the ice has melted, even though heat is being supplied.
- Water boils at **100 °C (373 K)** and again the temperature **stays constant** until all water turns to steam.

**Explanation.** Heating increases the kinetic energy of the particles; they vibrate faster and eventually overcome the forces of attraction; the solid melts.
- **Melting point**: the temperature at which a solid melts to become a liquid at atmospheric pressure. It is a measure of the strength of attraction between particles. (Ice: 273.15 K.)
- The process is **fusion**.
- **Latent heat of fusion**: the amount of heat energy required to change **1 kg of a solid into liquid** at atmospheric pressure **at its melting point**. ('Latent' means hidden — the heat does not show on the thermometer; it is used to break attraction between particles.) Particles in water at 0 °C (273 K) have **more energy** than particles in ice at the same temperature.
- **Boiling point**: the temperature at which a liquid starts boiling at atmospheric pressure. Boiling is a **bulk phenomenon** — particles from the whole liquid gain enough energy to become vapour.
- **Latent heat of vaporisation**: heat needed to change **1 kg of a liquid into gas** at atmospheric pressure at its boiling point. Particles in steam at 100 °C (373 K) have more energy than water at the same temperature — which is why **burns from steam are more severe** than from boiling water.

**Sublimation.** Some substances change **directly from solid to gas** (and back, called deposition) without becoming liquid: **camphor, naphthalene balls, ammonium chloride, iodine, dry ice (solid CO₂)**. *Activity:* heat camphor in a china dish covered by an inverted funnel with cotton in its stem — the vapours solidify on the cool funnel.

**Kelvin scale.** SI unit of temperature is the **kelvin (K)**. 0 °C = 273.15 K (use 273 for simplicity). K = °C + 273; °C = K − 273.
- 300 K = 300 − 273 = **27 °C**; 573 K = **300 °C**.
- 25 °C = **298 K**; 373 °C = **646 K**.
- All temperatures on the Kelvin scale are positive; 0 K is absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature.

check.q: Why do steam burns hurt more than burns from boiling water at the same temperature?
options: Steam carries extra latent heat of vaporisation
check.why: Steam at 100 °C holds the extra latent heat it absorbed while vaporising, and releases it on the skin.

sections.md:
We know that the difference in states is due to the differing distances between particles. What happens if we **squeeze** a gas in a cylinder with a piston? Its particles come closer.

- **Applying pressure and reducing temperature can liquefy gases.** LPG is liquefied petroleum gas stored under pressure.
- **Solid carbon dioxide (dry ice)** is stored under high pressure. When the pressure is reduced to 1 atmosphere, it changes **directly into gas** without becoming liquid — that is why it is called *dry* ice. It is used to keep ice-cream and vaccines cold during transport, and for stage 'fog'.

So the **state of a substance at a given temperature and pressure** depends on both. Pressure is measured in **atmospheres (atm)**; the SI unit is the **pascal (Pa)**. **1 atm = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa**. The pressure of air at sea level is 1 atm, the 'normal atmospheric pressure'.

**Did you know?** In the hills of Ladakh, at lower air pressure, water boils below 100 °C, so dal takes far longer to cook — which is why people use pressure cookers there. A pressure cooker raises the pressure so water boils at about 120 °C.

check.q: Dry ice is:
options: solid CO₂ that sublimes at 1 atm
check.why: Solid carbon dioxide turns directly into gas when the pressure drops to 1 atmosphere.

sections.md:
Do we always need to heat or change pressure to change a state? No! Wet clothes dry in the sun, water in a puddle disappears, a few drops of water on a plate vanish without boiling.

Particles of a liquid have **different kinetic energies**. At the surface, a small fraction of particles have enough energy to break away and become vapour. **The phenomenon of a liquid changing into vapour at any temperature below its boiling point is called evaporation.** It is a **surface phenomenon** (boiling is a bulk phenomenon).

### Factors affecting evaporation
1. **Surface area**: evaporation increases with larger surface area (we spread clothes to dry; tea in a saucer cools faster than in a cup).
2. **Temperature**: increases with temperature — more particles get enough energy.
3. **Humidity**: the amount of water vapour in air. When humidity is high (e.g. Mumbai in July), the air already holds a lot of water, so evaporation **decreases** — clothes take ages to dry in the monsoon.
4. **Wind speed**: increases with wind — moving air carries away the vapour, so more can escape.

*Activity:* Put 5 mL of water in a test tube, a china dish and a large dish; keep one set inside, one in the sun, one under a fan. Record how long each takes to evaporate.

| Evaporation | Boiling |
|---|---|
| At any temperature below b.p. | At a fixed temperature (b.p.) |
| Surface phenomenon | Bulk phenomenon |
| Slow, quiet | Fast, bubbles form |
| Causes cooling | Temperature stays constant |

check.q: Clothes dry slowly on a humid monsoon day because:
options: air already has a lot of water vapour, so evaporation is slow
check.why: High humidity reduces the rate of evaporation because air can take up less extra water vapour.

sections.md:
In an open vessel, the liquid keeps evaporating. The particles of the liquid **absorb energy from the surroundings** to regain the energy lost during evaporation. This absorption of energy makes the **surroundings cold**.

- Pour some **acetone (nail-polish remover)** on your palm: it feels cold as it evaporates, taking heat from your hand.
- After a hot sunny day, people in villages and towns **sprinkle water on the roof or open ground** — the large latent heat of vaporisation of water helps cool the surface.
- **Earthen pots (matka, surahi)**: water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates from the outer surface, cooling the water inside.
- **Cotton clothes in summer**: we sweat more in summer; cotton absorbs sweat and exposes it to the air for easy evaporation, so our body cools. Synthetic clothes do not absorb sweat well.
- **Water droplets on the outside of a glass of ice water**: water vapour in the air loses energy on the cold glass and **condenses** into liquid — the reverse process. This also proves air contains water vapour.
- Dogs pant and we sweat for the same reason.

**Did you know?** The 'desert cooler' used in Indian homes blows air through wet khus or wood-wool pads. Evaporation of water cools the air — and it works best in dry heat like Delhi in May, poorly in humid Chennai, exactly as humidity predicts.

**Beyond three states.** Scientists also talk of **plasma** (super-energetic, ionised gas found in stars, neon signs, lightning) and **Bose–Einstein condensate**, predicted by **Satyendra Nath Bose** and Albert Einstein and first made in 1995 by cooling a gas to a tiny fraction above absolute zero. (Older editions of this chapter mentioned these as extra states.)

sections.h: 9. The Kelvin scale and latent heat in detail
sections.md:
Scientists measure temperature in **kelvin (K)**, the SI unit. To convert: **K = °C + 273** (more exactly 273.15), and **°C = K − 273**. So water freezes at 273 K and boils at 373 K; a room at 25 °C is at 298 K. There are no negative temperatures on the Kelvin scale — 0 K (−273 °C) is absolute zero.

**Why does the thermometer stop rising while ice melts?** Heat goes on entering, but the temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted. The energy is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles, not to raise their kinetic energy. This 'hidden' heat is **latent heat** (Latin *latere*, to hide).

- **Latent heat of fusion** — heat needed to change 1 kg of a solid into liquid at its melting point, at atmospheric pressure. For ice, about 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg.
- **Latent heat of vaporisation** — heat needed to change 1 kg of a liquid into gas at its boiling point. For water, about 22.5 × 10⁵ J/kg.

So particles in **water at 0 °C (273 K) have more energy than particles in ice at the same temperature**, and particles in **steam at 100 °C have more energy than water at 100 °C**. That is why a **steam burn is more severe** than a burn from boiling water: steam releases its large latent heat as it condenses on the skin.

**Sublimation**: some solids, such as camphor, naphthalene and ammonium chloride, change directly to vapour on heating, and the vapour changes back to solid on cooling (**deposition**). **Dry ice** is solid carbon dioxide; it changes straight to gas when pressure is lowered to 1 atmosphere.

check.q: Convert 470 K to the Celsius scale.

sections.md:
Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour at any temperature **below its boiling point**, and it happens only at the **surface**. Its rate goes up with:

1. **Surface area** — clothes spread out dry faster than folded ones; tea in a saucer cools faster than in a cup.
2. **Temperature** — clothes dry faster in May sunshine than on a December morning; more particles get enough energy to escape.
3. **Lower humidity** — air holds only so much water vapour. On a humid monsoon day in Mumbai, washing stays damp for hours.
4. **Wind speed** — moving air carries vapour away, so clothes dry faster on a windy day.

**Everyday cooling by evaporation:**
- Water kept in an earthen pot (*matka*) becomes cool because water seeps through the pores and evaporates, taking latent heat from the pot.
- After a hot day people sprinkle water on the roof or open ground; evaporation cools the surface.
- We wear **cotton** clothes in summer because cotton absorbs sweat and exposes it to the air, helping evaporation and cooling us.
- Acetone (nail-polish remover) on the palm feels cold as it evaporates fast.
- Water droplets form on the outside of a glass of ice water because water vapour in the air condenses on the cold surface.

check.q: Why do wet clothes dry slowly on a humid day?
options: Air already holds much water vapour
check.why: When humidity is high the air is near saturation, so it takes up water vapour slowly and evaporation slows down.

sections.h: 11. More states of matter: plasma and BEC
sections.md:
Besides solid, liquid and gas, scientists talk about two more states.

**Plasma** is a state of super-energetic, super-excited particles in the form of ionised gases. Neon signs and fluorescent tubes contain gas that glows as plasma when electricity passes through it; the colour depends on the gas. The **Sun and stars** glow because of plasma created by very high temperatures.

**Bose–Einstein Condensate (BEC).** In 1920 the Indian physicist **Satyendra Nath Bose** did calculations for a fifth state; Albert Einstein built on them and predicted it. In 2001, Eric Cornell, Wolfgang Ketterle and Carl Wieman received the Nobel Prize in Physics for producing BEC, made by cooling a gas of extremely low density to super-low temperatures close to absolute zero. The particle called the **boson** is named after Bose.

**Gases are compressible** — this is why LPG cylinders and CNG cylinders (used in buses in Delhi) can hold large amounts of gas, and why oxygen cylinders supplied to hospitals are compressed gas. **Diffusion** of gases explains why the smell of hot food reaches you from far away, and why incense smell spreads in a room.
keyTerms: Plasma — ionised, super-energetic gas
BEC — state formed near absolute zero
Kelvin — SI unit of temperature

check.q: Which Indian scientist's work led to the prediction of BEC?
check.why: Satyendra Nath Bose's 1920s calculations, extended by Einstein, predicted the Bose–Einstein condensate.

rd-school-c9-science-a.structure-of-the-.title: Structure of the Atom
rd-school-c9-science-a.structure-of-the-.subtitle: Dalton said atoms can't be split. Then three experiments broke them open.

sections.md:
Comb your dry hair on a winter morning and hold the comb near tiny bits of paper: they jump up and cling. Rub a glass rod with silk: it attracts a balloon. Where does this electric charge come from? If atoms were solid, uncharged, indivisible balls — as Dalton imagined — rubbing should not produce charges at all.

By the end of the 19th century scientists realised that atoms are **divisible** and contain **sub-atomic particles**. The big challenge was to find how these particles are arranged.

In this chapter: discovery of **electrons, protons and neutrons**; atomic models of **Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr**; how electrons are distributed in **shells**; **valency**; **atomic number and mass number**; and **isotopes and isobars** and their uses.

check.q: The attraction of paper bits to a rubbed comb suggests that atoms contain:
check.why: Rubbing transfers charged particles (electrons), so atoms must contain charged parts.

sections.h: 2. Charged particles in matter — electrons and protons
sections.md:
**Canal rays (1886).** **E. Goldstein** passed electricity through a gas at very low pressure in a discharge tube and found new rays coming from the anode side, travelling through holes ('canals') in the cathode. These **canal rays** were **positively charged**. They led to the discovery of the **proton**.

**The electron (1897).** **J. J. Thomson** studied cathode rays — streams from the cathode in a discharge tube — and showed they are made of tiny **negatively charged** particles, the **electrons**. Electrons are the same for every gas used, so they must be part of all atoms.

| Particle | Symbol | Charge | Relative mass |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electron | e⁻ | −1 | ≈ 1/2000 of a proton (≈ 0) |
| Proton | p⁺ | +1 | 1 u |
| Neutron | n | 0 | 1 u |

An atom is electrically **neutral** overall, because the positive charge of its protons balances the negative charge of its electrons. Since electrons are so light and are easily removed, they are the ones transferred when you rub a comb — the comb gains electrons and becomes negative.

The neutron came last (1932, **J. Chadwick**) — see Section 6.

check.q: Canal rays led to the discovery of the:
check.why: Goldstein's canal rays were positive radiation, which led to the identification of the proton.

sections.h: 3. Thomson's model — the plum pudding (or watermelon)
sections.md:
Thomson was the first to propose a model for the structure of an atom. It resembled a **Christmas pudding** with electrons as dry fruits in a positive pudding — or, as NCERT suggests, a **watermelon**: the red edible part is the positive charge, and the seeds are the electrons scattered through it.

**Postulates:**
1. An atom consists of a **positively charged sphere** with **electrons embedded** in it.
2. The negative and positive charges are **equal in magnitude**, so the atom as a whole is **electrically neutral**.

Thomson's model explained the neutrality of atoms, but it could not explain the results of experiments carried out by other scientists — especially Rutherford's.

**Did you know?** J. J. Thomson won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906 for discovering the electron, and seven of his students and co-workers also went on to win Nobel Prizes.

check.q: In Thomson's watermelon model, the seeds represent:
check.why: Thomson pictured negative electrons scattered in a sphere of positive charge, like seeds in a watermelon.

sections.md:
**Ernest Rutherford** wanted to know how electrons are arranged. He designed an experiment in which fast-moving **alpha (α) particles** — doubly charged helium ions (mass 4 u, charge +2) with considerable energy — were made to fall on a **very thin gold foil**, about 1000 atoms thick. Gold was chosen because it can be beaten into an extremely thin layer. A zinc-sulphide screen around the foil flashed wherever an α-particle hit.

He expected, from Thomson's model, that the α-particles would be deflected only slightly by the thinly spread positive charge. What he saw:

1. **Most** of the fast-moving α-particles **passed straight** through the gold foil.
2. **Some** α-particles were **deflected by small angles**.
3. Surprisingly, **one out of every 12,000** particles **rebounded** back.

Rutherford said it was 'almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you'.

**Conclusions:**
1. Most of the space inside an atom is **empty** (most particles passed straight).
2. Very few particles were deflected, so the **positive charge occupies very little space**.
3. A very small fraction were deflected by 180°, so **all the positive charge and almost all the mass** of the gold atom were concentrated in a very **small volume** in the centre.
4. From his data he calculated that the radius of the nucleus is about **10⁵ times less** than the radius of the atom.

*Analogy:* A child stands in front of a wall with stones, eyes closed, throwing them. Every time a stone hits the wall he hears a sound. If the wall had wide gaps, most stones would pass through — and the rare thud would tell him where the solid parts are.

check.q: Most α-particles passed straight through the gold foil. This shows that:
options: most of the atom is empty space
check.why: If particles meet nothing in their path, most of the atom must be empty space.

sections.h: 5. Rutherford's nuclear model and its drawback
sections.md:
**Features of Rutherford's nuclear model:**
1. There is a **positively charged centre** in an atom called the **nucleus**. Nearly all the mass of an atom resides in the nucleus.
2. The **electrons revolve around the nucleus** in circular paths.
3. The **size of the nucleus is very small** compared with the size of the atom.

It looked like a tiny solar system, with the nucleus as the Sun and electrons as planets.

**Drawback.** Any particle moving in a circle is **accelerated**, and an accelerated charged particle should **radiate energy** (according to the physics of the time). An electron revolving around the nucleus would therefore lose energy steadily and **spiral into the nucleus**. The atom would be highly **unstable** and matter would not exist in the form we know. But atoms are quite stable. Rutherford's model could not explain this.

**Did you know?** Rutherford, born in New Zealand, received the Nobel Prize in **Chemistry** in 1908 — which amused him, as he thought of himself as a physicist. He is called the 'father of nuclear physics'.

check.q: The main drawback of Rutherford's model was that it could not explain:
check.why: A revolving electron should radiate energy and fall into the nucleus, so the model could not explain why atoms are stable.

sections.md:
To overcome the objections, **Niels Bohr** (Denmark, 1913) put forward these postulates:

1. Only certain special orbits known as **discrete orbits of electrons** are allowed inside the atom.
2. **While revolving in discrete orbits, electrons do not radiate energy.**

These orbits or shells are called **energy levels**. They are represented by the letters **K, L, M, N, …** or the numbers **n = 1, 2, 3, 4, …**, starting from the one nearest the nucleus.

### Neutrons
In **1932 James Chadwick** discovered another sub-atomic particle with **no charge** and a mass nearly equal to that of a proton: the **neutron**. Neutrons are present in the nucleus of all atoms **except ordinary hydrogen** (protium). The **mass of an atom** is therefore given by the **sum of the masses of protons and neutrons** in the nucleus. Protons and neutrons together are called **nucleons**.

**Did you know?** Bohr's model explained the bright line colours given off by hot hydrogen gas — the colours of neon-type lamps and fireworks come from electrons jumping between energy levels.

check.why: Bohr postulated that electrons in allowed orbits revolve without losing energy, making atoms stable.

sections.h: 7. How are electrons distributed in shells? (Bohr–Bury scheme)
sections.md:
The distribution of electrons into different orbits was suggested by **Bohr and Bury**. Rules:

1. The **maximum number of electrons** in a shell is given by **2n²**, where n is the shell number:
   - K (n = 1): 2 × 1² = **2**
   - L (n = 2): 2 × 2² = **8**
   - M (n = 3): 2 × 3² = **18**
   - N (n = 4): 2 × 4² = **32**
2. The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the **outermost** orbit is **8**.
3. Electrons are not accommodated in a given shell unless the **inner shells are filled** — shells are filled in a **step-wise** manner.

| Element | Symbol | Atomic no. | Protons | Neutrons | Electrons | K | L | M | Valency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hydrogen | H | 1 | 1 | – | 1 | 1 | – | – | 1 |
| Helium | He | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 | – | – | 0 |
| Lithium | Li | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | – | 1 |
| Beryllium | Be | 4 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 2 | 2 | – | 2 |
| Boron | B | 5 | 5 | 6 | 5 | 2 | 3 | – | 3 |
| Carbon | C | 6 | 6 | 6 | 6 | 2 | 4 | – | 4 |
| Nitrogen | N | 7 | 7 | 7 | 7 | 2 | 5 | – | 3 |
| Oxygen | O | 8 | 8 | 8 | 8 | 2 | 6 | – | 2 |
| Fluorine | F | 9 | 9 | 10 | 9 | 2 | 7 | – | 1 |
| Neon | Ne | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 2 | 8 | – | 0 |
| Sodium | Na | 11 | 11 | 12 | 11 | 2 | 8 | 1 | 1 |
| Magnesium | Mg | 12 | 12 | 12 | 12 | 2 | 8 | 2 | 2 |
| Aluminium | Al | 13 | 13 | 14 | 13 | 2 | 8 | 3 | 3 |
| Silicon | Si | 14 | 14 | 14 | 14 | 2 | 8 | 4 | 4 |
| Phosphorus | P | 15 | 15 | 16 | 15 | 2 | 8 | 5 | 3, 5 |
| Sulphur | S | 16 | 16 | 16 | 16 | 2 | 8 | 6 | 2 |
| Chlorine | Cl | 17 | 17 | 18 | 17 | 2 | 8 | 7 | 1 |
| Argon | Ar | 18 | 18 | 22 | 18 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 0 |

check.q: The maximum number of electrons the M shell can hold is:
check.why: For M, n = 3, so 2n² = 2 × 9 = 18.

sections.md:
The electrons in the **outermost shell** are called **valence electrons**. They decide how an atom reacts.

Atoms of **noble gases** (helium, neon, argon) have a completely filled outermost shell (an **octet** of 8, or a **duplet** of 2 for helium) and show **little chemical activity** — their valency is **zero**. Other atoms react to achieve such a stable octet, by **sharing, gaining or losing** electrons.

The **combining capacity** of an atom is its **valency**:
- If the atom has **1, 2 or 3** valence electrons, it tends to **lose** them; valency = number of valence electrons. Sodium (2, 8, 1) loses 1 → valency 1. Magnesium (2, 8, 2) → 2. Aluminium (2, 8, 3) → 3.
- If the atom has **5, 6 or 7** valence electrons, it tends to **gain** (8 − valence) electrons; valency = 8 − valence electrons. Oxygen (2, 6): 8 − 6 = 2. Chlorine (2, 8, 7): 8 − 7 = 1. Nitrogen (2, 5): 3.
- With **4** valence electrons (carbon, silicon), the atom usually **shares** — valency 4.

**Example.** Fluorine has 7 valence electrons. Is its valency 7? It is easier for fluorine to gain 1 electron than lose 7, so its valency is 8 − 7 = **1**.

check.q: The valency of sulphur (2, 8, 6) is:
check.why: Sulphur needs 2 more electrons to complete its octet, so its valency is 8 − 6 = 2.

sections.md:
**Atomic number (Z)**: the **total number of protons** present in the nucleus of an atom. All atoms of an element have the same atomic number — it *defines* the element. Hydrogen Z = 1, carbon Z = 6, oxygen Z = 8. In a neutral atom, number of electrons = number of protons = Z.

**Mass number (A)**: the **sum of the total number of protons and neutrons** (nucleons) in the nucleus. Carbon has 6 protons and 6 neutrons: A = 12 u. Aluminium: 13 protons + 14 neutrons = 27 u.

**Number of neutrons = A − Z.**

Notation: the atomic number is written as a subscript at the bottom left and the mass number as a superscript at the top left of the symbol: e.g. nitrogen ¹⁴₇N (A = 14, Z = 7).

**Example.** Find the composition of ²³₁₁Na: protons = 11, electrons = 11, neutrons = 23 − 11 = 12.

check.q: An atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Its mass number is:
check.why: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35.

sections.md:
### Isotopes
Some atoms of the same element have the **same atomic number but different mass numbers** — **isotopes**. Hydrogen has three: **protium** ¹₁H (no neutron), **deuterium** ²₁H or D (one neutron) and **tritium** ³₁H or T (two neutrons). Carbon: ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C. Chlorine: ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl.

Isotopes are pure substances. Their **chemical properties are similar** (same electrons), but **physical properties differ** (mass, density, melting point).

**Average atomic mass.** Chlorine occurs as ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl in the ratio 3 : 1. Average atomic mass = 35 × ¾ + 37 × ¼ = 26.25 + 9.25 = **35.5 u**. That is why chlorine's atomic mass is a fraction. (Any single atom has mass 35 or 37 u — the 35.5 is an average.)

### Applications of isotopes
- An isotope of **uranium** (U-235) is used as fuel in **nuclear reactors**.
- An isotope of **cobalt** (Co-60) is used in the **treatment of cancer**.
- An isotope of **iodine** is used in the treatment of **goitre**.
- Carbon-14 is used to find the age of fossils and old wood (radiocarbon dating).

### Isobars
Atoms of **different elements** with **different atomic numbers** but the **same mass number** are **isobars**. Calcium ⁴⁰₂₀Ca and argon ⁴⁰₁₈Ar: both A = 40, but Ca has 20 protons and Ar 18.

| | Isotopes | Isobars |
|---|---|---|
| Atomic number | Same | Different |
| Mass number | Different | Same |
| Element | Same | Different |
| Chemical properties | Similar | Different |

check.q: ⁴⁰₂₀Ca and ⁴⁰₁₈Ar are:
check.why: They have the same mass number (40) but different atomic numbers, so they are isobars.

workedExamples.q: Write the electron distribution of chlorine (Z = 17) and find its valency.
steps: K holds 2, L holds 8, the rest go to M.
Needs 1 more for an octet: valency 1.

steps: One valence electron, lost easily: valency 1.

summary: Atoms contain sub-atomic particles: electrons (−1, negligible mass), protons (+1, 1 u) and neutrons (0, 1 u).
Goldstein's canal rays (1886) led to the proton; J. J. Thomson discovered the electron (1897); Chadwick the neutron (1932).
Thomson's model: electrons embedded in a positive sphere (watermelon); explained neutrality only.
Rutherford's α-scattering: most of the atom is empty; a tiny, dense, positive nucleus holds nearly all the mass.
Rutherford's model could not explain the stability of the atom.
Bohr: electrons revolve in discrete orbits (K, L, M, N) without radiating energy.
Maximum electrons in a shell = 2n²; outermost shell holds at most 8; shells fill step-wise.
Valence electrons are in the outermost shell; valency = number lost (1–3) or 8 minus number (5–7); noble gases have valency 0.
Atomic number Z = number of protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons; neutrons = A − Z.
Isotopes: same Z, different A — similar chemistry; used in reactors, cancer and goitre treatment, dating.
Isobars: different Z, same A (⁴⁰Ca and ⁴⁰Ar).
Fractional atomic masses (Cl = 35.5 u) are averages over isotopes.

sections.md:

sections.h: 12. Average atomic mass and uses of isotopes
sections.md:
Most elements occur as a mixture of isotopes, so the atomic mass written in tables is an **average** weighted by natural abundance. Chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, in the ratio about 3 : 1. That is why chlorine's atomic mass is 35.5 u and not a whole number.

**Isotopes** of an element have the **same chemical properties** (same electrons) but **different physical properties** such as mass and density. Hydrogen has three: protium (¹H), deuterium (²H, D) and tritium (³H, T).

**Uses of isotopes:**
- **Uranium-235** is used as fuel in nuclear reactors (such as those at Tarapur and Kudankulam).
- An isotope of **cobalt (Co-60)** is used in treating cancer.
- An isotope of **iodine (I-131)** is used in the treatment of goitre.

**Isobars** are atoms of *different* elements with the *same mass number*, e.g. calcium (Z = 20) and argon (Z = 18), both with mass number 40.

**Did you know?** Not every isotope is radioactive; carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable, while carbon-14 is radioactive and is used to date ancient remains.

check.q: Why do isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties?
check.why: Chemical properties depend on electrons, and isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons, hence the same configuration.

rd-school-c9-science-a.tissues.title: Tissues
rd-school-c9-science-a.tissues.subtitle: How trillions of cells team up into the fabrics of plants and animals

sections.h: 1. From one cell to teams of cells
sections.md:
An *Amoeba* is a single cell that does everything — eats, moves, breathes, gets rid of waste. A mango tree or a human being cannot work like that. In multicellular organisms there are millions of cells, and most of them are **specialised** to carry out a few functions very efficiently. Muscle cells contract and relax to cause movement; nerve cells carry messages; blood flows to transport oxygen, food, hormones and wastes; in plants, vascular tissues conduct food and water from one part to another.

Cells specialising in one function are often grouped together in the body. **A group of cells that are similar in structure and/or work together to achieve a particular function forms a tissue.** Blood, phloem and muscle are tissues. This arrangement is called **division of labour**.

This chapter covers: why plant and animal tissues differ; **plant tissues** — meristematic and permanent (simple and complex); and **animal tissues** — epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.

check.q: A tissue is best described as:
options: a group of similar cells working together for a function
check.why: Tissues are groups of cells similar in structure and/or working together to perform a specific function.

sections.h: 2. Are plants and animals made of the same types of tissues?
sections.md:
Compare a neem tree and a dog.

- **Plants are stationary** — they do not move. Since they have to be upright, they have a large quantity of **supportive tissue**, most of which is **dead** (dead cells can give mechanical strength as easily as live ones and need less maintenance).
- **Animals move around** in search of food, mates and shelter. They consume more energy. Most of their tissues are **living**.
- **Growth pattern**: plant growth is **limited to certain regions** (tips of roots and shoots, etc.), where dividing tissues stay throughout life. Cell growth in animals is **more uniform** — there is no such demarcation of dividing and non-dividing regions.
- **Organisation**: the structural organisation of organs and organ systems is **far more specialised and localised in complex animals** than in very complex plants. This fits their different ways of feeding — plants make their own food and stay put; animals must hunt or graze and react quickly.

check.q: Why do plants have a lot of dead supportive tissue?
options: They are stationary and need strength to stand upright; dead cells need less maintenance
check.why: Being fixed and upright, plants need much mechanical support, which dead tissues provide efficiently.

sections.md:
**Activity (onion roots).** Place two onion bulbs over two glass jars of water so the roots grow into the water. After a few days, cut 1 cm off the tips of the roots of the second onion. Measure the roots of both onions daily for five days. Roots of the first keep growing; roots of the cut onion stop growing in length. The growing region was at the very tip.

The growth of plants occurs only in certain specific regions, because the dividing tissue — **meristematic tissue** — is located only at these points. Depending on where they are present, meristems are:

1. **Apical meristem** — at the **growing tips of stems and roots**; increases the **length**.
2. **Lateral meristem (cambium)** — on the sides; increases the **girth** (thickness) of the stem or root.
3. **Intercalary meristem** — at the **base of leaves or internodes** (on either side of the node) on twigs; seen clearly in grasses and bamboo, which regrow after grazing or mowing.

**Features of meristematic cells:** very **active**, with **dense cytoplasm**, **thin cellulose walls** and **prominent nuclei**; they **lack vacuoles** (vacuoles give rigidity and storage — meristems need neither, as they must divide quickly).

As new cells are produced, they take up a specific role and **lose the ability to divide**, forming **permanent tissue**. This process of taking up a permanent shape, size and function is called **differentiation**.

check.q: Which meristem increases the girth of a stem?

sections.md:
**Activity.** Take a thin cross-section of a stem, stain it with safranin, mount it in glycerine and observe. You see several types of cells — the different permanent tissues.

### Parenchyma
A few layers of cells form the basic **packing tissue**. Cells are **relatively unspecialised**, **living**, with **thin cell walls**, **loosely arranged** with **large intercellular spaces**. Functions: support and **storage of food**.
- **Chlorenchyma**: parenchyma containing **chlorophyll** — performs photosynthesis.
- **Aerenchyma**: in **aquatic plants**, large air cavities in parenchyma help them **float**.

### Collenchyma
Gives **flexibility** to plants and allows easy bending of parts like the **tendrils** and **stems of climbers** without breaking. Also provides mechanical support. Found in **leaf stalks below the epidermis**. Cells are **living, elongated** and **irregularly thickened at the corners**; very little intercellular space.

### Sclerenchyma
Makes the plant **hard and stiff**. The husk of a **coconut** is made of sclerenchymatous tissue. Cells are **dead**, **long and narrow**, with walls **thickened due to lignin** (a chemical substance acting like cement). Often walls are so thick that there is **no internal space** inside the cell. Present in **stems, around vascular bundles, in the veins of leaves and in the hard covering of seeds and nuts**. Gives strength. Jute and coir fibres are sclerenchyma.

### Protective tissues: epidermis
The outermost layer of cells is the **epidermis**, usually a **single layer**. In plants of very dry habitats it may be thicker, to protect against water loss. The entire surface is covered with it; it **protects all parts of the plant**. Outer epidermal cells often secrete a **waxy, water-resistant layer** on their outer surface — aiding protection against **loss of water, mechanical injury and invasion by parasitic fungi**. Cells form a **continuous layer without intercellular spaces**.

- **Stomata**: small pores in the epidermis of the leaf, enclosed by two kidney-shaped **guard cells**. Needed for **gas exchange** with the atmosphere and for **transpiration** (loss of water as water vapour).
- Epidermal cells of **roots**, whose function is absorbing water, bear long hair-like parts (**root hairs**) that greatly increase the absorptive surface.
- In desert plants, the epidermis has a thick waxy coating of **cutin** (a waterproof chemical).

### Protective tissues: cork
As plants grow older, the outer protective tissue undergoes changes. A strip of **secondary meristem** replaces the epidermis of the stem. Cells on the outside are cut off from this layer, forming the **several-layer thick cork** or the **bark** of the tree. Cork cells are **dead**, **compactly arranged** without intercellular spaces, and have a chemical called **suberin** in their walls that makes them **impervious to gases and water**. Bottle corks are made from the bark of the cork oak.

check.q: The husk of a coconut is made of:
check.why: Coconut husk consists of dead, lignified sclerenchyma fibres that make it hard and strong.

sections.h: 5. Permanent tissue — complex tissues (xylem and phloem)
sections.md:
Simple tissues are made of one type of cell. **Complex tissues** are made of **more than one type of cells**, all coordinating to perform a common function. **Xylem and phloem** are complex tissues; they are **conducting (vascular) tissues** and together form a **vascular bundle**. Vascular tissue is a distinctive feature of complex plants and has made their survival on land possible.

### Xylem
Conducts **water and minerals** **vertically upwards** from roots to other parts. It consists of:
- **Tracheids** and **vessels** — tubular structures with thick walls; **many are dead** when mature. They transport water and minerals.
- **Xylem parenchyma** — stores food.
- **Xylem fibres** — mainly supportive.

### Phloem
Transports **food** (made in leaves) **from leaves to other parts** of the plant — and, unlike xylem, it can move material **in both directions**. It is made of:
- **Sieve tubes** — tubular cells with **perforated walls** (sieve plates).
- **Companion cells**.
- **Phloem fibres**.
- **Phloem parenchyma**.

Except for **phloem fibres**, phloem cells are **living cells**.

**Did you know?** When you see 'rings' in a cut log, each ring is a year's growth of xylem made by the cambium — counting them tells the tree's age.

left.title: Xylem
points: Tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres

right.title: Phloem
points: Sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres
Sieve plates allow flow between cells

check.q: Which of these is a dead component of phloem?
check.why: All phloem cells are living except the phloem fibres, which are dead.

sections.md:
When we breathe, our chest moves; this is due to muscle tissue. The oxygen we breathe is carried by blood — a connective tissue. Messages travel through nervous tissue. Let us look at the four types, starting with **epithelial tissue**.

**Epithelium** forms the **covering or protective tissue** in the animal body. It covers most organs and cavities within the body and forms a **barrier to keep different body systems separate**. Skin, the lining of the mouth, the lining of blood vessels, lung alveoli and kidney tubules are all made of epithelium.

**Features:** cells are **tightly packed** and form a **continuous sheet**; there is **little cementing material** between them and **almost no intercellular space**. Anything entering or leaving the body must cross at least one layer of epithelium, so the **permeability** of the cells plays an important role in exchange between the body and the outside, and between body parts. A fibrous **basement membrane** separates epithelium from the tissue below.

**Types:**
1. **Simple squamous epithelium** — extremely **thin and flat** cells forming a delicate lining. Lines **blood vessels** and **lung alveoli**, where transport by diffusion happens through a selectively permeable surface. Also the lining of the **oesophagus and mouth**.
2. **Stratified squamous epithelium** — the **skin** epithelium, where cells are arranged in **many layers** to prevent wear and tear.
3. **Columnar epithelium** — tall, pillar-like cells; found in the **inner lining of the intestine**, where absorption and secretion occur. Where it bears **cilia** (hair-like projections) — **ciliated columnar epithelium** — as in the **respiratory tract**, the cilia beat and push mucus forward to clear it.
4. **Cuboidal epithelium** — cube-shaped cells; forms the lining of **kidney tubules and ducts of salivary glands**, providing mechanical support.
5. **Glandular epithelium** — epithelial cells often acquire extra specialisation as **gland cells**, which secrete substances at the epithelial surface. Sometimes a portion of epithelium **folds inward** and a **multicellular gland** forms.

check.q: The lining of lung alveoli is made of:
check.why: Alveoli need a very thin lining for gas diffusion, so they are lined by simple squamous epithelium.

sections.md:
Cells of connective tissue are **loosely spaced** and **embedded in an intercellular matrix**. The matrix may be **jelly-like, fluid, dense or rigid**, and its nature differs with the function of the tissue. Connective tissue connects, binds and supports.

1. **Blood** — has a fluid (liquid) matrix called **plasma**, in which **red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs)** and **platelets** are suspended. Plasma also contains proteins, salts and hormones. Blood flows and **transports gases, digested food, hormones and waste** materials to different parts of the body.
2. **Bone** — a **strong and non-flexible** tissue. It forms the **framework** that supports the body, anchors the muscles and supports the main organs. Bone cells are embedded in a **hard matrix** composed of **calcium and phosphorus** compounds.
3. **Ligament** — connects **bone to bone**. It is **very elastic** and has considerable strength, with very little matrix.
4. **Tendon** — connects **muscle to bone**. Fibrous tissue with **great strength but limited flexibility**.
5. **Cartilage** — has **widely spaced cells**; the solid matrix is made of **proteins and sugars**. It **smoothens bone surfaces at joints**, and is present in the **nose, ear, trachea and larynx**. Fold the cartilage of your ear: it bends; try the bones of your arm: they do not!
6. **Areolar connective tissue** — found **between the skin and muscles, around blood vessels and nerves**, and in the **bone marrow**. It **fills the space inside organs, supports internal organs** and helps in **repair of tissues**.
7. **Adipose tissue** — **fat-storing** tissue found **below the skin and between internal organs**. Its cells are filled with **fat globules**; storage of fat also lets it act as an **insulator**.

**Did you know?** A sprained ankle usually means an injured ligament — which is why doctors advise rest; ligaments heal slowly.

check.q: Which tissue connects a muscle to a bone?
check.why: Tendons are strong fibrous tissues joining muscles to bones; ligaments join bones to bones.

sections.md:
**Muscular tissue** consists of **elongated cells**, also called **muscle fibres**. It is responsible for **movement** in our body. Muscles contain special proteins called **contractile proteins**, which **contract and relax** to cause movement.

| Feature | Striated (skeletal) | Smooth (unstriated) | Cardiac |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | Voluntary — we move them at will | Involuntary | Involuntary |
| Location | Attached to bones (limbs) | Iris of eye, ureters, bronchi of lungs, alimentary canal, blood vessels | Heart |
| Cell shape | Long, cylindrical, unbranched | Long, spindle-shaped (pointed ends) | Cylindrical, branched |
| Nuclei | Many (multinucleate) | One (uninucleate) | One (uninucleate) |
| Striations | Alternate light and dark bands | None | Faint |
| Fatigue | Tire quickly | Slow | Rhythmic contraction and relaxation **throughout life** |

- **Striated muscles** are also called **skeletal muscles** because they are mostly attached to bones and help in body movement. Under the microscope they show **alternate light and dark bands** (striations).
- **Smooth muscles** control movements we cannot start or stop at will: movement of food in the alimentary canal, contraction and relaxation of blood vessels.
- **Cardiac muscles** of the heart show **rhythmic contraction and relaxation** from before birth till death — about 70 times a minute at rest.

check.q: Which muscle works rhythmically throughout life without tiring?
check.why: Cardiac muscle of the heart contracts and relaxes rhythmically from before birth until death.

sections.md:
All cells can respond to stimuli. However, cells of **nervous tissue** are **highly specialised** for being **stimulated and then transmitting the stimulus very rapidly** from one place to another within the body. The **brain, spinal cord and nerves** are all composed of nervous tissue.

The cells are called **nerve cells or neurons**. A neuron consists of:
- a **cell body** with a **nucleus and cytoplasm**,
- many short, branched parts called **dendrites**, which receive signals,
- usually one long part, the **axon**, which carries the signal away.

An individual nerve cell may be up to **a metre long**. Many nerve fibres bound together by connective tissue make up a **nerve**.

The signal that passes along a nerve fibre is called a **nerve impulse**. Nerve impulses allow us to **move our muscles when we want to**. The **combination of nerve and muscle tissue** is fundamental to most animals; it enables them to move rapidly in response to stimuli — like pulling your hand away from a hot tawa.

**Did you know?** Plant tissues and animal tissues are arranged into **organs** (leaf, heart) and **organ systems** (shoot system, digestive system) — the next levels of organisation after tissues: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.

check.why: The axon is usually a single long extension carrying the nerve impulse away from the cell body.

summary: A tissue is a group of cells similar in structure and/or function; tissues allow division of labour.
Plants are stationary with much dead support tissue and localised growth; animals move and have mostly living tissues.
Meristematic tissue divides: apical (length), lateral/cambium (girth), intercalary (at nodes, e.g. grasses).
Meristem cells: dense cytoplasm, thin walls, prominent nucleus, no vacuoles; they differentiate into permanent tissue.
Simple permanent tissues: parenchyma (storage; chlorenchyma, aerenchyma), collenchyma (flexibility), sclerenchyma (dead, lignified, strength).
Epidermis protects, has stomata with guard cells and root hairs; cork (with suberin) replaces it in old stems.
Complex tissues: xylem (water upward — tracheids, vessels, parenchyma, fibres) and phloem (food both ways — sieve tubes, companion cells, parenchyma, fibres).
Animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.
Epithelium: squamous (simple, stratified), columnar (ciliated), cuboidal and glandular.
Connective tissue: blood, bone, ligament, tendon, cartilage, areolar and adipose — cells in a matrix.
Muscle: striated (voluntary), smooth (involuntary), cardiac (rhythmic, branched).
Nervous tissue: neurons with cell body, dendrites and axon carry nerve impulses.
