rd-school-c9-science-a.tissues-2.title: Tissues (part 2)
rd-school-c9-science-a.tissues-2.subtitle: The root-tip activity, stomata and epidermis up close, comparison tables and exam practice

sections.h: 10. The onion-root activity: where does growth happen?
sections.md:
Take two glass jars of water and place an onion on each so that its base touches the water. Let roots grow for a few days. Measure root length on day 1, 2 and 3. On day 4, **cut about 1 cm from the tips of the roots of the onion in jar 2**. Keep measuring both sets for five more days.

**What you find:** roots in jar 1 keep growing; roots in jar 2 stop growing (or barely grow). The tips contained the **apical meristem**, the dividing tissue responsible for increase in length. Remove it and growth in length stops.

This activity sets up the chapter's point that **plant growth is limited to certain regions**, while animal growth is more uniform. Plants are mostly stationary, and much of their body is **dead supportive tissue** (like sclerenchyma and xylem); animals move to find food and shelter, so they need more energy and most of their tissues are **living**. Animal organs also tend to be more specialised and localised than plant tissues.

**Where meristem lives:**
- **Apical** — tips of stems and roots → length.
- **Lateral (cambium)** — sides → girth (thickness).
- **Intercalary** — base of leaves or internodes, e.g. in grasses → regrowth after grazing or mowing.

check.q: Why did roots stop growing after their tips were cut off?
check.why: Growth in length comes from dividing cells of the apical meristem at the root tip, so removing the tip stops it.

sections.h: 11. Protective tissues: epidermis, stomata and cork
sections.md:
**Epidermis** is the outermost single layer of cells covering a plant. On aerial parts it often secretes a waxy, water-resistant layer that protects against water loss, mechanical injury and fungal attack. Desert plants have a thick waxy **cutin** coat. Epidermal cells of roots carry long hair-like extensions (**root hairs**) that greatly increase the area for absorbing water.

**Stomata** are small pores in the epidermis of the leaf, each enclosed by two kidney-shaped **guard cells**. They are needed for exchange of gases with the atmosphere and for **transpiration** (loss of water as vapour), which pulls water up and cools the leaf.

**Activity.** Peel the lower surface of a *Rhoeo* leaf (or any fleshy leaf), mount it in water with safranin and observe the guard cells and pores.

**Cork.** As trees age, a strip of secondary meristem replaces the epidermis of the stem, forming several layers of thick, dead cells — the **bark**. Cork cells are dead, compactly arranged without intercellular spaces, and have a substance called **suberin** in their walls that makes them impervious to gases and water. Cork from the cork oak is used for bottle stoppers, notice boards and sports balls.
keyTerms: Stomata — leaf pores with guard cells
Transpiration — water loss as vapour from leaves
Suberin — waterproofing chemical in cork walls

check.q: Which chemical makes cork cells impermeable to water and gases?
check.why: Cork cell walls are impregnated with suberin, so water and gases cannot pass through.

sections.md:
**Simple permanent tissues:**

| Tissue | Cells | Wall | Job | Where |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parenchyma | living, loosely packed, large spaces | thin, cellulose | storage, food; with chloroplasts = chlorenchyma; with air cavities = aerenchyma (floating in water plants) | soft parts of plant |
| Collenchyma | living, elongated | thick at corners | flexibility, mechanical support | leaf stalks, below epidermis |
| Sclerenchyma | dead, long, narrow | thick, lignified | strength, hardness | husk of coconut, veins, seed coats, jute fibres |

**Muscles:**

| Feature | Striated (skeletal) | Smooth (unstriated) | Cardiac |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | voluntary | involuntary | involuntary |
| Shape | long, cylindrical, unbranched | spindle-shaped | cylindrical, branched |
| Nuclei | many | one | one |
| Bands | light and dark | none | faint |
| Where | limbs, attached to bones | gut, iris, ureters, bronchi | heart |

**Xylem vs phloem:** xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres) carries water and minerals upward and is mostly dead; phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres, phloem parenchyma) carries food both ways and is mostly living — only phloem fibres are dead.

**Connective tissue quick list:** blood (plasma + RBC, WBC, platelets), bone (hard, calcium and phosphorus in matrix), ligament (bone to bone, elastic), tendon (muscle to bone, strong, limited flexibility), cartilage (smoothens joints; nose, ear, trachea), areolar (fills space in organs, repairs tissue), adipose (fat storage, insulation).

check.q: Which tissue connects a muscle to a bone?
check.why: Tendons are fibrous tissues of great strength that join skeletal muscles to bones.

steps: Many nuclei and unbranched cylindrical cells confirm skeletal muscle.
It is voluntary and attached to bones.
workedExamples.answer: Striated (skeletal) muscle, found in the limbs.

workedExamples.q: Why can water hyacinth float on water?
steps: Its stems and leaves contain parenchyma with large air cavities.

rd-school-c9-science-b.motion.title: Motion
rd-school-c9-science-b.motion.subtitle: From a Rajdhani pulling out of Howrah to a satellite circling Earth — describing how things move

sections.h: 1. Is it moving? It depends who's asking
sections.md:
You sit in a train at Howrah. The train on the next track starts sliding past, and for a moment you feel *your* train is moving. Then you look at the platform and realise you are still. Motion, it turns out, is not as obvious as it seems.

We see birds fly, a dog run, clouds drift, leaves fall. Some motion we infer: air moving because the leaves sway; the Earth spinning and orbiting because of day, night and seasons — though we feel nothing. Sitting in a moving bus, you are **at rest** with respect to your seat but **in motion** with respect to the trees outside.

To describe the position of an object we need a **reference point**, called the **origin**. 'The school is 2 km north of the railway station' uses the station as the reference point. **An object is in motion if its position changes with time with respect to a reference point.**

This chapter covers: describing motion (distance, displacement, uniform and non-uniform motion); speed and velocity; acceleration; distance–time and velocity–time graphs; the three equations of motion; and uniform circular motion.

check.q: A passenger sitting in a moving bus is at rest with respect to:
check.why: The passenger's position does not change relative to the seat, so relative to it he is at rest.

sections.h: 2. Motion along a straight line — distance and displacement
sections.md:
The simplest motion is along a straight line. Let an object start from O, go to C, and come back to B on a straight road, where OA = … let us use numbers. O is at 0 km, B at 25 km, C at 60 km.

Object goes O → C → B.

- **Distance** travelled = OC + CB = 60 + 35 = **95 km**. Distance is the **actual length of the path** covered. It needs only a **numerical value** (magnitude) — it is a **scalar**.
- **Displacement** = the **shortest distance** from the initial to the final position = OB = **25 km**, in the direction from O to B. It needs both **magnitude and direction** — it is a **vector**.

Important cases:
- Displacement can be **equal** to distance (motion in one direction along a straight line, O → C: both 60 km).
- Displacement is **less than or equal to** distance, never more.
- If the object returns to its starting point, **displacement = 0** though distance is not zero. A runner completing one lap of a 400 m track covers 400 m distance with zero displacement.

**Example.** A farmer walks around a square field of side 10 m in 40 s. What is the magnitude of his displacement after 2 min 20 s? Time = 140 s. In 40 s he walks 40 m (one round), so his speed is 1 m/s, and in 140 s he walks 140 m = 3 rounds (120 m) + 20 m — two sides more. He is now at the corner diagonally opposite to the start. Displacement = √(10² + 10²) = 10√2 ≈ **14.1 m**.

### Uniform and non-uniform motion
- **Uniform motion**: an object covers **equal distances in equal intervals of time**, however small the intervals — e.g. a car on an expressway on cruise control at a steady 80 km/h in a straight line.
- **Non-uniform motion**: **unequal distances in equal intervals** — a car in city traffic, a person jogging in a park, a ball rolling down a slope.

check.q: An athlete completes one full lap of a circular track of circumference 400 m. His displacement is:
check.why: He ends where he started, so the shortest distance between initial and final positions is zero.

sections.h: 3. Measuring the rate of motion — speed
sections.md:
A bus from Pune to Mumbai and a car on the same road may cover the same distance in different times. To compare, we use **speed**: **the distance travelled by an object in unit time**.

**Speed = distance ÷ time**; SI unit **metre per second (m/s or m s⁻¹)**. Other units: cm/s, km/h.

Most objects move non-uniformly, so we use **average speed**:

**Average speed = total distance travelled ÷ total time taken.**

**Example 1.** An object travels 16 m in 4 s and then another 16 m in 2 s. Average speed = (16 + 16)/(4 + 2) = 32/6 = **5.33 m/s**. (Note: it is *not* the average of 4 m/s and 8 m/s, which would be 6 m/s.)

**Example 2.** The odometer of a car reads 2000 km at the start of a trip and 2400 km at the end. The trip took 8 h. Average speed = 400/8 = **50 km/h**. In m/s: 50 × 1000/3600 = **13.9 m/s**.

**Unit conversion trick:** 1 km/h = 1000 m/3600 s = **5/18 m/s**. So 72 km/h = 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s; 10 m/s = 10 × 18/5 = 36 km/h.

**Example 3.** Usha swims in a 90 m long pool. She covers 180 m in one minute by swimming from one end to the other and back. Average speed = 180/60 = **3 m/s**; average velocity = 0 (she is back where she started).

check.q: 72 km/h equals:
check.why: Multiply by 5/18: 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s.

sections.md:
Speed does not tell us the direction. A cyclist going north at 5 m/s and one going south at 5 m/s have the same speed but are moving very differently.

**Velocity** is the **speed of an object moving in a definite direction** — more precisely, **displacement per unit time**. Velocity is a **vector**; speed is a scalar. SI unit: m/s.

The velocity of an object can be changed by changing its **speed**, its **direction**, or **both**.

When velocity changes uniformly, the **average velocity** is the arithmetic mean of the initial and final velocities:

**v_av = (u + v)/2**, where u = initial velocity, v = final velocity.

**Example.** A car's velocity increases uniformly from 18 km/h to 36 km/h. In m/s: u = 5 m/s, v = 10 m/s. v_av = (5 + 10)/2 = 7.5 m/s.

**Speed vs velocity — quick comparison**

| Speed | Velocity |
|---|---|
| Distance/time | Displacement/time |
| Scalar | Vector |
| Always positive (or zero) | Can be positive, negative or zero |
| Average speed ≥ magnitude of average velocity | Average velocity can be zero for a round trip |

check.q: Which of these can be zero while speed is not zero (for a journey)?
check.why: If the object returns to the start, displacement and hence average velocity are zero, though distance and speed are not.

sections.h: 5. Rate of change of velocity — acceleration
sections.md:
When a Mumbai local train pulls out of Dadar, its velocity increases; as it approaches Bandra, it slows down. **Acceleration** is a measure of the **change in velocity of an object per unit time**:

**a = (v − u)/t**

SI unit: **m/s² (m s⁻²)**.

- If acceleration is in the **direction of velocity**, it is **positive** (speeding up).
- If it is **opposite** to velocity, it is **negative** — called **retardation** or deceleration (slowing down).
- **Uniform acceleration**: velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time — e.g. a freely falling body, or a ball rolling down a smooth slope.
- **Non-uniform acceleration**: velocity changes by unequal amounts — e.g. a car in city traffic.

**Example 4.** Rahul pedals his bicycle from rest and reaches 6 m/s in 30 s. Then he brakes, and velocity falls to 4 m/s in the next 5 s. Acceleration in the first case: (6 − 0)/30 = **0.2 m/s²**. In the second: (4 − 6)/5 = **−0.4 m/s²** (retardation).

**Example 5.** A bus decreases its speed from 80 km/h to 60 km/h in 5 s. u = 80 × 5/18 = 22.22 m/s; v = 60 × 5/18 = 16.67 m/s. a = (16.67 − 22.22)/5 = **−1.11 m/s²**.

**Example 6.** A train starting from a railway station attains a speed of 40 km/h (11.11 m/s) in 10 minutes (600 s). a = 11.11/600 ≈ **0.0185 m/s²**.

check.q: A car slows from 20 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 s. Its acceleration is:
check.why: a = (v − u)/t = (10 − 20)/5 = −2 m/s², a retardation.

sections.md:
Graphs show at a glance how motion changes. For a **distance–time graph**, time goes on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis.

- **Uniform speed** → a **straight line** sloping upward. Distance is directly proportional to time. The **slope** of the line = **speed**: from two points (t₁, s₁) and (t₂, s₂), v = (s₂ − s₁)/(t₂ − t₁).
- **Non-uniform speed (accelerated motion)** → a **curve** (getting steeper as speed increases).
- **At rest** → a **horizontal line** parallel to the time axis — distance does not change.

**Example (table to graph).** A car's distance at 8:00, 8:15, 8:30, 8:45, 9:00 am is 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 km. Plot: straight line. Slope = 40 km/1 h = 40 km/h.

If instead the distances were 0, 1, 4, 9, 16 m at t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 s, the graph is a curve rising ever more steeply — accelerated motion.

sections.md:
On a **velocity–time graph**, time is on the x-axis and velocity on the y-axis.

- **Uniform velocity** → a **horizontal line** parallel to the time axis.
- **Uniform acceleration** → a **straight line sloping upward**. The **slope = acceleration**.
- **Uniform retardation** → a straight line sloping **downward**.
- **Non-uniform acceleration** → a curve.

**The area under a v–t graph = displacement (distance for motion in one direction).**

*Uniform velocity:* a car moves at 40 km/h for 2 h. The area of the rectangle = 40 × 2 = **80 km**.

*Uniform acceleration:* a car accelerates from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s. The area is a triangle = ½ × 10 × 20 = **100 m**.

If it starts at u and reaches v in time t, the area is a **trapezium** = rectangle (u × t) + triangle (½ × (v − u) × t).

**Example.** A train's velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 30 m/s in 20 s, stays at 30 m/s for 40 s, then falls uniformly to 0 in 30 s. Distance = ½ × 20 × 30 + 30 × 40 + ½ × 30 × 30 = 300 + 1200 + 450 = **1950 m**. Accelerations: 30/20 = 1.5 m/s², 0, and −30/30 = −1 m/s².

sections.h: 8. Equations of motion by the graphical method
sections.md:
For an object moving along a straight line with **uniform acceleration**, three equations connect velocity, position, acceleration and time. Let initial velocity = u, final velocity = v, time = t, acceleration = a, displacement = s.

Consider a v–t graph: the line goes from point A (0, u) to point B (t, v). Drop BC perpendicular to the time axis, and draw AD parallel to the time axis meeting BC at D. O is the origin, so OA = u, BC = v, OC = t, and BD = v − u.

### First equation: v = u + at (velocity–time relation)
Acceleration = slope = BD/AD = (v − u)/t. So v − u = at, giving **v = u + at**.

### Second equation: s = ut + ½at² (position–time relation)
Displacement = area of trapezium OABC = area of rectangle OADC + area of triangle ABD = (u × t) + ½ × t × (v − u) = ut + ½ × t × at, so **s = ut + ½at²**.

### Third equation: v² = u² + 2as (position–velocity relation)
Area of trapezium = ½ × (OA + BC) × OC = ½ (u + v) t. From the first equation, t = (v − u)/a. So s = ½ (u + v)(v − u)/a = (v² − u²)/2a, giving **v² = u² + 2as**.

**Example 7.** A train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 0.1 m/s² for 2 minutes. u = 0, a = 0.1, t = 120 s. v = 0 + 0.1 × 120 = **12 m/s**. s = ½ × 0.1 × 120² = 0.05 × 14400 = **720 m**.

**Example 8.** The brakes applied to a car produce an acceleration of 6 m/s² opposite to its motion. If the car takes 2 s to stop, how far does it travel? a = −6, t = 2, v = 0. u = v − at = 0 + 12 = 12 m/s. s = ut + ½at² = 24 − 12 = **12 m**. *This is why drivers must keep a safe distance.*

**Example 9.** A car accelerates uniformly from 18 km/h (5 m/s) to 36 km/h (10 m/s) in 5 s. a = (10 − 5)/5 = **1 m/s²**; s = 5 × 5 + ½ × 1 × 25 = **37.5 m**.

**Example 10.** A stone is thrown vertically upward with 5 m/s; it decelerates at 10 m/s². How high does it go and how long does it take? At top v = 0. v² = u² + 2as ⇒ 0 = 25 − 20s ⇒ s = **1.25 m**. t = (0 − 5)/(−10) = **0.5 s**.

sections.md:
When the velocity of an object changes, it is accelerating — and velocity changes if **direction** changes, even at constant speed.

Imagine an athlete running along a closed path of a **rectangular** track at constant speed: he changes direction only at the four corners. On a **hexagonal** track, six times; an octagon, eight times. As the number of sides increases, the track becomes a **circle**, and the athlete changes direction **at every point**.

When an object moves along a circular path at **uniform speed**, the motion is **uniform circular motion**. Its velocity changes continuously in direction, so it is an **accelerated motion**.

**Speed in circular motion:** if a body takes time t to go once around a circle of radius r, v = **2πr/t** (circumference ÷ time).

**Activity (stone on a thread).** Tie a stone to a thread and whirl it in a horizontal circle. Release the thread: the stone flies off **along a straight line tangent** to the circle at the point of release. This shows that at every instant the direction of motion is along the tangent. Sparks from a knife sharpener's grinding wheel fly off tangentially for the same reason; an athlete releases the hammer or discus at the right moment so it flies in the desired direction.

Examples: the Moon around the Earth, artificial satellites in circular orbits, a cyclist on a circular track at constant speed, the tip of a clock's second hand.

**Example 11.** An artificial satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 42,250 km and takes 24 h per revolution. v = 2 × 3.14 × 42,250/24 = 265,330/24 ≈ **11,055 km/h ≈ 3.07 km/s**. (Such 'geostationary' satellites keep pace with the Earth's rotation — India's INSAT/GSAT satellites use these orbits for TV and weather.)

rd-school-c9-social-a.ch1-french-revolut.title: The French Revolution
rd-school-c9-social-a.ch1-french-revolut.subtitle: How hungry crowds, bold ideas and an empty treasury turned a kingdom upside down
tags: India and the Contemporary World I

sections.md:
Imagine Paris on the morning of **14 July 1789**. The city is tense. Rumours fly that the king has ordered troops to march in. Bread prices have shot up so high that a labourer spends most of a day's wage on a single loaf. About seven thousand men and women gather, arm themselves at the town hall, and march towards a grim old fortress-prison in the east of the city: the **Bastille**.

The Bastille held only seven prisoners that day. But it was hated as a symbol of the king's despotic power — a place where people could be locked up on the king's order without trial. In the fight that followed, the commander of the fortress was killed and the prisoners were released. Within days the fortress was being demolished, and people bought its broken stones as souvenirs.

Why does a school textbook in India begin its world history with this event? Because the ideas that came out of France in those years — **liberty, equality and fraternity**, the idea that power comes from the people and not from God-given kings, the idea of rights that belong to every human being — travelled across the world. They reached Indian thinkers like **Tipu Sultan** and **Raja Rammohan Roy**, and they shaped the language of freedom movements everywhere.

In this read we will follow the same path as your chapter:

1. French society at the end of the 18th century
2. The outbreak of the Revolution
3. France abolishes monarchy and becomes a republic
4. Did women have a revolution?
5. The abolition of slavery
6. The Revolution and everyday life
7. Napoleon, and the legacy of the Revolution

> *Did you know?* The 14th of July is still France's national day, celebrated with parades and fireworks.

sections.h: French society: three estates and one burden
sections.md:
In 1774 **Louis XVI** of the Bourbon family became king of France at the age of twenty, married to the Austrian princess **Marie Antoinette**. He inherited an empty treasury. Long wars had drained it — including France's help to the thirteen American colonies in their war of independence against Britain. France now owed more than **2 billion livres**, and lenders were charging 10 per cent interest. The court at Versailles was extravagant, and the cost of running the army, the government and the universities kept rising.

To pay for all this, the state needed taxes. But who paid them? French society was divided into **three estates**:

| Estate | Who | Share of population (approx.) | Paid taxes? |
|---|---|---|---|
| First | Clergy (church officials) | small | Exempt |
| Second | Nobility | small | Exempt |
| Third | Merchants, lawyers, officials, peasants, artisans, servants, labourers | about 97% | Paid everything |

The first two estates enjoyed **privileges by birth** — above all, exemption from taxes paid to the state. Nobles also enjoyed **feudal privileges**: peasants had to work in their houses and fields, serve in the army, or help build roads. The Church took its own tax, the **tithe** — one-tenth of agricultural produce. And every member of the third estate paid the direct state tax, the **taille**, plus indirect taxes on everyday goods like salt and tobacco.

Peasants made up about 90 per cent of the population, yet only a small number of them owned the land they tilled. About 60 per cent of the land was owned by nobles, the Church and richer members of the third estate.

**The struggle to survive.** France's population rose from about 23 million in 1715 to 28 million in 1789. More mouths meant more demand for food grains, and grain production could not keep pace. The price of bread — the staple diet of the majority — rose rapidly. Wages did not. Labourers working in workshops whose owners fixed wages could not keep up. When drought or hail ruined a harvest, the gap between rich and poor widened, and a **subsistence crisis** followed: people could not afford even the basic means of living.

**A growing middle class.** Earlier, peasants had sometimes rioted against taxes and food scarcity, but they lacked the means to change the whole social order. That leadership came from the **middle class** — people who had earned their wealth through overseas trade and the manufacture of goods like woollen and silk textiles, plus professionals such as lawyers and administrators. They were educated, and they believed no group should be privileged by birth. A person's position, they argued, should depend on **merit**.

sections.md:
The middle class did not invent its arguments out of thin air. It read the **philosophers** of the Enlightenment.

- **John Locke**, in *Two Treatises of Government*, attacked the idea of the divine and absolute right of a monarch.
- **Jean-Jacques Rousseau**, in *The Social Contract*, proposed a form of government based on a contract between people and their representatives.
- **Montesquieu**, in *The Spirit of the Laws*, proposed dividing power between the **legislative, executive and judiciary** — an idea put into practice in the government of the USA, whose new constitution and its guarantee of individual rights were an important example for French thinkers.

These ideas were discussed intensely in **salons** and **coffee-houses** and spread through books and newspapers. Because many people could not read, the texts were often read aloud in groups. So when news spread that Louis XVI planned to impose further taxes, there was anger and protest against privilege.

> *Think about it:* Montesquieu's separation of powers is present in India's Constitution too — Parliament makes laws, the executive carries them out, and courts judge disputes.
keyTerms: Enlightenment — 18th-century movement valuing reason, liberty and questioning tradition
Separation of powers — dividing government into legislature, executive and judiciary

sections.h: 1789: from the Estates General to the Bastille
sections.md:
**5 May 1789.** Louis XVI called together the **Estates General**, an old political body that the king could summon to approve new taxes. It had last met in 1614! The first and second estates sent 300 representatives each, seated in rows facing each other. The third estate's 600 members stood at the back. Peasants, artisans and women were denied entry altogether, though their grievances were listed in about 40,000 letters.

Voting had always been by estate: **each estate one vote**. So the two privileged estates could always outvote the third, 2 to 1. This time the third estate demanded **one member, one vote**, a democratic principle borrowed from Rousseau. When the king rejected this, the third-estate members walked out.

**20 June 1789.** They assembled in the indoor tennis court of Versailles and declared themselves the **National Assembly**. In the famous **Tennis Court Oath** they swore not to disperse until they had drafted a constitution for France that would limit the monarch's powers. They were led by **Mirabeau**, a nobleman who believed in ending feudal privilege, and **Abbé Sieyès**, a priest who wrote an influential pamphlet called *What is the Third Estate?*

While the Assembly worked at Versailles, the rest of France seethed. A severe winter had ruined the harvest; bread prices rose; bakers hoarded supplies. After hours in long queues, angry women stormed the shops. When the king ordered troops into Paris, the crowd stormed the **Bastille on 14 July**.

In the countryside, rumours spread that lords had hired bands of brigands to destroy ripe crops. Gripped by what historians call the **Great Fear**, peasants attacked châteaux, looted hoarded grain and burnt the documents that recorded their feudal dues. Many nobles fled, some to neighbouring countries.

Faced with the power of his revolting subjects, Louis XVI recognised the National Assembly and accepted that his powers would now be checked by a constitution. On the night of **4 August 1789**, the Assembly passed a decree **abolishing the feudal system** of obligations and taxes. The clergy lost their privileges, tithes were abolished, and lands owned by the Church were confiscated. The government acquired assets worth at least 2 billion livres.

sections.h: The Constitution of 1791 and the Rights of Man
sections.md:
The National Assembly completed a draft constitution in **1791**. Its main aim was to limit the powers of the monarch. Power was now separated and assigned to different institutions — legislature, executive and judiciary — making France a **constitutional monarchy**.

But who would vote? The constitution gave the power to make laws to the **National Assembly**, which was **indirectly elected**. Citizens voted for a group of electors, who in turn chose the Assembly. And not all citizens could vote:

- **Active citizens**: men above 25 years of age who paid taxes equal to at least 3 days of a labourer's wage. Only they could vote.
- **Passive citizens**: the remaining men and **all women**. No vote.
- To become an **elector** or a member of the Assembly, a man had to belong to the highest bracket of taxpayers.

So the Revolution's first constitution was, by today's standards, far from democratic. Still, it opened with a ringing **Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen**. Rights such as the right to life, freedom of speech, freedom of opinion and equality before law were declared **natural and inalienable** — belonging to every human being by birth and impossible to take away. It was the duty of the state to protect each citizen's natural rights.

**Reading the symbols.** Most people could not read, so revolutionaries used images to spread ideas:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Broken chain | Being freed (chains fettered slaves) |
| Bundle of rods (fasces) | Strength lies in unity |
| Eye within a triangle radiating light | Knowledge, the all-seeing eye dispelling ignorance |
| Sceptre | Royal power |
| Snake biting its tail | Eternity |
| Red Phrygian cap | Worn by a slave on becoming free |
| Blue-white-red | The national colours of France |
| Winged woman | Personification of the law |
| Law tablet | The law is the same for all |

> *Did you know?* Jean-Paul Marat, a journalist, wrote that the rich used the laws to keep the poor in their place — a sign that many felt the Revolution had not gone far enough.
keyTerms: Constitutional monarchy — a monarchy whose powers are limited by a constitution
Active citizen — tax-paying man over 25 with the right to vote
Inalienable — cannot be taken away

check.q: Under the 1791 Constitution, who could vote?
options: Men over 25 who paid a minimum tax
check.why: Only 'active citizens' — men above 25 paying taxes equal to at least three days' wages — had the right to vote.

sections.h: France becomes a republic; the Reign of Terror
sections.md:
Louis XVI had signed the Constitution, but he was secretly negotiating with the king of **Prussia** and other rulers who feared the revolution would spread. In April 1792 the National Assembly voted to declare **war against Prussia and Austria**. Thousands of volunteers joined the army. Marching to Paris, volunteers from Marseilles sang a patriotic song composed by Roget de L'Isle — the **Marseillaise**, today France's national anthem.

The war brought losses and economic hardship. Large sections of the population felt the revolution had to be carried further, since the 1791 Constitution gave rights only to the richer sections. **Political clubs** became meeting places. The most successful was the **Jacobin club**, named after the former convent of St Jacob in Paris. Its members were mainly from the less prosperous sections: small shopkeepers, artisans like shoemakers, pastry cooks, watch-makers and printers, servants and daily-wage workers. Its leader was **Maximilian Robespierre**.

Many Jacobins wore long striped trousers like dock workers, to set themselves apart from nobles who wore knee breeches. They were called **sans-culottes** — 'those without knee breeches'. Men wore the red cap of liberty; women were not allowed to.

In summer 1792 the Jacobins planned an insurrection of Parisians angered by food shortages. On **10 August** they stormed the Palace of the Tuileries, massacred the king's guards and held the king hostage. Elections followed in which **all men of 21 and above**, regardless of wealth, got the vote. The new assembly was called the **Convention**. On **21 September 1792** it abolished the monarchy and declared France a **republic** — a form of government where people elect the government, including its head, and there is no hereditary monarchy. Louis XVI was sentenced to death by a court for treason and executed publicly on **21 January 1793**; Queen Marie Antoinette met the same fate shortly after.

**The Reign of Terror (1793–1794).** Robespierre followed a policy of severe control and punishment. All those he saw as 'enemies' of the republic — ex-nobles, clergy, members of other political parties, even members of his own party who disagreed — were arrested, tried by a revolutionary tribunal and, if found guilty, guillotined. The **guillotine** was a device of two poles and a blade, named after Dr Guillotin who invented it.

Robespierre's government also issued laws placing a **maximum ceiling on wages and prices**. Meat and bread were rationed. Peasants had to sell grain at government-fixed prices. Expensive white flour was forbidden; everyone had to eat the *equality bread* made of wholewheat. Instead of Monsieur and Madame, people were addressed as **Citoyen** and **Citoyenne** (citizen). Churches were shut down and their buildings converted into barracks or offices.

Robespierre pursued his policies so relentlessly that even his supporters began to demand moderation. Finally he was convicted by a court in **July 1794**, arrested and guillotined.

**The Directory.** The fall of the Jacobins allowed the wealthier middle classes to seize power. A new constitution denied the vote to non-propertied sections. It provided for two elected legislative councils, which then appointed a **Directory** — an executive of five members — to guard against concentrating power in one man as under Jacobin rule. But Directors often clashed with the councils. The resulting political instability paved the way for a military dictator: **Napoleon Bonaparte**.

Priests who refused the new laws

sections.md:
From the very beginning, women were active participants. Most third-estate women worked for a living: as seamstresses or laundresses, selling flowers, fruits and vegetables at the market, or as domestic servants in wealthy homes. Most had no access to education or job training; only daughters of nobles or wealthy families could study at a convent and then be married off. Working women also had to care for their families — cooking, fetching water, queuing for bread, looking after children. Their wages were lower than men's.

To voice their interests, women started their own **political clubs and newspapers**. About sixty women's clubs came up in different French cities. The **Society of Revolutionary and Republican Women** was the most famous. A main demand was that women enjoy the **same political rights as men** — the right to vote, to be elected, and to hold political office.

The early revolutionary government did introduce laws that helped women:
- State schools were created and schooling became **compulsory for all girls**.
- Fathers could no longer force daughters into marriage against their will. Marriage became a contract entered into freely and registered under civil law.
- **Divorce** was made legal and could be applied for by both women and men.
- Women could now train for jobs, become artists or run small businesses.

But the fight for political rights continued. During the Reign of Terror, the new government issued laws ordering the **closure of women's clubs** and banning their political activities. Many prominent women were arrested, and a number of them executed. One of the best known, **Olympe de Gouges**, had written a *Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen*, which she addressed to the Queen and the Assembly asking them to act on it. In 1793 she criticised the Jacobin government for forcibly closing down women's clubs; she was tried by the National Convention, charged with treason and executed.

Women's movements for voting rights continued across the world through the next 150 years. It was only in **1946** that women in France finally won the right to vote.

> *Compare:* In India, the Constitution gave every adult citizen — woman or man — the vote from the very first general election in 1951–52.

check.q: When did women in France finally get the right to vote?
check.why: Despite their active role in the Revolution, French women won the vote only in 1946.

sections.md:
One of the most revolutionary social reforms of the Jacobin regime was the **abolition of slavery in the French colonies**. The Caribbean colonies — **Martinique, Guadeloupe and San Domingo** — supplied tobacco, indigo, sugar and coffee. But Europeans were reluctant to go and work in distant, unfamiliar lands, so there was a shortage of labour on the plantations.

This was met by the **triangular slave trade** between Europe, Africa and the Americas, which began in the 17th century. French merchants sailed from ports like **Bordeaux and Nantes** to the African coast, where they bought enslaved people from local chieftains. Branded and shackled, the enslaved were packed tightly into ships for the three-month voyage across the Atlantic to the Caribbean, where they were sold to plantation owners. Their labour met the growing European demand for sugar, coffee and indigo. Port cities like Bordeaux and Nantes owed their economic prosperity to the flourishing trade.

Throughout the 18th century there was little criticism of slavery in France. The National Assembly held long debates about whether the rights of man should be extended to all French subjects, including those in the colonies, but it did not pass any laws, fearing opposition from businessmen whose incomes depended on the trade.

It was finally the **Convention** which in **1794** legislated to free all slaves in the French overseas possessions. This, however, turned out to be short-term: ten years later **Napoleon reintroduced slavery**. Plantation owners understood their freedom as including the right to enslave African Negroes in pursuit of their economic interests. Slavery was finally abolished in French colonies in **1848**.

sections.h: Everyday life, Napoleon and the legacy
sections.md:
**The Revolution and everyday life.** Could politics change the clothes people wore, the language they spoke or the books they read? The years after 1789 saw many such changes. One important law, soon after the storming of the Bastille in summer 1789, was the **abolition of censorship**. In the Old Regime, all written material and cultural activities — books, newspapers, plays — could be published or performed only after approval by the king's censors. Now the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen proclaimed **freedom of speech and expression** a natural right.

Newspapers, pamphlets, books and printed pictures flooded the towns of France, and from there spread rapidly into the countryside. They described and discussed the events and changes taking place. Freedom of the press also meant that opposing views could be expressed. Each side sought to convince others through print. Plays, songs and festive processions attracted large numbers of people — a way they could grasp and identify with ideas like liberty or justice that political philosophers wrote about at length in texts only a handful of educated people could read.

**Napoleon.** In **1804**, Napoleon Bonaparte crowned himself **Emperor of France**. He set out to conquer neighbouring European countries, dispossessing dynasties and creating kingdoms where he placed members of his family. Napoleon saw his role as a moderniser of Europe. He introduced many laws such as the **protection of private property** and a **uniform system of weights and measures** provided by the **decimal system**. Initially many saw him as a liberator who would bring freedom to the people. But soon his armies came to be viewed everywhere as an invading force. He was finally defeated at **Waterloo in 1815**. Many of his measures that carried revolutionary ideas of liberty and modern laws to other parts of Europe had an impact on people long after he had gone.

**The legacy.** The ideas of **liberty and democratic rights** were the most important legacy of the French Revolution. These spread from France to the rest of Europe during the 19th century, where feudal systems were abolished. Colonised peoples reworked the idea of freedom from bondage into their movements to create a sovereign nation state. Tipu Sultan and Rammohan Roy are two examples of individuals who responded to the ideas coming from revolutionary France. Tipu is remembered for having planted a 'tree of liberty' in his capital, Seringapatam, and for joining a Jacobin club — a story historians cite from French records; and Rammohan Roy admired the Revolution's ideals so much that, on his way to England in 1830–31, he is said to have insisted on visiting a French ship flying the revolutionary flag.

> *Did you know?* The metre and the kilogram — the units you use in every science class — come from the decimal metric system first created in revolutionary France in the 1790s.

workedExamples.q: Explain the circumstances that led to the outbreak of revolutionary protest in France.
steps: Empty treasury: wars, including help to the American colonies, left a debt of over 2 billion livres.
Unfair taxes: only the third estate paid; the clergy and nobility were exempt.
Subsistence crisis: population grew from 23 to 28 million; bread prices rose faster than wages.
New ideas: Locke, Rousseau and Montesquieu questioned divine right and privilege, discussed in salons and coffee-houses.
Trigger: the Estates General of 1789 refused 'one member, one vote', leading to the National Assembly, and the Bastille fell on 14 July.
workedExamples.answer: A financial crisis, unjust taxation, a subsistence crisis and Enlightenment ideas combined; the dispute over voting at the Estates General set off the Revolution.

workedExamples.q: Which groups benefited from the Revolution and which were disappointed?
steps: Benefited: the middle class (end of privilege, careers by merit, property protected); peasants (end of feudal dues and tithes).
Disappointed: women (no political rights; clubs closed in 1793); the poor (could not vote under the 1791 constitution and again after 1795); enslaved people when Napoleon restored slavery.
Nobles and clergy lost privileges and lands.
workedExamples.answer: The wealthy middle classes gained most; women, the propertyless and colonised slaves were let down.

summary: In 1789 France was an absolute monarchy under Louis XVI with an empty treasury.
Society had three estates; only the third (about 97%) paid taxes like the taille, plus the tithe to the Church.
Population growth and poor harvests caused a subsistence crisis; bread was unaffordable.
The educated middle class, inspired by Locke, Rousseau and Montesquieu, opposed privilege by birth.
At the Estates General (May 1789) the third estate demanded 'one member, one vote' and formed the National Assembly (Tennis Court Oath, 20 June).
The Bastille was stormed on 14 July 1789; the Great Fear swept the countryside; feudalism was abolished on 4 August.
The 1791 Constitution created a constitutional monarchy; only active citizens (tax-paying men over 25) could vote.
The Declaration of the Rights of Man made rights like life, speech and equality before law natural and inalienable.
France became a republic on 21 September 1792; Louis XVI was executed in January 1793.
Robespierre's Reign of Terror (1793–94) used the guillotine, price ceilings and equality bread.
The Directory (five-member executive) followed; instability led to Napoleon, emperor in 1804, defeated at Waterloo in 1815.
Women won education, divorce and marriage-by-consent laws but no vote until 1946; Olympe de Gouges was executed.
Slavery was abolished in 1794, restored by Napoleon, and finally ended in 1848.
Liberty and democratic rights were the lasting legacy, inspiring people from Europe to India.

sections.md:
In February 1917, the Tsar of Russia ruled over one of the largest empires on Earth. By October of the same year, a small party of revolutionaries had seized power in its capital and announced that, for the first time in history, a country would be run in the name of **workers and peasants**. Factories, banks and land would belong to society, not to private owners.

This was the **Russian Revolution**. Like the French Revolution, it began a debate that lasted a century: should society be organised around private property and individual freedom, or around collective ownership and equality? To understand it, we first need to go back to 19th-century Europe and look at three families of ideas: **liberals, radicals and conservatives** — and then the newcomer, **socialism**.

In this read we follow your chapter:
1. The age of social change — liberals, radicals, conservatives; industrial society; socialism
2. The Russian Revolution — the empire in 1914, the 1905 revolution, World War I, February and October 1917
3. What changed after October — civil war, collectivisation
4. The global influence of the Revolution and the USSR, including in India

check.q: In the name of which groups did the October 1917 revolutionaries claim to rule?
check.why: The Bolsheviks claimed to run the country on behalf of workers and peasants, with property owned by society.

sections.md:
After the French Revolution, people across Europe argued about how society should change. Broadly, three groups emerged.

**Liberals** wanted a nation that **tolerated all religions** — remember that European states then usually favoured one religion. They opposed the uncontrolled power of dynastic rulers and wanted to safeguard individual rights against governments. They argued for a representative, elected parliamentary government, subject to laws interpreted by a well-trained judiciary independent of rulers. **But** they were not 'democrats': they did not believe in universal adult franchise. They felt men of property should mainly have the vote, and they did not want the vote for women.

**Radicals** wanted a nation in which government was based on the **majority of a country's population**. Many supported women's suffragette movements. They opposed the privileges of great landowners and wealthy factory owners. They were not against private property, but disliked its concentration in the hands of a few.

**Conservatives** opposed radicals and liberals. After the French Revolution, however, even they had begun to accept that some change was inevitable. Earlier, in the 18th century, they had generally opposed change; by the 19th century they accepted change but believed **the past had to be respected** and change brought about slowly.

**Industrial society.** These debates happened during a time of huge social and economic change. New cities came up, new industrialised regions developed, railways expanded and the **Industrial Revolution** occurred. Men, women and children were pushed into factories. Work hours were often long and wages poor. Unemployment was common, especially in times of low demand for industrial goods. Housing and sanitation were problems because towns were growing rapidly. Liberals and radicals searched for solutions.

Many liberals and radicals were themselves property owners and employers. Having made wealth through trade or industry, they felt effort, labour and enterprise should be encouraged. If freedom of individuals was ensured, if the poor could labour, and those with capital could operate without restraint, they believed societies would develop. Many working men and women who wanted changes rallied around them in the early 19th century. Some nationalists, liberals and radicals wanted revolutions to end the kind of governments established in Europe in 1815. In France, Italy, Germany and Russia they became revolutionaries. **Giuseppe Mazzini**, an Italian nationalist, conspired with others to achieve this in Italy. Nationalists elsewhere — including India — were influenced by him.

sections.md:
By the mid-19th century in Europe, **socialism** was a well-known body of ideas that attracted widespread attention. Socialists were **against private property** and saw it as the root of all social ills. Why? Individuals who owned property did provide employment, but the propertied were concerned only with personal gain and not with the welfare of those who made the property productive. So if society as a whole rather than single individuals controlled property, more attention would be paid to collective social interests.

Socialists had different visions of the future:

- **Robert Owen** (1771–1858), a leading English manufacturer, sought to build a cooperative community called **New Harmony** in Indiana (USA).
- Others felt cooperatives could not be built on a wide scale through individual initiative; they demanded that **governments encourage cooperatives**. In France, **Louis Blanc** (1813–1882) wanted the government to encourage cooperatives and replace capitalist enterprises. Cooperatives were associations of people who produced goods together and divided profits according to work done.
- **Karl Marx** (1818–1883) and **Friedrich Engels** (1820–1895) added other ideas. Marx argued that industrial society was 'capitalist'. Capitalists owned the capital invested in factories, and the profit of capitalists was produced by workers. The conditions of workers could not improve as long as this profit was accumulated by private capitalists. Workers had to overthrow capitalism and the rule of private property. Marx believed that to free themselves from capitalist exploitation, workers had to construct a radically socialist society where all property was socially controlled. This would be a **communist society**, and he was convinced workers would triumph in their conflict with capitalists.

**Support for socialism.** By the 1870s, socialist ideas spread through Europe. Socialists formed an international body — the **Second International**. Workers in England and Germany began forming associations to fight for better living and working conditions; they set up funds to help members in times of distress and demanded a reduction of working hours and the right to vote. In Germany, these associations worked closely with the **Social Democratic Party (SPD)**. By 1905, socialists and trade unionists formed a **Labour Party** in Britain and a **Socialist Party** in France. However, till 1914, socialists never succeeded in forming a government in Europe.
keyTerms: Socialism — ideas favouring social (collective) ownership of property
Cooperative — group that produces together and shares profits by work done
Capitalism — system where private owners invest capital and keep profits
Communism — Marx's ideal society where all property is socially controlled

check.why: Robert Owen, an English manufacturer, set up the cooperative community New Harmony in Indiana, USA.

sections.md:
In 1914, **Tsar Nicholas II** ruled Russia and its empire. Besides the territory around Moscow, the empire included present-day Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, parts of Poland, Ukraine and Belarus. It stretched to the Pacific and comprised today's Central Asian states, as well as Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan. The majority religion was **Russian Orthodox Christianity**, but the empire also included Catholics, Protestants, Muslims and Buddhists.

**Economy and society.** About **85 per cent** of the empire's population earned their living from agriculture — a higher proportion than in most European countries (in France and Germany it was 40–50 per cent). Cultivators produced for the market and for their own needs, and Russia was a major exporter of grain. Industry existed in pockets — **St Petersburg and Moscow** were prominent industrial areas. Craftsmen did much of the production, but large factories existed alongside. Many factories were set up in the 1890s when Russia's railway network was extended and foreign investment in industry increased. Coal production doubled and iron and steel output quadrupled.

Most industry was the private property of industrialists. The government supervised large factories to ensure minimum wages and limited hours of work, but factory inspectors could not prevent rules being broken. In craft units and small workshops, the working day was sometimes **15 hours**, compared with 10 or 12 in factories. Accommodation varied from rooms to dormitories.

Workers were a divided group. Some had strong links with villages; others had settled in cities permanently. They were divided by skill: metalworkers considered themselves aristocrats among workers because their occupations demanded more training. Women made up **31 per cent** of the factory labour force by 1914 but were paid less than men (between half and three-quarters of a man's wage). Despite divisions, workers united to strike when they disagreed with employers about dismissals or work conditions — in the textile industry in 1896–97 and the metal industry in 1902.

**Peasants.** In the countryside peasants cultivated most of the land, but the nobility, the crown and the Orthodox Church owned large properties. Peasants had no respect for the nobility, unlike in France. Nobles got their power and position through services to the Tsar, not local popularity. Peasants wanted the land of the nobles to be given to them. Frequently they refused to pay rent and even murdered landlords. In 1902 this occurred on a large scale in south Russia, and in 1905 such incidents took place all over Russia. Russian peasants were different in one way: they **pooled their land together periodically**, and their commune (**mir**) divided it according to the needs of individual families.

**Socialism in Russia.** All political parties were illegal before 1914. The **Russian Social Democratic Workers Party** was founded in 1898 by socialists who respected Marx's ideas. Because of government policing, it had to operate as an illegal organisation. It set up a newspaper, mobilised workers and organised strikes. Some socialists felt the peasant custom of dividing land periodically made them natural socialists, so the **Socialist Revolutionary Party** (formed 1900) struggled for peasants' rights and demanded that land belonging to nobles be transferred to peasants. Social Democrats disagreed: Lenin felt peasants were not one united group — some were rich, some poor.

The Social Democratic party was itself divided over strategy. **Vladimir Lenin**, who led the **Bolshevik** group, thought that in a repressive society like Tsarist Russia the party should be disciplined and should control the number and quality of its members. Others — the **Mensheviks** — thought the party should be open to all, as in Germany.

check.why: About 85% of the empire's population earned a living from agriculture, far more than in France or Germany.

sections.h: 1905, the war, and the February Revolution
sections.md:
**The 1905 Revolution.** Russia was an autocracy; unlike other European rulers, even at the beginning of the 20th century the Tsar was not subject to parliament. Liberals in Russia campaigned to end this. Together with Social Democrats and Socialist Revolutionaries, they worked with peasants and workers during the revolution of 1905 to demand a constitution.

The year 1904 was bad for workers. Prices of essential goods rose so quickly that real wages declined by 20 per cent. Membership of workers' associations rose dramatically. When four members of the Assembly of Russian Workers were dismissed at the **Putilov Iron Works**, there was a call for industrial action. Over the next few days over **110,000 workers in St Petersburg** went on strike demanding a reduction in the working day to eight hours, an increase in wages and improvement in working conditions.

When the procession of workers led by **Father Gapon** reached the Winter Palace, it was attacked by police and Cossacks. Over 100 workers were killed and about 300 wounded. This incident, known as **Bloody Sunday**, started a series of events that became the 1905 Revolution. Strikes took place all over the country; universities closed when students walked out. Lawyers, doctors, engineers and other middle-class workers established the Union of Unions and demanded a constituent assembly.

During 1905, the Tsar allowed the creation of an elected consultative parliament, the **Duma**. But he dismissed the first Duma within 75 days and re-elected a second Duma within three months. He did not want any questioning of his authority. He changed voting laws and packed the third Duma with conservative politicians. Liberals and revolutionaries were kept out.

**The First World War and the Russian empire.** In 1914, war broke out between two European alliances — **Germany, Austria and Turkey** (the Central powers) versus **France, Britain and Russia** (later Italy and Romania). Each country had a global empire, so the war was fought outside Europe as well as in Europe. This was the First World War.

In Russia the war was initially popular and people rallied around Nicholas II. As the war continued, though, the Tsar refused to consult the main parties in the Duma. Support wore thin. Anti-German sentiments ran high: St Petersburg — a German name — was renamed **Petrograd**. The **Tsarina Alexandra's** German origins and poor advisers, especially a monk called **Rasputin**, made the autocracy unpopular.

The war on the 'eastern front' differed from the 'western front'. Russian armies lost badly in Germany and Austria between 1914 and 1916. There were over **7 million casualties by 1917**. As they retreated, the army destroyed crops and buildings to prevent the enemy from living off the land — creating over **3 million refugees** in Russia. The war also hurt industry: Russia was cut off from other suppliers of industrial goods by German control of the Baltic Sea. Industrial equipment disintegrated more rapidly. By 1916, railway lines began to break down. Able-bodied men were called up to the war, causing labour shortages. Large supplies of grain were sent to feed the army. For people in the cities, bread and flour became scarce. By the winter of 1916, **riots at bread shops** were common.

**The February Revolution in Petrograd.** In the winter of 1917, conditions in the capital were grim. In February 1917, food shortages were deeply felt in workers' quarters. The winter was very cold — frost and heavy snow. Parliamentarians wishing to preserve elected government were opposed to the Tsar's wish to dissolve the Duma.

On **22 February**, a lockout took place at a factory on the right bank of the river Neva. The next day, workers in fifty factories called a strike in sympathy. In many factories, **women led the way** to the strikes — this came to be called **International Women's Day**. Demonstrating workers crossed from the factory quarters to the centre of the capital and surrounded government buildings. On 25 February the government suspended the Duma. On the 27th, the police headquarters were ransacked. Cavalry was called out but refused to fire on the demonstrators. By evening, soldiers and striking workers had gathered to form a 'soviet' or 'council' in the same building where the Duma met — the **Petrograd Soviet**.

The very next day, a delegation went to see the Tsar. Military commanders advised him to abdicate. He followed their advice and **abdicated on 2 March**. Soviet leaders and Duma leaders formed a **Provisional Government** to run the country.

sections.h: After February: Lenin and the October Revolution
sections.md:
The army officials, the landowners and the industrialists were influential in the Provisional Government. But liberals and socialists among them worked towards an elected government. Restrictions on public meetings and associations were removed. 'Soviets' like the Petrograd Soviet were set up everywhere, though no common system of election was followed.

In **April 1917**, the Bolshevik leader **Vladimir Lenin** returned to Russia from exile. He and the Bolsheviks had opposed the war since 1914. Now he felt it was time for soviets to take over power. He declared that the war be brought to a close, land be transferred to the peasants, and banks be nationalised. These three demands were Lenin's **'April Theses'**. He also argued that the Bolshevik Party rename itself the **Communist Party** to indicate its new radical aims. Most others in the party were initially surprised by the April Theses, thinking the time was not yet ripe for a socialist revolution. But events of the following months changed their attitude.

Through the summer the workers' movement spread. In industrial areas, **factory committees** were formed which began questioning the way industrialists ran their factories. Trade unions grew in number. Soldiers' committees were formed in the army. In June, about 500 soviets sent representatives to an All Russian Congress of Soviets. As the Provisional Government saw its power reduce and Bolshevik influence grow, it decided to take stern measures. It resisted attempts by workers to run factories and began arresting leaders. Popular demonstrations staged by the Bolsheviks in July 1917 were sternly repressed. Many Bolshevik leaders had to go into hiding or flee.

Meanwhile in the countryside, peasants and their Socialist Revolutionary leaders pressed for a redistribution of land. Land committees were formed. Encouraged by the Socialist Revolutionaries, peasants seized land between July and September 1917.

**The revolution of October 1917.** As conflict between the Provisional Government — led by **Kerenskii** — and the Bolsheviks grew, Lenin feared the Provisional Government would set up a dictatorship. In September, he began discussions for an uprising against the government. Bolshevik supporters in the army, soviets and factories were brought together.

On **16 October 1917**, Lenin persuaded the Petrograd Soviet and the Bolshevik Party to agree to a socialist seizure of power. A **Military Revolutionary Committee** was appointed by the Soviet under **Leon Trotskii** to organise the seizure. The date of the event was kept a secret.

The uprising began on **24 October**. Sensing trouble, Prime Minister Kerenskii had left the city to summon troops. At dawn, military men loyal to the government seized the buildings of two Bolshevik newspapers. Pro-government troops were sent to take over telephone and telegraph offices and protect the **Winter Palace**. In a swift response, the Military Revolutionary Committee ordered its supporters to seize government offices and arrest ministers. Late in the day, the ship **Aurora** shelled the Winter Palace. Other vessels sailed down the Neva and took over various military points. By nightfall, the city was under the committee's control and the ministers had surrendered. At a meeting of the All Russian Congress of Soviets in Petrograd, the majority approved the Bolshevik action. Uprisings took place in other cities. There was heavy fighting — especially in Moscow — but by December, the Bolsheviks controlled the **Moscow–Petrograd area**.

> *Did you know?* Russia then used the old Julian calendar, 13 days behind ours. So the 'October' Revolution happened on 7 November by today's calendar, and the 'February' Revolution on 12 March.

sections.h: What changed after October: civil war and Stalin
sections.md:
The Bolsheviks were totally opposed to private property. Most industry and banks were **nationalised in November 1917** — the government took over ownership and management. Land was declared social property and peasants were allowed to seize the land of the nobility. In cities, Bolsheviks enforced partition of large houses according to family requirements. They banned the use of the old titles of aristocracy. To assert the change, new uniforms were designed for the army and officials — the Soviet hat (**budeonovka**) was introduced in 1918.

The Bolshevik Party was renamed the **Russian Communist Party (Bolshevik)**. In November 1917 the Bolsheviks conducted elections to the Constituent Assembly, but they failed to gain majority support. In January 1918, the Assembly rejected Bolshevik measures and Lenin dismissed it. He thought the All Russian Congress of Soviets was more democratic. In March 1918, despite opposition by their political allies, the Bolsheviks made peace with Germany at **Brest Litovsk**. In the years that followed, the Bolsheviks became the only party to participate in elections to the All Russian Congress of Soviets, which became the Parliament of the country. Russia became a **one-party state**. Trade unions were kept under party control. The secret police (first called the Cheka, later OGPU and NKVD) punished those who criticised the Bolsheviks. Many young writers and artists rallied to the Party because it stood for socialism and change. But many felt the Party was moving away from the ideals of a socialist revolution through censorship.

**The civil war.** When the Bolsheviks ordered land redistribution, the Russian army began to break up. Soldiers, mostly peasants, wished to go home for the redistribution and deserted. Non-Bolshevik socialists, liberals and supporters of autocracy condemned the uprising. Their leaders moved to south Russia and organised troops to fight the Bolsheviks — the **'reds'**. During 1918 and 1919, the **'greens'** (Socialist Revolutionaries) and **'whites'** (pro-Tsarists) controlled most of the Russian empire. They were backed by French, American, British and Japanese troops — all worried at the growth of socialism in Russia. As these troops and the Bolsheviks fought a civil war, looting, banditry and famine became common.

By January 1920, the Bolsheviks controlled most of the former Russian empire. They succeeded due to cooperation with non-Russian nationalities and Muslim jadidists. Cooperation did not work where Russian colonists themselves turned Bolshevik. In Khiva, in Central Asia, Bolshevik colonists brutally massacred local nationalists in the name of defending socialism. In this situation, many were confused about what the Bolshevik government represented. Partly to remedy this, most non-Russian nationalities were given **political autonomy** in the **Soviet Union (USSR)** — the state the Bolsheviks created from the Russian empire in **December 1922**. But since this was combined with unpopular policies the Bolsheviks forced on the local government — like harsh discouragement of nomadism — attempts to win over different nationalities were only partly successful.

**Making a socialist society.** During the civil war, the Bolsheviks kept industries and banks nationalised. They permitted peasants to cultivate the land that had been socialised. Bolsheviks used confiscated land to demonstrate what collective work could be. A process of **centralised planning** was introduced. Officials assessed how the economy could work and set targets for a five-year period. On this basis they made the **Five Year Plans**. The government fixed all prices to promote industrial growth during the first two Plans (1927–1932 and 1933–1938). Centralised planning led to economic growth. Industrial production increased (between 1929 and 1933 by 100 per cent in the case of oil, coal and steel). New factory cities came into being. However, rapid construction led to poor working conditions. In the city of Magnitogorsk, the construction of a steel plant was achieved in three years. An expanded schooling system developed, and arrangements were made for factory workers and peasants to enter universities. Crèches were established in factories for the children of women workers. Cheap public health care was provided. Model living quarters were set up for workers. The effect of all this was uneven, though, as government resources were limited.

**Stalinism and collectivisation.** The period of the early Planned Economy was linked to the disasters of the **collectivisation of agriculture**. By 1927–1928, towns in Soviet Russia were facing an acute problem of grain supplies. The government fixed prices at which grain must be sold, but peasants refused to sell to government buyers at these prices. **Stalin**, who headed the party after the death of Lenin, introduced firm emergency measures. He believed rich peasants and traders in the countryside were holding stocks in the hope of higher prices. Speculation had to be stopped and supplies confiscated. In 1928, Party members toured the grain-producing areas, supervising enforced grain collections and raiding '**kulaks**' — the name for well-to-do peasants.

It was argued that the shortage was partly due to the small size of holdings. After 1917, land had been given over to peasants. These small-sized peasant farms could not be modernised. To develop modern farms and run them along industrial lines with machinery, it was necessary to 'eliminate kulaks', take away land from peasants, and establish state-controlled large farms. From **1929**, the Party forced all peasants to cultivate in collective farms (**kolkhoz**). The bulk of land and implements were transferred to the ownership of collective farms. Peasants worked on the land, and the kolkhoz profit was shared. Enraged peasants resisted the authorities and destroyed their livestock: between 1929 and 1931, the number of cattle fell by one-third. Those who resisted collectivisation were severely punished; many were deported and exiled. Collectivisation did not immediately increase production. In fact, the bad harvests of 1930–1933 led to one of the most devastating famines in Soviet history, when over **4 million** died. Many within the Party criticised the confusion in industrial production under the Planned Economy and the consequences of collectivisation. Stalin and his sympathisers charged these critics with conspiracy against socialism. Accusations were made throughout the country, and by 1939, over **2 million** were in prisons or labour camps. Most were innocent of the crimes, but no one spoke for them. A large number were forced to make false confessions under torture and were executed — several among them were talented professionals.
keyTerms: Nationalisation — the government taking over ownership of industry or banks
Five Year Plan — central plan setting economic targets for five years
Kulak — Russian term for a well-to-do peasant
Kolkhoz — collective farm in the USSR

sections.h: The global influence of the Revolution — and India
sections.md:
Existing socialist parties in Europe did not wholly approve of the way the Bolsheviks took power and kept it. However, the possibility of a workers' state fired people's imagination across the world. In many countries, **communist parties** were formed — like the Communist Party of Great Britain. The Bolsheviks encouraged colonial peoples to follow their experiment. Many non-Russians from outside the USSR participated in the **Conference of the Peoples of the East (1920)** and the Bolshevik-founded **Comintern** — an international union of pro-Bolshevik socialist parties. Some received education in the USSR's Communist University of the Workers of the East. By the time of the outbreak of the Second World War, the USSR had given socialism a global face and world stature.

Yet by the 1950s it was acknowledged within the country that the style of government in the USSR was not in keeping with the ideals of the Russian Revolution. In the world socialist movement too, it was recognised that all was not well. A backward country had become a great power. Its industries and agriculture had developed, and the poor were being fed. But it had denied the essential freedoms to its citizens and carried out its developmental projects through repressive policies. By the end of the 20th century, the international reputation of the USSR as a socialist country had declined — though it was recognised that socialist ideals still enjoyed respect among its people. But in each country, the ideas of socialism were rethought in a variety of different ways.

**India and the Russian Revolution.** Among the many people inspired by the Russian Revolution were many Indians. Several attended the Communist University. By the mid-1920s, the **Communist Party** was formed in India. Its members kept in touch with the Soviet Communist Party. Important Indian political and cultural figures took an interest in the Soviet experiment and visited Russia — among them **Jawaharlal Nehru** and **Rabindranath Tagore**, who wrote about Soviet socialism. Writings gave Indians impressions of the new society. Tagore, in his *Letters from Russia* (1930s), was struck by the spread of education, while also noting his unease at the lack of freedom of thought.

> *Think about it:* India later borrowed the idea of **Five Year Plans** (from 1951), but within a democracy with elections and fundamental rights. That combination — planning plus freedoms — was India's own path.

sections.md:
In the spring of 1945, as the Second World War ended in Europe, Allied soldiers entering camps in Germany and Poland found evidence of something almost impossible to believe: a modern, educated state had organised the systematic killing of millions of civilians. Between 1945 and 1946, an **International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg** tried leading Nazis for crimes against peace, war crimes and **crimes against humanity**.

How could this happen in Germany — the land of great scientists, musicians and philosophers? How did a party that won under 3 per cent of the vote in 1928 rule the country by 1933? And why did so many ordinary people go along with it?

This chapter asks those questions calmly and carefully. It is not a story about villains alone; it is a warning about how democracies can fail — through economic despair, fear, propaganda and silence. Following your textbook, we will look at:

1. The birth of the Weimar Republic and its troubles
2. Hitler's rise to power
3. The Nazi worldview
4. Youth in Nazi Germany
5. Ordinary people and the crimes against humanity

> A note before we begin: this read describes persecution and genocide factually, without graphic detail. If any part troubles you, talk about it with a teacher or a family member.

sections.h: The Weimar Republic: born in defeat
sections.md:
At the start of the 20th century Germany was a powerful empire. In the **First World War (1914–1918)** it fought alongside the Austrian empire against the Allies (England, France and Russia). Everyone expected a quick victory; instead the war dragged on for four exhausting years. Germany made early gains, occupying France and Belgium, but the Allies — strengthened by the USA joining in 1917 — won in **November 1918**.

Defeat brought the fall of the emperor. A **National Assembly** met at **Weimar** and drew up a democratic constitution with a federal structure. Deputies were elected to the German Parliament, the **Reichstag**, on the basis of **equal and universal votes cast by all adults including women**.

But the new republic was not welcomed by everyone, because it was forced to sign the harsh **Treaty of Versailles** (1919):
- Germany lost its overseas colonies, about **13 per cent of its territory**, **75 per cent of its iron** and **26 per cent of its coal** to France, Poland, Denmark and Lithuania.
- The Allies **demilitarised** Germany to weaken its power.
- The **War Guilt Clause** held Germany responsible for the war and damage the Allies suffered. Germany had to pay compensation of **£6 billion**.
- The Allied armies occupied the resource-rich **Rhineland** for much of the 1920s.

Many Germans blamed the Weimar Republic itself for the defeat and the humiliation. Supporters of the republic — mainly **socialists, Catholics and Democrats** — were mocked as the **'November criminals'**.

**The effects of the war.** The war had a devastating impact on the entire continent, psychologically and financially. Europe moved from a continent of creditors to one of debtors. The young republic was made to pay for the sins of the old empire. Soldiers came to be placed above civilians. Politicians and publicists laid great stress on the need for men to be aggressive, strong and masculine. The media glorified trench life — though in reality soldiers lived miserable lives in trenches, trapped with rats feeding on corpses, facing poisonous gas and enemy shelling. **Aggressive war propaganda and national honour** occupied centre stage, while popular support grew for conservative dictatorships that had recently come into being.

**Political radicalism.** The birth of the republic coincided with a revolutionary uprising of the **Spartacist League**, on the pattern of the Bolshevik Revolution in Russia. Soviets of workers and sailors were established in many cities. The Weimar Republic crushed the uprising with the help of a war veterans' organisation called the **Free Corps**. The Spartacists later founded the Communist Party of Germany. Communists and socialists thereafter became irreconcilable enemies and could not make common cause against Hitler.
