sections.md:
India occupies an important strategic position in **South Asia**. India has **28 States and 8 Union Territories** (after the reorganisation of 2019–2020, when Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh became UTs and Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu were merged into one UT).

India shares its **land boundaries** with:

| Direction | Neighbours |
|---|---|
| North-west | **Pakistan** and **Afghanistan** |
| North | **China (Tibet)**, **Nepal** and **Bhutan** |
| East | **Myanmar** and **Bangladesh** |

Our southern neighbours across the sea consist of two island countries:

- **Sri Lanka**, separated from India by a narrow channel of sea formed by the **Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar**. (A chain of shoals between them, Adam's Bridge / Ram Setu, lies in this area.)
- **Maldives**, situated to the **south of the Lakshadweep Islands**.

India has had **strong geographical and historical links** with its neighbours. Buddhism spread from India to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Tibet and beyond; trade, languages, food, festivals and family ties cross these borders even today.

**Map skills.** On an outline map of India, mark: the Tropic of Cancer; the Standard Meridian; the southernmost, northernmost, easternmost and westernmost points; the states through which the Tropic of Cancer passes; the neighbouring countries; the Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar; Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.
keyTerms: Palk Strait — narrow sea channel between India and Sri Lanka
Gulf of Mannar — sea area south of the Palk Strait
Standard Meridian — the longitude whose local time is taken as the country's standard time
Peninsula — land surrounded by water on three sides

check.q: Which country is India's neighbour to the south of Lakshadweep?
check.why: The Maldives lies in the Arabian Sea/Indian Ocean to the south of the Lakshadweep Islands.

sections.h: 7. States, capitals and why location shapes life
sections.md:
India's location and size explain a great deal about everyday life:

- **Climate variety.** Because India spans about 29° of latitude and the Himalayas wall off the north, it has everything from snowfields in Ladakh to tropical rainforests in Kerala and the Andamans, and the Thar desert in Rajasthan. The Tropic of Cancer marks the rough boundary between the hotter tropical south and the cooler sub-tropical north.
- **Monsoon.** India's position at the head of the Indian Ocean, with land heating up faster than sea in summer, helps produce the **monsoon** winds that bring most of its rain (studied in the Climate chapter).
- **Long coast.** A 7,516.6 km coastline supports fishing, ports, shipbuilding, salt pans and tourism, and gives India a large **Exclusive Economic Zone** at sea.
- **Strategic position.** Sitting astride the sea lanes between the Gulf (oil) and East Asia (factories), India has an important role in the security of the Indian Ocean.
- **Diversity.** India's size and history of contacts give it many languages, cuisines and cultures — 'unity in diversity'.

**Exercise idea (states and capitals).** Make a table listing all 28 states and 8 UTs with their capitals. Identify: states with no coastline; states that border other countries; the smallest and largest states by area (Goa and Rajasthan); states through which the Tropic of Cancer passes; states bordering Bangladesh (West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram).

**Did you know?** Uttar Pradesh borders Nepal; Sikkim borders Nepal, Bhutan and China; Arunachal Pradesh borders Bhutan, China and Myanmar. And the island territories — Lakshadweep (coral islands) and Andaman & Nicobar (mostly volcanic/mountain islands) — are very different in origin.

check.q: Which is the largest state of India by area?
check.why: Rajasthan is the largest state by area; Goa is the smallest.

summary: India lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere, between 8°4′N–37°6′N and 68°7′E–97°25′E (mainland).
The Tropic of Cancer (23°30′N) divides India almost in half and passes through 8 states.
Andaman & Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal (south-east); Lakshadweep in the Arabian Sea (south-west).
Kanniyakumari is the southern tip of the mainland; Indira Point (6°45′N) was the southernmost point of the Union, submerged in 2004.

North–south extent ≈ 3,214 km; east–west ≈ 2,933 km — east–west looks smaller because longitudes converge.
About 30° of longitude gives a 2-hour time lag between Gujarat and Arunachal Pradesh.

India's central position in the Indian Ocean and its Deccan Peninsula link it to West Asia, Africa, Europe and East Asia; the ocean is named after India.
Ideas (Upanishads, Ramayana, Panchatantra, numerals, decimal system) went out; spices and muslin were exported; Greek sculpture and West Asian architecture came in.
The Suez Canal (1869) cut India's distance to Europe by 7,000 km.
Neighbours: Pakistan, Afghanistan (NW); China, Nepal, Bhutan (N); Myanmar, Bangladesh (E); Sri Lanka (via Palk Strait and Gulf of Mannar) and Maldives across the sea.
India has 28 states and 8 union territories.

sections.h: 8. Key numbers every student must know
sections.md:
Geography questions on this chapter are full of numbers. Here they are in one place.

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Latitudinal extent (mainland) | 8°4′N to 37°6′N |
| Longitudinal extent | 68°7′E to 97°25′E |
| Area | about 3.28 million sq km |
| Share of world area | about 2.4% |
| World rank by area | 7th |
| Land boundary | about 15,200 km |
| Coastline (mainland + islands) | about 7,516.6 km |
| N–S and E–W extent | each a little over 30° of latitude/longitude; actual distance N–S about 3,214 km, E–W about 2,933 km |
| Standard Meridian | 82°30′E, passing near Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh) |
| Time difference Gujarat–Arunachal | about 2 hours |
| IST vs GMT | 5 hours 30 minutes ahead |

**Why is the E–W distance smaller though the degrees are similar?** Lines of longitude come closer together as we move away from the Equator towards the poles, so 30° of longitude covers less ground than 30° of latitude.

**Why 2 hours?** Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, i.e. 1° every 4 minutes. From 68°7′E to 97°25′E is almost 30°, and 30 × 4 = 120 minutes = 2 hours. The Sun rises in Arunachal Pradesh about two hours before it rises in Gujarat's Kachchh, yet watches in both places show the same time because of IST.

**The southernmost point.** The mainland ends at Kanniyakumari (8°4′N), but the southernmost point of the Union, **Indira Point** (about 6°45′N) in Great Nicobar, lies further south. (The name is sometimes written Pygmalion Point in older maps.)

check.q: Why was 82°30′E chosen as the Standard Meridian?
options: It lies roughly midway between India's east and west limits
It is a multiple of 15° exactly
check.why: 82°30′E lies close to the middle of India's longitudinal extent, so the time difference with both ends is minimised.

sections.h: 9. The Tropic of Cancer and India's states
sections.md:
The **Tropic of Cancer (23°30′N)** divides India into almost two equal parts. The southern part lies in the tropical zone and the northern part in the sub-tropical (warm temperate) zone, which affects temperature and the length of day and night. At Kanniyakumari the difference between day and night is hardly felt; in Kashmir it can be several hours in winter and summer.

The Tropic passes through **eight states**, from west to east:

1. Gujarat
2. Rajasthan
3. Madhya Pradesh
4. Chhattisgarh
5. Jharkhand
6. West Bengal
7. Tripura
8. Mizoram

A memory trick: **"Good Rains Make Crops Joyful With Tasty Mangoes"** — G-R-M-C-J-W-T-M.

**Island groups.** India has two island groups. The **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** lie in the Bay of Bengal, to the south-east. The **Lakshadweep Islands** lie in the Arabian Sea, to the south-west; they are coral islands. Both are Union Territories. Exam tip: *Bay of Bengal → Andaman & Nicobar; Arabian Sea → Lakshadweep.*

sections.h: 10. India's central position on world routes
sections.md:
The Indian landmass sits centrally between **West Asia and East Asia**, and is a southward extension of the Asian continent. The **trans-Indian Ocean routes** connecting Europe in the west and East Asia pass close to India, which gives it a strategic central location. The **Deccan Peninsula** protrudes into the Indian Ocean, letting India keep close contact with West Asia, Africa and Europe from the western coast and with Southeast and East Asia from the eastern coast. **No other country has as long a coastline on the Indian Ocean as India** — that is why the ocean is named after it.

**Opening of the Suez Canal (1869)** reduced India's distance from Europe by about 7,000 km.

**Over land.** India's contacts with the world are older than its sea links. Passes across the mountains in the north gave passage to ancient travellers. These routes carried **ideas and commodities**: the *Upanishads*, the *Ramayana*, the *Panchatantra* stories, Indian numerals and the decimal system reached many parts of the world, while spices and muslin were traded. In return, the influence of Greek sculpture and the architectural styles of domes and minarets from West Asia can be seen in parts of India.

**Neighbours recap.** India shares land boundaries with Pakistan and Afghanistan (north-west), China, Nepal and Bhutan (north), Myanmar and Bangladesh (east). Across the sea lie **Sri Lanka**, separated by the narrow **Palk Strait** and **Gulf of Mannar**, and the **Maldives**, to the south of Lakshadweep.

check.q: By roughly how much did the Suez Canal shorten India's distance to Europe?
check.why: The 1869 canal let ships avoid going round Africa, cutting about 7,000 km from the route.

sections.h: 11. Map work and model exam answers
sections.md:
**Map work (practise on an outline map of India):** mark the Tropic of Cancer and the Standard Meridian; label the southernmost, northernmost, easternmost and westernmost points; mark Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar, Palk Strait, Gulf of Mannar, Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal; shade the states crossed by the Tropic; mark the states that have a coastline and those that share a boundary with each neighbouring country.

**Model answer 1 — Why is India said to have a strategic location?** (1) It lies at the head of the Indian Ocean, centrally between East and West Asia. (2) Trans-Indian Ocean routes between Europe and East Asia pass nearby. (3) The peninsula gives contact by sea on both sides. (4) Overland passes allowed old exchanges of goods and ideas.

**Model answer 2 — Why do we need a Standard Meridian?** Local time changes by 4 minutes per degree. Across India's 30° that is 2 hours. If each place kept local time, trains, flights, offices and broadcasts would be confusing. One meridian (82°30′E) gives the whole country a single clock, IST.

**Model answer 3 — Size facts.** India's area is about 3.28 million sq km, 2.4% of the world's land, seventh largest. Its land frontier is about 15,200 km and its coastline about 7,516.6 km. It is bounded by young fold mountains in the north-west, north and north-east, and tapers south of 22°N into the Indian Ocean, splitting it into the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal.

check.q: Which water body separates India from Sri Lanka?
check.why: Sri Lanka is separated from India by the Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar.

rd-school-c9-social-b.ch2-physical-featu.subtitle: Young mountains, ancient plateaus, golden plains, dunes, coasts and coral islands — and how plates built them all

sections.md:
Climbers on the high slopes of the Himalayas sometimes find something astonishing: **fossils of sea creatures** — shells and ammonites — embedded in rock at 5,000 metres above sea level. How did the bottom of a sea end up on the roof of the world?

The answer is one of the greatest stories in Earth science, and it explains almost every landform in India. India has every kind of relief: mountains, plains, deserts, plateaus, coasts and islands. Some rocks of the peninsula are among the **oldest on Earth**; the Himalayas are among the **youngest** mountains. India's land is also made of many kinds of rock — some hard like marble (used in the Taj Mahal), some soft like soapstone used in carving. In this read we will follow the chapter:

1. How were these landforms made? — the **Theory of Plate Tectonics**
2. The major physiographic divisions:
   - The Himalayan Mountains
   - The Northern Plains
   - The Peninsular Plateau
   - The Indian Desert
   - The Coastal Plains
   - The Islands

Keep a physical map of India open — colours on it show heights: greens for low plains, yellows and browns for plateaus and hills, white for snow.

check.q: What do sea fossils high in the Himalayas tell us?
options: Seas once covered the whole Earth's surface forever
The rocks were once at the bottom of a sea and were later pushed up
The Himalayas are the oldest mountains
check.why: Marine fossils show that sediments laid down in an ancient sea were folded and raised up to form the Himalayas.

sections.h: How the land was built: plate tectonics
sections.md:
Geologists explain the formation of continents and oceans with the **Theory of Plate Tectonics**. According to it, the crust (upper part) of the Earth is made of **seven major and some minor plates**. These plates are always moving, very slowly — a few centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

The movement of plates produces stresses that cause **folding, faulting and volcanic activity**. Plate movements are of three types:

| Type | What happens | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Convergent** | Plates come towards each other | Collide, crumble, or one slides under the other — fold mountains, volcanoes |
| **Divergent** | Plates move away from each other | New crust forms; rift valleys, mid-ocean ridges |
| **Transform** | Plates slide past each other horizontally | Earthquakes along faults |

**India's journey.** The oldest landmass, the **Peninsular part**, was part of the **Gondwana land**. Gondwana included India, Australia, South Africa, South America and Antarctica as one single landmass. The **convectional currents** in the mantle split the crust into pieces. The **Indo-Australian plate** broke away from Gondwana and **drifted northwards**. This northward drift resulted in the **collision with the much larger Eurasian Plate**.

Between the two plates lay a sea called the **Tethys**. Due to the collision, the sedimentary rocks accumulated in the Tethys geosyncline were **folded** to form the mountain system of western Asia and the **Himalayas**. That's where the sea fossils came from!

The uplift of the Himalayas out of the Tethys Sea and the subsidence of the northern flank of the Peninsular plateau created a large **basin**. In due course of time, this depression got filled by sediments deposited by the rivers flowing from the mountains in the north and the peninsular plateau in the south. A flat land of extensive alluvial deposits formed the **Northern Plains**.

So, in terms of age:
- **Peninsular Plateau**: among the oldest landmasses, made of igneous and metamorphic rocks; a stable block (though recent earthquakes show some stress).
- **Himalayas and Northern Plains**: most recent landforms. The Himalayas are geologically young, weak and flexible — still rising, which is why the region faces earthquakes.

check.q: Which type of plate boundary formed the Himalayas?
check.why: The Indian and Eurasian plates moved towards each other (convergent), folding the Tethys sediments into the Himalayas.

sections.md:
The Himalayas, geologically young and structurally **fold mountains**, stretch over the northern borders of India. These mountain ranges run in a **west–east direction from the Indus to the Brahmaputra**. They represent the loftiest and one of the most rugged mountain barriers of the world. They form an **arc** that covers a distance of about **2,400 km**. Their width varies from **400 km in Kashmir to 150 km in Arunachal Pradesh**. The altitudinal variations are greater in the eastern half than in the western half.

The Himalaya consists of **three parallel ranges** in its longitudinal extent, with a number of valleys between them:

**1. Great or Inner Himalayas — the Himadri.** The northernmost range is the most continuous range, consisting of the loftiest peaks with an average height of **6,000 metres**. It contains all the prominent Himalayan peaks. The folds of the Great Himalayas are asymmetrical in nature. The core of this part is composed of **granite**. It is **perennially snowbound**, and a number of glaciers descend from this range.

| Peak | Country | Height (m) |
|---|---|---|
| Mt. Everest | Nepal | 8,848 |
| Kanchenjunga | India | 8,598 |
| Makalu | Nepal | 8,481 |
| Dhaulagiri | Nepal | 8,172 |
| Nanga Parbat | (J&K region) | 8,126 |
| Annapurna | Nepal | 8,078 |
| Nanda Devi | India | 7,817 |
| Kamet | India | 7,756 |
| Namcha Barwa | China (Tibet) | 7,756 |

(Everest's height was revised to 8,848.86 m in 2020 by a joint Nepal–China survey.)

**2. Lesser Himalaya — the Himachal.** The range lying to the south of the Himadri forms the most rugged mountain system. The ranges are mainly composed of highly compressed and altered rocks. The altitude varies between **3,700 and 4,500 metres** and the average width is **50 km**. While the **Pir Panjal** range forms the longest and the most important range, the **Dhaula Dhar and the Mahabharat ranges** are also prominent ones. This range consists of the famous **valley of Kashmir, the Kangra and Kullu valleys** in Himachal Pradesh. This region is well known for its **hill stations** (Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital, Darjeeling…).

**3. Outer Himalayas — the Shiwaliks.** The outermost range. They extend over a width of **10–50 km** and have an altitude varying between **900 and 1,100 metres**. These ranges are composed of **unconsolidated sediments** brought down by rivers from the main Himalayan ranges located farther north. These valleys are covered with thick gravel and alluvium. The longitudinal valleys lying between the Lesser Himalaya and the Shiwaliks are known as **Duns**. **Dehra Dun, Kotli Dun and Patli Dun** are some of the well-known Duns.

**Regional divisions (west to east), by river valleys:**
- Between the **Indus and the Satluj**: **Punjab Himalaya** (also called Kashmir and Himachal Himalaya from west to east)
- Between the **Satluj and Kali**: **Kumaon Himalayas**
- Between the **Kali and Teesta**: **Nepal Himalayas**
- Between the **Teesta and Dihang**: **Assam Himalayas**

The **Brahmaputra** marks the easternmost boundary of the Himalayas. Beyond the **Dihang gorge**, the Himalayas bend sharply to the south and spread along the eastern boundary of India. They are known as the **Purvachal or the Eastern hills and mountains**. These hills, running through the northeastern states, are mostly composed of strong **sandstones**, which are sedimentary rocks. Covered with dense forests, they mostly run as parallel ranges and valleys. The Purvachal comprises the **Patkai hills, the Naga hills, the Manipur hills and the Mizo hills**.

sections.md:
The northern plain has been formed by the interplay of the **three major river systems** — the **Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra** — along with their tributaries. This plain is formed of **alluvial soil**. The deposition of alluvium in a vast basin lying at the foothills of the Himalaya over millions of years formed this fertile plain. It spreads over an area of **7 lakh sq km**. The plain is about **2,400 km long and 240 to 320 km broad**. It is a densely populated physiographic division. With rich soil cover, an adequate water supply and a favourable climate, it is agriculturally a very productive part of India.

The rivers coming from the northern mountains are involved in depositional work. In the lower course, due to the gentle slope, the velocity of the river decreases, which results in the formation of **riverine islands** — **Majuli** in the Brahmaputra is the largest inhabited riverine island in the world. The rivers in their lower course split into numerous channels due to the deposition of silt. These channels are known as **distributaries**.

**Three sections (west to east):**
1. **Punjab Plains** — western part, formed by the Indus and its tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Satluj). The larger part lies in Pakistan. These plains are dominated by **doabs** ('do' = two, 'ab' = water: the land between two rivers).
2. **Ganga Plains** — extend between the Ghaggar and Teesta rivers, spread over the states of North India: Haryana, Delhi, UP, Bihar, partly Jharkhand and West Bengal.
3. **Brahmaputra Plains** — in the east, particularly in Assam.

**Four regions by relief (north to south):**

| Region | Where | Features |
|---|---|---|
| **Bhabar** | Narrow belt, about 8–16 km wide, at the foot of the Shiwaliks, parallel to the slopes | Rivers deposit pebbles; streams **disappear** underground |
| **Terai** | South of the bhabar | Streams **re-emerge**; wet, swampy, marshy; once thick forests and wildlife (much cleared for agriculture after Partition to settle migrants; Dudhwa National Park is in this region) |
| **Bhangar** | The largest part of the plain | **Older alluvium**; lies above flood level; terrace-like; contains calcareous deposits called **kankar** |
| **Khadar** | Flood plains | **Newer, younger alluvium**; renewed almost every year; very fertile, ideal for intensive agriculture |

sections.md:
The Peninsular plateau is a **tableland** composed of the **old crystalline, igneous and metamorphic rocks**. It was formed due to the breaking and drifting of the Gondwana land, making it a part of the oldest landmass. The plateau has broad and shallow valleys and rounded hills. It consists of two broad divisions: the **Central Highlands** and the **Deccan Plateau**. The **Narmada river** divides them.

**Central Highlands.** The part lying to the north of the Narmada river, covering a major area of the **Malwa plateau**. The **Vindhyan range** is bounded by the Central Highlands on the south and the **Aravalis** on the northwest. Further westward it gradually merges with the sandy and rocky desert of Rajasthan. The flow of the rivers draining this region — the **Chambal, Sind, Betwa and Ken** — is from **southwest to northeast**, indicating the slope. The Central Highlands are wider in the west but narrower in the east. The eastward extensions of this plateau are locally known as the **Bundelkhand and Baghelkhand**. The **Chotanagpur plateau** marks the further eastward extension, drained by the **Damodar river**.

**Deccan Plateau.** A **triangular landmass** that lies to the south of the Narmada. The **Satpura range** flanks its broad base in the north, while the **Mahadev, the Kaimur hills and the Maikal range** form its eastern extensions. The Deccan Plateau is **higher in the west and slopes gently eastwards**. An extension of the plateau is also visible in the northeast — locally known as the **Meghalaya, Karbi-Anglong Plateau and North Cachar Hills**. It is separated by a fault from the Chotanagpur Plateau. Three important ranges from west to east are the **Garo, Khasi and Jaintia Hills**.

The western and eastern edges of the Deccan Plateau are marked by the **Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats**:

| Western Ghats | Eastern Ghats |
|---|---|
| Lie parallel to the western coast | Stretch from Mahanadi valley to the Nilgiris in the south |
| **Continuous**, can be crossed only through passes (Thal, Bhor, Pal ghats) | **Discontinuous and irregular**, dissected by rivers draining into the Bay of Bengal |
| Higher: average 900–1,600 m | Lower: average about 600 m |
| Height increases from north to south | Highest peak **Mahendragiri (1,501 m)** |
| Highest peak **Anai Mudi (2,695 m)**; second **Doda Betta (2,637 m)** | Shevroy and Javadi Hills to the southeast |
| Cause orographic rain from moist winds | Receive less rain |

**Udagamandalam (Ooty)** and **Kodaikanal** are famous hill stations in the region where the Eastern and Western Ghats meet.

One distinct feature of the Peninsular plateau is the **black soil** area known as the **Deccan Trap** — of **volcanic origin**, hence igneous rocks. Over time these rocks have been denuded and are responsible for the formation of black soil, excellent for cotton.

The **Aravali Hills** lie on the western and northwestern margins of the peninsular plateau. These are **highly eroded hills** found as broken hills, stretching from **Gujarat to Delhi** in a southwest–northeast direction — among the oldest fold mountains in the world.

check.q: Which is the highest peak of the Western Ghats?
check.why: Anai Mudi at 2,695 m in Kerala is the highest peak of the Western Ghats (and of peninsular India).

sections.md:
The Indian desert lies towards the **western margins of the Aravali Hills**. It is an undulating sandy plain covered with **sand dunes**. This region receives very low rainfall — **below 150 mm per year**. It has an arid climate with low vegetation cover. Streams appear during the rainy season; soon after, they disappear into the sand as they do not have enough water to reach the sea. **Luni** is the only large river in this region.

**Barchans** — **crescent-shaped dunes** — cover larger areas, but **longitudinal dunes** become more prominent near the India–Pakistan boundary. Wind blows sand up the gentle windward slope; it slides down the steep slip face; the 'horns' of the crescent point downwind.

If you visit Jaisalmer, you may see the **Sam sand dunes**, where tourists ride camels at sunset. The Raikas you met in the history chapter on pastoralists live in this desert.

> *Did you know?* Under Rajasthan's sand, a satellite survey traced the dried-up channel of an ancient river that many scholars identify with the Vedic Saraswati — historians and geologists still debate the details.

sections.h: The Coastal Plains and the Islands
sections.md:
**The Coastal Plains.** The Peninsular plateau is flanked by a stretch of narrow coastal strips, running along the **Arabian Sea on the west** and the **Bay of Bengal on the east**.

**Western coast** — sandwiched between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea, it is a **narrow plain**. It consists of three sections:
- northern part: **Konkan** (Mumbai to Goa)
- central stretch: **Kannad Plain**
- southern stretch: **Malabar coast**

**Eastern coast** — the plains along the Bay of Bengal are **wide and level**. In the northern part it is referred to as the **Northern Circar**, while the southern part is known as the **Coromandel Coast**. Large rivers such as the **Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri** have formed extensive **deltas** on this coast. **Lake Chilika** (in Odisha, south of the Mahanadi delta) is an important feature along the eastern coast — the largest saltwater lake in India.

**The Islands.** India has two groups of islands.

**Lakshadweep** — lies close to the **Malabar coast of Kerala**. This group of islands is composed of small **coral islands**. Earlier they were known as Laccadive, Minicoy and Amindive. In 1973 they were named **Lakshadweep**. It covers a small area of **32 sq km**. **Kavaratti** island is the administrative headquarters. The group has great diversity of flora and fauna. The **Pitti island**, which is uninhabited, has a **bird sanctuary**.

*Corals* are short-lived microscopic organisms that live in colonies in shallow, mud-free and warm waters. They secrete calcium carbonate. The coral secretion and their skeletons form coral deposits in the form of reefs: barrier reefs, fringing reefs and **atolls** (circular reefs).

**Andaman and Nicobar Islands** — an elongated chain of islands in the **Bay of Bengal**, extending from north to south. They are bigger in size, more numerous and scattered. The entire group is divided into two broad categories: the **Andaman in the north** and the **Nicobar in the south**. It is believed these islands are an **elevated portion of submarine mountains**. They are of great strategic importance for the country. There is great diversity of flora and fauna. These islands lie close to the Equator and experience an **equatorial climate** with thick forest cover. India's only active volcano is on **Barren Island** in the Andaman group.

**Putting it all together.** The mountains are the major sources of water and forest wealth. The northern plains are the granaries of the country — they provided the base for early civilisations. The plateau is a storehouse of minerals, which has played a crucial role in the industrialisation of the country. The coastal region and island groups provide sites for fishing and port activities. Thus, the diverse physical features of the land have immense future possibilities of development — each region **complements** the others.

sections.h: Map work and writing great answers
sections.md:
The exercise section of this chapter asks you to **locate features on an outline map of India** and to **write comparisons**. Here is how to master both.

**Map work checklist.** Practise marking these on a blank map until you can do it from memory:
- **Mountain ranges:** Karakoram, Zaskar, Pir Panjal, Patkai Bum, Naga hills, Mizo hills, Aravali, Vindhya, Satpura, Western Ghats, Eastern Ghats.
- **Peaks:** K2 (in the Karakoram, in the Pakistan-administered region), Kanchenjunga (Sikkim), Nanda Devi (Uttarakhand), Anai Mudi (Kerala), Mahendragiri (Odisha), Doda Betta (Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu).
- **Plateaus:** Chotanagpur (Jharkhand), Malwa (Madhya Pradesh), Meghalaya.
- **Desert:** the Thar, west of the Aravalis.
- **Islands:** Lakshadweep (Arabian Sea), Andaman and Nicobar (Bay of Bengal).

A trick that helps: trace India's outline with your finger and *say* the features aloud from northwest to northeast, then down the west coast and up the east coast. Your hand learns the order.

**How to answer a 'distinguish' question.** Examiners love pairs: bhangar vs khadar, Western vs Eastern Ghats, Western vs Eastern coastal plains, Himadri vs Shiwaliks. Always write in a **two-column table** with the *same basis of comparison* in each row — location, height, rocks, continuity, rainfall, examples. Three or four solid rows beat ten vague ones.

**How to answer 'describe the formation of…'.** Use a chain: *cause → process → result*. For the Himalayas: Gondwana breaks up (cause) → Indo-Australian plate drifts north and collides with Eurasia; Tethys sediments fold (process) → young, lofty fold mountains with marine fossils (result). For the Northern Plains: Himalayas rise and the peninsula's northern edge sinks (cause) → rivers fill the basin with alluvium over millions of years (process) → flat, fertile, densely populated plain (result).

**Activity idea from the chapter's spirit.** Make a 'relief sandwich': a strip of cardboard showing a cross-section from the Thar desert to the Bay of Bengal, or from Ladakh to Kanyakumari, with heights labelled. You will see at once why rivers of the Deccan flow east and why the Western Ghats catch the monsoon.

> *Did you know?* The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the world's biodiversity hotspots — older than the Himalayas, and home to the lion-tailed macaque and many frogs found nowhere else.

options: The east coast has no sea

steps: So about 6.6 lakh sq km — close to the area of the Northern Plains (7 lakh sq km)

workedExamples.q: A plate moves 5 cm a year. How far does it move in 10 million years?
workedExamples.answer: 500 km — enough to close a sea like the Tethys over geological time

summary: India has mountains, plains, plateaus, desert, coasts and islands of very different ages.
Plate tectonics: seven major plates move by convergent, divergent and transform motion.
The Indo-Australian plate broke from Gondwana, drifted north and collided with the Eurasian plate.
Folding of Tethys sediments formed the Himalayas; the basin in front filled with alluvium to form the Northern Plains.
The Himalayas (2,400 km arc) have three ranges: Himadri (~6,000 m, snowbound), Himachal (Pir Panjal, Dhaula Dhar, Mahabharat; hill stations), Shiwaliks (unconsolidated sediments; Duns).
Regional divisions: Punjab, Kumaon, Nepal and Assam Himalayas; Purvachal in the northeast.
The Northern Plains (7 lakh sq km) are formed by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; divided into Punjab, Ganga and Brahmaputra plains.
By relief: bhabar (pebbles, streams vanish), terai (marshy), bhangar (old alluvium, kankar), khadar (new alluvium).
The Peninsular Plateau is an old tableland split by the Narmada into the Central Highlands and the Deccan Plateau.
Western Ghats are continuous and higher (Anai Mudi 2,695 m); Eastern Ghats are discontinuous and lower (Mahendragiri 1,501 m).
The Deccan Trap is of volcanic origin and gives black soil; the Aravalis are old, eroded hills.
The Indian Desert receives under 150 mm rain; barchans dominate; Luni is its only large river.
Western coastal plain is narrow (Konkan, Kannad, Malabar); eastern is wide (Northern Circar, Coromandel) with deltas and Chilika lake.
Lakshadweep = coral islands (Kavaratti HQ); Andaman & Nicobar = submarine mountain peaks with Barren Island volcano.
The divisions complement each other: water, food, minerals and trade.
